text:
Pillar 1: The Intended Message of the Scriptures (Contextual & Exegetical Analysis)
1 Samuel 11–13 marks the critical transition from the theocratic judgeship under Samuel to the monarchy of Saul, detailing his inaugural military triumph, the formal renewal of the kingdom, and his precipitous spiritual collapse at Gilgal.
Chapter 11: The Mobilization of the Spirit and Deliverance at Jabesh-gilead
Nahash* the Ammonite, besieges Jabesh-gilead, proposing a covenant conditioned upon gouging out the right eye of every inhabitant to bring reproach upon Israel. When messengers arrive at Gibeah, Saul—plowing behind his oxen—is seized by the Holy Spirit: "And the Spirit of God came upon Saul when he heard those tidings, and his anger was kindled greatly" (1 Sam. 11:6). Saul hews his oxen into pieces and sends them throughout Israel with a summons of judgment: "Whosoever cometh not forth after Saul and after Samuel, so shall it be done unto his oxen" (11:7). The fear of the Lord falls on the people, assembling 330,000 men. Saul launches a dawn watch assault, routing the Ammonites. When the people demand the execution of those who had previously rejected Saul's kingship (cf. 1 Sam. 10:27), Saul demonstrates magnanimity: "There shall not a man be put to death this day: for to day the Lord hath wrought salvation in Israel" (11:13). The chapter concludes at Gilgal, where the kingdom is renewed through peace offerings before the Lord.
Chapter 12: Samuel’s Covenant Defense and the Witness of the Storm
Samuel delivers his farewell address, establishing his personal integrity: he took no man’s ox, ass, or bribe, challenging the nation to convict him of extortion, to which they attest his blamelessness (12:3–5). Samuel then rehearses Yahweh’s historical covenant faithfulness from Moses and Aaron through the period of the judges (Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, Samuel). He directly confronts their core sin: demanding an earthly monarch because of fear of Nahash, while Yahweh was already their sovereign King (12:12). To confirm their transgression, Samuel calls upon the Lord during the dry wheat harvest (May–June), and Yahweh sends unseasonable thunder and rain (12:17–18). The terrified people plead for intercession. Samuel comforts them with covenant reassurance: "For the Lord will not forsake his people for his great name's sake: because it hath pleased the Lord to make you his people" (12:22). He charges them to serve God in truth with all their heart, pledging his own continued ministry: "God forbid that I should sin against the Lord in ceasing to pray for you" (12:23), warning that persistence in wickedness will consume both them and their king.
Chapter 13: The Unlawful Sacrifice and Saul’s Deposition at Gilgal
Jonathan strikes the Philistine garrison at Geba, inciting a massive Philistine mobilization: 30,000 chariots, 6,000 horsemen, and troops like sand on the seashore encamping at Michmash (13:5). Terrified, the men of Israel hide in caves, rocks, and pits, while some flee across the Jordan. Saul waits seven days at Gilgal according to the appointment set by Samuel (cf. 1 Sam. 10:8). Seeing his army scattering and Samuel delayed, Saul capitulates to fear and usurps the priestly office: "Bring hither a burnt offering to me, and peace offerings. And he offered the burnt offering" (13:9). As soon as he finishes, Samuel arrives. Saul justifies his disobedience with pragmatic excuses: the people were scattering, Samuel was late, the Philistines were gathering, and he "forced" himself to seek Yahweh's favor (13:11–12). Samuel delivers God’s irrevocable verdict: "Thou hast done foolishly: thou hast not kept the commandment of the Lord thy God... but now thy kingdom shall not continue: the Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart" (13:13–14). The chapter concludes with the strategic destitution of Israel: the Philistines maintain a blacksmith monopoly, stripping Israel of swords and spears, leaving only Saul and Jonathan armed among the remaining six hundred men (13:19–22).
Pillar 2: Deeper Theological Meanings
The Spirit’s Anointing vs. Unregenerate Character
In 1 Samuel 11:6, the Spirit of God rushes upon Saul, enabling supernatural courage and military unity. However, the subsequent events of Chapter 13 expose that charismatic empowerment for external service is distinct from inward, sanctifying regeneration. Saul could operate as a conduit of divine power in battle, yet remain an insecure, self-directed man who refuses submission to divine command when external props collapse. Spiritual gifting does not equal spiritual maturity or obedient faith.
The Presumption of Sacramental Manipulation
Saul’s action at Gilgal (13:9–12) exposes the pagan view of ritual: treating the sacrifice as an autonomous, mechanical talisman to secure divine favor before battle, rather than an act of covenantal obedience. Saul operates under the delusion that the outward performance of a burnt offering could compel God's intervention, even while defying the prophetic command to wait. Samuel’s confrontation unmasks the reality that formal ritual without obedience is rebellion. God seeks absolute surrender to His revealed will, not pragmatic religious maneuvers designed to ease psychological panic.
Covenant Continuity and the Lord’s Great Name
Samuel’s address in Chapter 12 anchors Israel's preservation entirely to divine monergism, the theological doctrine that God alone, through the Holy Spirit, effects the regeneration and salvation of an individual without any cooperative assistance, contribution, or decisive initiative from the human will. The people’s demand for a king was an act of covenantal apostasy (12:12, 17), yet God does not abandon them: "For the Lord will not forsake his people for his great name's sake: because it hath pleased the Lord to make you his people" (12:22). Salvation and perseverance do not rest on human merit, but upon God’s unalterable commitment to His own glory and covenant oath.
The Principle of Divine Succession: The Man After God’s Own Heart
The judgment pronounced in 13:14 ("the Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart") introduces the foundational criteria for true kingdom leadership. Saul measured reality by visible optics: counting troops, assessing enemy chariots, and managing panic. A man after God's own heart—typified ultimately in David and fulfilled in Jesus Christ—submits unconditionally to the Word of God, waits upon the divine timetable, and refuses to compromise divine jurisdiction for immediate pragmatic gain.
Pillar 3: The Daily Walk of the Truth Seeker
Rejecting Pragmatic Compromise Under Pressure
Saul's excuse—"I forced myself therefore, and offered a burnt offering" (1 Sam. 13:12)—is the classic confession of human pragmatism overriding revealed truth. A truth seeker does not allow escalating crises, evaporating support, or running out of time to justify stepping outside God's prescribed boundaries. When duty demands waiting, moving ahead without divine warrant is disobedience, regardless of how pressing the crisis appears.
Distinguishing Godly Boldness from Carnal Self-Preservation
In 1 Samuel 11, Saul used his authority to defend the oppressed inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead and gave glory to Yahweh. In Chapter 13, Saul focused entirely on retaining his fleeing soldiers and securing personal survival. The truth seeker must continually examine the motives behind their actions: are you acting out of Spirit-wrought zeal for God's righteousness, or out of anxious manipulation to preserve your own standing, reputation, or control?
Fulfilling the Intercessory Obligation
Samuel declared: "God forbid that I should sin against the Lord in ceasing to pray for you: but I will teach you the good and the right way" (1 Sam. 12:23). Scripture frames the abandonment of intercession and sound instruction for God’s people not merely as a lack of discipline, but as a sin against the Lord. Walking faithfully requires persistent intercession for the Body of Christ and an unyielding commitment to proclaim unvarnished truth, even when those being addressed have acted foolishly.
Trusting the Sovereign Sovereign Over Visible Metrics
Israel faced 30,000 chariots and an innumerable army with only two swords between Saul and Jonathan (13:5, 22). Their terror arose because they evaluated their security by material armaments and troop counts. The truth seeker walks by faith in the unseen Sovereign, knowing that the outcome of spiritual warfare is never determined by earthly resources, superior numbers, or technological monopolies, but by the arm of the Lord.
Synthesized Guide for the Truth Seeker
The transition of the kingdom in 1 Samuel 11–13 establishes an enduring law of God’s government: External gifting and initial victories are worthless if the heart remains governed by fear and self-will rather than total obedience to the written Word.
Israel’s history proves that God can take a reluctant man plowing behind oxen, clothe him with His Spirit, and shatter the enemy; yet that same man, left to his own carnal heart, will reduce worship to an instrumental tactic when his earthly securities vanish. The fall of Saul at Gilgal warns every seeker that God does not accept religious activity as a substitute for waiting upon His commands.
When circumstances press, when allies scatter, and when human reason screams that immediate action is necessary to avert catastrophe, the command of God remains absolute: wait. The Sovereign Lord does not preserve His people because of their military readiness, their institutional strength, or their tactical brilliance; He preserves them for His own great Name’s sake. The duty of the truth seeker is to stand immovable in their appointed jurisdiction, refuse the temptation of unauthorized compromise, and remember that obedience to the Word of God is the only true measure of faithfulness.
*Footnote on Nahash: Linguistic Root and Spiritual Typology
The linguistic root of Nahash (נָחָשׁ, nachash—literally "serpent") connects directly to the broader biblical motif of adversarial malice, subtle distortion of God's Word, and tyrannical subjugation.
1. The Typology of Nahash the Ammonite In 1 Samuel 11, Nahash personifies serpentine cruelty:
The Demanded Mutilation: He refuses terms of peace unless he can thrust out the right eye of every man of Jabesh-gilead (1 Sam. 11:2). The intent was twofold: to leave them militarily incapacitated behind their shields (which covered the left eye) and to "lay it for a reproach upon all Israel."
The Spiritual Parallel: Adversarial worldly authority seeks to blind the spiritual perception of God's people, strip away their defensive posture, and render them an object of public humiliation. It does not offer genuine covenant peace, but permanent mutilation and bondage.
2. Spiritual Masquerade Over Carnal Distraction Scripture defines adversarial deception not as physical alteration, but as a calculated moral masquerade:
"And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light. Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers also be transformed as the ministers of righteousness; whose end shall be according to their works." (2 Corinthians 11:14–15)
The danger in fallen leadership is subtle and ideological:
Decrees that subvert divine law are cloaked in the language of compassion, equity, and public order.
The transcendent moral law of the Creator is systematically undermined or redefined.
Trust is redirected away from the Sovereign God toward human administrative systems, technical infrastructure, and financial leverage.

3. The Historical Alignment of Earthly Rulers Psalm 2 exposes the perpetual rebellion of worldly authorities:
"The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the Lord, and against his anointed, saying, Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us." (Psalm 2:2–3)
Whether in the 11th century BC under Nahash or across modern governing structures, fallen authority consistently seeks to sever human society from divine law. The objective remains identical: replacing the Kingship of God with autonomous human control, convincing men that survival demands capitulation to predatory decrees rather than trust in the Sovereign Lord.

text:
in 2015, mark zuckerberg revealed a story he had kept private for years: when facebook was struggling and people were telling him to sell the company for as much as $1 billion, steve jobs gave him a very different piece of advice.

go to a temple in india.

zuckerberg told the story while sitting on stage with indian prime minister narendra modi, saying, “this is a story that i haven’t told publicly and very few people know.”

facebook was still young, and there was serious interest from people who wanted to buy the company. instead of giving zuckerberg another business strategy, jobs told him to visit the same temple in india that he had gone to years earlier while trying to figure out what he wanted apple to become.

zuckerberg eventually went and spent almost a month traveling through india.

the trip changed the way he looked at facebook.

he saw people connecting with each other in ways that had little to do with technology itself, and he said the experience reminded him why he had started building facebook in the first place.

zuckerberg kept that feeling with him for the next decade as the company grew far beyond what it had been when the offers started coming in.

he didn't sell.

today, meta is worth more than a trillion dollars.

the strange part is that jobs didn't tell him what price to accept or what feature to build next. he sent him somewhere he thought might help him remember why he was building the company in the first place.

would you have taken the $1 billion, or gone to india?

text:
Spectrum AI Accelerator Brings AI Computing Closer to Where Data Is Created, Enabling Faster, More Responsive Applications

Spectrum Business Brings AI Computing to the Edge of the Network as shown at SCTE TechExpo 26

At SCTE TechExpo 26, Spectrum Business made several announcements demonstrating how its Spectrum AI Accelerator Platform combines Spectrum Edge Computing Infrastructure (ECI) and connectivity to bring AI computing closer to where data is created.

This approach enables low-latency, secure, and scalable AI applications across enterprise, cloud, and edge environments. Spectrum is working with leading AI innovators, including Cast AI, HP, Hydra Host, World Wide Technology (WWT), and NVIDIA, to expand the possibilities for AI at the network edge.

Here is a closer look at these collaborations:
Cast AI: Integrates NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs hosted on Spectrum’s Edge Computing      Infrastructure, helping provide access to AI computing resources across hyperscale cloud environments through Spectrum’s network.

HP: HP Z Boost delivers on-demand shared GPU resources for AI, rendering, and visualization workloads. HP ZGX Nano and ZGX Fury provide enterprise ready      AI workstations designed to bring AI capabilities closer to where data is generated and used.

Hydra Host: Partners with Spectrum to commercialize its AI Factory platform on ECI, expanding access to AI infrastructure and GPU resources for organizations seeking advanced AI capabilities.

World Wide Technology (WWT) and NVIDIA: Collaborate with Spectrum to advance distributed edge AI infrastructure for physical AI applications, including robotics and industrial automation. These applications can benefit from secure, low-latency computing closer to the devices and machines they control.

Bringing AI Computing Closer to the Action

Spectrum has begun distributing computing power across its network, using more than 1,000 smaller edge facilities already embedded in its infrastructure.

The company says this approach can place computing capacity within milliseconds of hundreds of millions of connected devices in homes and businesses across the United States.

This brings computing closer to where data is generated. Spectrum aims to make AI applications faster, more responsive, and better suited to real-time tasks.

This is an important development as AI evolves beyond answering questions and generating content.

Increasingly, AI is being used to control or interact with physical machines, robots, sensors, real-time video systems, and other connected devices. These applications require speed, reliability, and security.

A robot must respond immediately to changing conditions on a factory floor. If its instructions must travel to a distant data center and back, the delay could affect how quickly and accurately it responds. In applications such as robotics and industrial automation, even small delays can matter.

That is where edge computing becomes increasingly important. By moving computing resources closer to the devices they serve, Spectrum’s ECI, enhanced by NVIDIA accelerated computing platforms, is designed to support applications that require rapid responses and reliable connectivity.

Working with Cast AI, HP, Hydra Host, WWT, and NVIDIA, Spectrum demonstrates how this distributed infrastructure can support emerging AI workloads. The demonstrations include robotics applications that illustrate the potential of combining AI computing with low-latency network connectivity.

Why AI at the Edge Matters

AI is moving from the digital world into the physical world. As that transition continues, computing power must be available closer to the places where decisions are made and actions take place.

Cloud computing will remain important, but not every AI application can depend on sending information to a distant data center. Some applications need to process information and respond immediately.

Spectrum Business is positioning its network and edge infrastructure to address this growing need. The combination of distributed computing, advanced GPUs, and connectivity could help businesses develop and deploy new AI applications across industries.

The broader lesson is that the future of artificial intelligence will depend on more than increasingly capable AI models. It will also depend on the infrastructure that delivers computing power where it is needed, when it is needed.

Spectrum’s AI Accelerator initiative offers a look at how network providers can play a larger role in that future, helping bring AI out of centralized data centers and closer to the people, businesses, devices, and machines that will use it.

text:
Space Tortuga and the mystery of At Attin

Skeleton Crew's second episode is a clear step up for me. After a mostly dull first episode, the pirate port, familiar ships and all those aliens finally gave me more of that Star Wars feeling. 

Port Borgo is basically Tortuga in space, and it has a great atmosphere. There are familiar alien species everywhere, even Twi'leks heading into what looks like a brothel. The kids don't quite grasp what sort of place it is, but they know it's not for them xD. The better pace also helped me get into the adventure.

Fern still gets on my nerves. I can't quite tell whether it's the performance or the character herself, but I find her exhausting. Her bluff to get SM-33 to accept her as captain fits the way she's been leading the group, though.

SM-33, though, actually wowed me a little. I'm a droid fan, and he reminds me a little of an Imperial KX droid, without the black finish and with a lot more damage. I also like KB, the tech nerd whose fascination with everything around her is obvious. She understands a lot of what she sees and seems like the most useful member of the group to me.

The Old Republic credits really got me thinking about At Attin. There's the Barrier, that system of preparing children for assigned roles, and now money that outsiders treat as treasure. Has this society been cut off from the galaxy, carrying on while wars and political upheavals passed it by? It reminds me of Fallout's Vaults: people stepping outside an isolated community and discovering a world they barely know. For these kids, that could mean a completely new life.

And their home turns out to be basically Atlantis to everyone else, a lost planet of treasure xD. People have heard the legend; they just don't believe the kids actually come from there.

I'm also guessing the prisoner at the end is Captain Silvo. Brutus is back from the opening episode, so finding his former captain locked up would make sense to me. Wim immediately sees a Jedi when the stranger uses the Force. That doesn't make the man trustworthy. If my guess is right, I suspect he wants to use the kids to find At Attin, get rich and regain his position. His offer of help could be very convenient for him.

I still feel that this is a live-action series aimed at kids. Maybe I'd be more swept up in it as the target audience, although my dad took me to see Revenge of the Sith when I was a little over ten, and I already preferred that more serious side of Star Wars. This kind of kids' adventure doesn't captivate me quite as much. Still, the atmosphere, faster pace and mystery made this a much more enjoyable episode. 7/10.

text:
I draw three lessons from the report: reach, vendor reviews and detection.

The first lesson is reach. A bid is an offer to show an ad. Discover-Tech left its bidding records open online, and about 76.7% of its bids were for ads inside mobile apps.

From March to June 2026, the lab counted 75,373 apps and 120,768 websites. Each showed ads carrying the attacker's script tag.

A browser ad blocker doesn't touch an ad inside an app. So the control has to sit on the network, where every app's traffic passes.

Frank Dickson of Dickson Research gave CSO Online a list for defenders. It includes blocking ad and tracking domains at the DNS or secure web gateway layer.

He says blocking at that layer reaches in-app ads on managed phones. He also says to switch off advertising IDs on company phones through your MDM.

The advertising ID is one of the two items an ad sent to Discover-Tech: the other is the IP address.

If you already run DNS filtering and MDM, both are settings you can change this week. If you don't, those two tools are your budget line.

text:
Charlie Munger says he turned $70 million into "a billion dollars worth of property in about two seconds."

The property is a ranch of about 1,800 acres near Santa Barbara, per the Independent, with two miles of ocean frontage, avocado trees and a private lake.

Munger says its owner, the widow of the last grandchild of a major California oilman, needed to sell but could not. The county had denied the family's request to subdivide it, according to Noozhawk. The Independent reported the asking price fell from $108 million to $90 million.

So Munger offered UC Santa Barbara $70 million. He had already given the school $65 million in 2014, its largest gift at the time, per Noozhawk. He knew, he says, that the university "is not subject to the damn Santa Barbara zoning rules." You can hear him say it.

"I didn't get the billion, the university did, but I like helping the university."

Both the Independent and Noozhawk reported that Munger bought the ranch to donate it to the school.

The billion is Munger's own estimate. The university's chancellor said the school plans to keep it "as a working ranch."

By his account, the same land was worth far more in a university's hands than in a family's.

Clever workaround, or a billion-dollar guess?

text:
𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐒𝐮𝐦𝐨 𝐀𝐮𝐭𝐮𝐦𝐧 𝐓𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐑𝐞𝐜𝐚𝐩 (𝐎𝐜𝐭.𝟏𝟐 𝐭𝐨 𝟏𝟕)
A collection of news from each location of the autumn tour in translation.

𝐎𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟏𝟐 - 𝐊𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐳𝐚𝐰𝐚 (𝐈𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐤𝐚𝐰𝐚)
The Autumn Grand Sumo Tour was held on the 12th at the Ishikawa Prefectural General Sports Center in Kanazawa City.

Juryo Kagayaki, a native of Nanao City, Ishikawa Prefecture, joined the tour and interacted with local fans through handshakes and "chibikko sumo" (children's sumo). Having spent his three middle school years in Kanazawa City, he had many opportunities to speak with visitors. Expressing his gratitude, he said, "Everyone came early in the morning and offered kind words like, 'You did well this tournament.' I am truly grateful."

During the last tournament, Kagayaki achieved his first undefeated 10-game winning streak from day one, but went 1–4 in the final stretch. He lost in a three-way playoff, missing out on his first Juryo championship title. Looking back, he reflected, "It was a tournament where I felt in great condition. That's precisely why I feel I could have won it all, leaving me with immense regret. I will use this disappointment as motivation to win the title next tournament and work hard to return to Makuuchi and succeed."

Over the past few days, Kagayaki stayed in Thailand to promote the upcoming Bangkok performance scheduled for next June. He attended press conferences and other events locally, returning to Japan late on the 10th to join the Autumn Tour. Since overseas performances are primarily intended for Makuuchi-ranked wrestlers, he enthusiastically stated, "(Bangkok) was a great place, so I want to participate in the event as a Makuuchi wrestler."

𝐎𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟏𝟑 - 𝐊𝐚𝐡𝐨𝐤𝐮 (𝐈𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐤𝐚𝐰𝐚)
The Autumn Tour was held on the 13th at the BLUECATS ARENA in Kahoku City, Ishikawa Prefecture.

Makuuchi Toshinofuji joined a butsukari-geiko session against Yokozuna Onosato for the first time. For about four minutes, Toshinofuji charged with all his might, but was repeatedly thrown down and covered in sand. Feeling inspired, he remarked, "He's huge and heavy. Our heights are about the same [Onosato is 190 cm, while Toshinofuji is around 195 cm], but he has incredible weight. It made me realize I need to gain more weight and work on my fundamentals."

The 26-year-old, who made his Makuuchi debut last tournament, is participating in his first tour as a sekitori. He has been sweating it out vigorously in the daily moshiai among sekitori wrestlers, saying with a fulfilled expression, "It’s fun to spar with members I usually don't face. I want to wrestle as many opponents as possible whom I might face next tournament." Having graduated from Doshisha University, he looked forward to the tour stopping in Kyoto on the 16th, where he spent his university days: "I love Kyoto, so I'm happy to go back."

-

Makuuchi Asasuiryu rejoined the tour. He had been absent since day one after submitting a medical certificate citing a "left orbital medial wall fracture."

According to Asasuiryu, he injured his left eye during a bout on Day 5 of the Autumn Basho, his Makuuchi debut tournament. For the first few days, his vision was blurred to the point where he "couldn't see ahead at all," but he completed all 15 days, securing a winning record. An examination after the tournament revealed the fracture.

Fortunately, doctors determined that surgery was unnecessary, and he monitored his progress while resting. Although not fully healed, his recovery is progressing well, with his doctor noting that "compared to individual variations, recovery is on the faster side." Aiming for the Kyushu Basho, he rejoined the tour mid-way, stating, "I will hold off on actual sumo bouts for now and move my body within reasonable limits."

𝐎𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟏𝟒 - 𝐓𝐚𝐤𝐚𝐲𝐚𝐦𝐚 (𝐆𝐢𝐟𝐮)
The Autumn Grand Sumo Tour was held in Takayama City, Gifu Prefecture.

This marks the first time in nine years that a sumo tour has been held in Takayama City. On the 14th, a large crowd gathered as soon as the doors opened at 9:00 AM.
At the venue, a handshake session was held featuring Fujiryoga from Aichi Prefecture and other wrestlers.

On the dohyo, heavy butsukari-geiko took place. The collision practice between Yokozuna Onosato and Yokozuna Hoshoryu drew particularly enthusiastic cheers from the audience.
Toward the end of the morning session, local children squared off against the wrestlers, filling the arena with a warm and friendly atmosphere.
Bouts for the Takayama tour took place in the afternoon.

𝐎𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟏𝟓 - 𝐍𝐚𝐠𝐚𝐡𝐚𝐦𝐚 (𝐒𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐚)
The Nagahama tour of the Autumn Grand Sumo Tour was held on the 15th at the Prefectural Kyosai Dome Nagahama in Tamura-cho, Nagahama City. Approximately 5,000 spectators attended to catch a glimpse of the tour's return to Nagahama after a 27-year hiatus.

Around 110 rikishi participated, including Yokozuna Onosato and Yokozuna Hoshoryu. The event featured shokkiri, and during Hoshoryu’s dohyo-iri, the crowd rhythmically shouted "Yoisho!" in time with his stomping. When the tournament matches began and intense collisions unfolded right before their eyes, cheers and applause erupted throughout the venue.

Visitors enjoyed interacting with the wrestlers through events like handshake sessions and children's sumo. Twenty elementary school students from the city participated in the children's sumo, taking on Yokozuna Onosato on the ring.

𝐎𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟏𝟔 - 𝐊𝐲𝐨𝐭𝐨 (𝐊𝐲𝐨𝐭𝐨)
On the 16th, the Autumn Tour visited Kyoto City. Yokozuna Hoshoryu, who underwent right knee surgery in late July, completed 19 bouts in total with Yokozuna Onosato and others, recording 8 wins and 11 losses. Among these, 14 bouts were against Onosato, resulting in 6 wins and 8 losses. The two had also fought 10 bouts on the 14th in Takayama, Gifu, where Hoshoryu won 7–3. After missing the Autumn Basho entirely, Hoshoryu has smoothly resumed ring practice toward his return at the Kyushu Basho.

"Wins and losses don't matter right now. I just recovered from an injury. Up until now, I only did basic exercises, so I think this is a good start."

Hoshoryu expressed confidence after handling more bouts than expected. In moshiai with Ozeki Kirishima and Ozeki Kotozakura, he showed moments of overwhelming speed. However, when moving into a 12-bout sanban-geiko with Onosato, he repeatedly succumbed to raw power, particularly in the latter half. Nearly three months after his surgery, his lack of conditioning was hard to hide.

Chairman Hakkaku, who inspected the training that day, offered strict criticism: "If you don't intend to compete in the Kyushu Basho, you shouldn't be training like this. Without putting in a higher volume of bouts, you won't regain heavy, effective movement." During practice, the Chairman called Hoshoryu over to instruct him to increase his bout count.

Commenting on practice among Yokozuna and Ozeki where Hoshoryu stepped off the ring after losing a bout, Chairman Hakkaku demanded higher discipline: "Once a Yokozuna enters the ring, he shouldn't step down. He should keep going. Younger wrestlers are watching. He needs to be a role model."

"I want to increase my bout count [as Chairman Hakkaku pointed out]. I was tired in the second half. My body has recovered, so now I want to rebuild my stamina."

With the 19-day Autumn Tour past its halfway point on Day 11 and only 10 days remaining until the Kyushu Basho banzuke announcement, Hoshoryu looked ahead positively: "I will train hard with every intention of competing."

-

Newly promoted Juryo wrestler Ryuho, a native of Uji City, made a special appearance. A large banner celebrating his promotion to new Juryo status was prominently displayed in the arena. Dressed in a black mawashi, he was welcomed with loud cheers as he stepped onto the dohyo. Having secured his promotion after the Autumn Basho, he remarked, "My father and junior members from my Kyoto sumo club came to watch. It was a nice milestone." He also returned to his family home to recharge.

At the end of practice, he engaged in butsukari-geiko against Ozeki Kotozakura, who acted as his training partner. Expressing his gratitude, Ryuho thanked Kotozakura after the session. Looking ahead to the Kyushu Basho, he said, "I want to do my best to achieve a kachi-koshi." His shikona incorporates the character "鳳" from Byodoin Phoenix Hall (平等院鳳凰堂), located about a 10-minute drive from his family home in Uji City. Ryuho aims to spread his wings wide in the final tournament of the year.

𝐎𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟏𝟕 - 𝐎𝐬𝐚𝐤𝐚 (𝐎𝐬𝐚𝐤𝐚)
The Grand Sumo Maishima regional tour was held in Osaka City on the 17th, marking the return of komusubi Hakunofuji.

Having started on the 6th, the autumn tour saw him pull out on the 9th due to pain flaring up in his old left Achilles tendon injury. Because the pain typically leaves him unable to walk for two to three days, he had been fully dedicated to treatment.

On this day of his return, he entered into a bout with sekiwake Fujinokawa. Regarding participation in practice starting from tomorrow's Himeji tour on the 18th, while monitoring his physical condition, he noted, "I want to adjust my body starting around tomorrow and think about it."

This is the 12th day of the 19-day autumn tour. There are now less than 10 days left until the banzuke announcement on the 26th for the Kyushu Tournament. In September's Autumn Tournament, where he served as a new san'yaku, he finished with only 5 wins despite defeating two Ozeki, Aonishiki and Kotozakura. He relinquished his san'yaku rank and hopes to use the upcoming Kyushu Tournament—where he will make a fresh start from the maegashira ranks—as a springboard for a counter-offensive.

-

Juryo-ranked Kazuma, a local native, took on 8 bouts in sparring practice before having former ozekiTakayasu give him a long round of butsukari-geiko.

A native of Minato Ward, Osaka City, the venue for the day—Ookini Arena Maishima—is a mere 15-minute drive from his parents' home. During the previous day's Kyoto tour, where he pushed his heavy body against Yokozuna Onosato while completely out of breath, he expressed gratitude for the local fans' support, saying, "Since it was my hometown, there were cheers. I somehow managed to push through to the end."

Visiting the venue was his younger brother, Kazusa Kawabuchi, the Japanese middleweight boxing champion. Kawabuchi captured the Japanese national title in August during his 5th professional fight. Because that bout—a 7th-round TKO victory—happened while the summer tour was underway, he was unable to watch it live at Korakuen Hall in Tokyo, but it served as a great inspiration.

Kazuma's theme for the regional tour is: "You can gain experiences here that you normally can't. I have to absorb these lessons so that everyone is willing to grant me practice." Tour practices are a precious opportunity to lock arms with sekitori from other stables. He made his debut starting from the makushita lowest-rank tsukedashi at the 2024 Nagoya Tournament, where he tore his right anterior cruciate ligament and subsequently sat out five consecutive tournaments. Although he dropped all the way down to jonokuchi, he achieved promotion to the makuuchi division at this year's Nagoya Tournament. He hopes to use this as a turning point to bounce back from consecutive losing records over the past two tournaments.

𝐔𝐩𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐥𝐞:

October 18 - Himeji (Hyogo)

text:
India’s Submarine Future Is Already Taking Shape in Mumbai: Why Naval Group’s Proven Scorpène Offers a Faster, Lower-Risk Path to Expanding India’s Underwater Warfare Capability

India’s submarine fleet is entering a critical phase. The Navy needs more conventional attack submarines, but the real choice is between building on an ecosystem India has already developed and taking on another long development cycle.

Naval Group’s Scorpène offers a powerful advantage: India already knows how to build it.

Under Project-75, Naval Group designed the submarine and transferred its technology to Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, which built six Kalvari-class boats now operational with the Indian Navy. Indian crews know the platform, and an industrial base exists around its construction and maintenance.

Submarine programmes require specialised tooling, trained engineers, certified suppliers and testing infrastructure. A design new to India would need much of this rebuilt, with fresh investment and another learning curve.

Localisation is easy to promise and hard to deliver. Here, it has already been delivered: Naval Group developed Indian suppliers and qualified Indian partners to manufacture components across the Navy’s “float, move and fight” categories.

The bigger opportunity is the integration of Indian technology. Naval Group is working with DRDO’s Naval Materials Research Laboratory to integrate India’s indigenous fuel-cell Air Independent Propulsion system into the Kalvari class, turning a proven design into a carrier for Indian innovation.

The same logic extends beyond construction. Naval Group supports maintenance, spares, repairs and lifecycle services, training Indian engineers and bringing Indian firms into the ecosystem. These skills stay in India and grow with the fleet.

The platform also has room to grow. Six weapon tubes carry heavyweight torpedoes and SM39 Exocet anti-ship missiles, and the combat system can accommodate future weapons and sensors, backed by a country that builds its own submarine-launched missiles.

Behind it stands a partner that has stood by India. France chose engagement over sanctions after the 1998 nuclear tests, and Indian Mirage 2000s played a major role at Kargil in 1999.

For a Navy operating across the Indian Ocean, time matters. Every additional year spent stabilising a platform new to India is a year in which the underwater fleet remains under pressure.

The Scorpène may therefore represent more than another submarine order. It represents a chance to turn an established French-Indian programme into a deeper Indian submarine ecosystem.

text:
In Toronto’s finance district, a piece of history disappears
 John Robarts hosted one of Canada’s most important political gatherings right in downtown Toronto. You wouldn’t know it by walking there
 Written by Steve Paikin
 Oct 16, 2026 
 I always think about John Robarts at this time of year.
 Ontario’s 17th premier was one of our finest. He had the job from 1961–1971, which was a great decade to be sitting in the second floor corner office at Queen’s Park.  
 Ontario got so much good stuff during those years: GO Transit, our first nuclear power plants, five new universities, the college system, an expansion of civil rights, OISE, TVO, a massive new school building plan, Medicare (for which the feds actually paid half the tab), and a burgeoning cultural scene.
 But it was another item in which Robarts took particular interest. He was a unilingual anglophone from London but, when he served in the Navy during World War II, his bunkmate was a unilingual francophone from Quebec. Robarts saw his ship as a metaphor for the country — as in, we’re all in the same boat now.
 When bombs began blowing up in mailboxes in Quebec as the spectre of separatism rose, Robarts wanted a much better understanding of the phenomenon. And so, he tasked one of his top advisers, Ian Macdonald (a future president of York University), with mounting the Confederation of Tomorrow conference to study the issue. It would be the most important gathering of political heavy-hitters since Sir John A. Macdonald gathered the Fathers of Confederation in Charlottetown in 1864.  
 Robarts was the only premier with the gravitas to assemble all the country’s premiers in our centennial year in hopes of discussing Quebec’s future. He even offered the country’s justice minister the option of chairing the conference. But Pierre Trudeau, a year away from becoming prime minister, declined, thus Robarts chaired the event himself.
 a library
 The premier also used the occasion to show off one of Ontario’s newest spectacles, the dazzling Toronto-Dominion Centre, comprised of three soaring towers. The building was so new, they hadn’t even laid the carpeting in yet. Nevertheless, Robarts held the conference on the top floor of the TD Bank Tower and put it all on television so Canadians could follow along.
 For many years, the TD Centre celebrated its important historic role by featuring a large plaque on the north wall of the tower’s lobby. The plaque displayed the circular table configuration of the attendees, complete with their names. The circular seating plan aimed to convey that all the premiers were on an equal footing, working together for a common cause.
 But several years ago, I got an email from someone who worked in the financial district that something was amiss — the plaque had seemingly been removed. Apparently, the TD Tower’s landlord, Cadillac Fairview, took down the plaque after the lobby was redecorated with some large Indigenous artwork. The passerby inquired with CF as to the plaque’s whereabouts but never heard back. That was a bit strange since the person who inquired about where the plaque was Richard Robarts: Yes, a cousin of the former premier.
 I decided to stick my nose in as well. I began emailing CF to find out where the plaque had been taken, and whether the company had any plans to put the historic plaque back. At first, I was handed off to a public relations firm, which confirmed the plaque had been removed so the lobby could be redecorated.
 I thanked the rep for that information but assured them I knew that already. Where was the plaque now? And what were the plans to bring it out of hiding and remount it?
 Suddenly, I was ghosted. No further information was forthcoming. Many months later, I’ve tried once again to get some answers out of Cadillac Fairview, and again, received no response at all. Nothing.
 (Update: After publication, I received a follow-up from a spokesperson for Cadillac Fairview. "The TD Bank Tower lobby went through extensive renovations beginning in 2009, as part of a comprehensive, complex-wide upgrade," the note reads. "The plaques would have been removed during that work, and we expect they were stored or donated, but unfortunately we haven’t found records showing where they were moved. It remains an open question for us, and one we haven’t set aside. If we learn more, you’ll be the first to know. We really wish we had better news for you at this time.")
 I started this column by saying I always think of Robarts when mid-October comes. That’s because on October 18, 1982, John Parmenter Robarts died by suicide. He was 65.
 This Sunday repreents the 44th anniversary of Robarts’s death. Wouldn’t it be the decent thing for Cadillac Fairview at least to answer some basic questions about this important memento to a great Canadian’s attempts to keep this country together?
 And isn’t it important to give Canadians a chance to even casually bump into reminders of our history?
 You’d think so, wouldn’t you?

It waits on the permit.

The pipeline got the only help since the post below. On October 14, attorneys general from 12 states asked the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to approve it without widening its environmental review. The commission has still set no decision date. Bloom fell on Thursday anyway.

The strongest fact against the worry: Oracle is rewriting the permit to keep Bloom, not to replace it, and its computing plans did not shrink. Friday's selling was also broad. The extraordinary physiological and experimental investigations of Dr. Robert H. Collyer (1873) and Dr. Robert Hare (1855) preserve two remarkably elaborate nineteenth-century systems of invisible agency, nervous transformation, molecular activity, cerebral exaltation, organic metamorphosis, and the alleged interaction of material and spiritual existence. Their combined intellectual significance emerges from an unusual convergence of medical experimentation, electrochemical philosophy, anomalous mechanics, comparative antiquity, biblical cosmography, and speculative theories of the vital principle. Within these investigations, the living organism appears as an exceptionally responsive configuration of sensory faculties, electrical activity, nervous excitation, retained impressions, muscular volition, and transformative developmental processes, while the external world becomes the proposed theatre of forces whose operations extend beyond immediately visible mechanical phenomena.

Collyer's Exalted States of the Nervous System introduces an extensive physiological investigation of consciousness under extraordinary conditions. Anaesthesia, somnambulism, trance, ecstatic insensibility, cerebral congestion, visual fixation, nervous exhaustion, magnetic induction, respiratory excitation, and the restoration of dormant faculties are interpreted through his proposed nervo-vital principle. 

The resulting model attributes exceptional importance to the concentration, redistribution, and expenditure of nervous activity, particularly where ordinary sensory relationships appear suspended or radically altered. 

His comparisons between inhalational anaesthesia, mesmerism, concentrated attention, and natural sleep establish a striking historical theory of state-dependent cerebral transformation. 

Especially important are the reports of forgotten languages reappearing during illness, unusual intellectual accomplishments during somnambulism, and memories apparently inaccessible to waking consciousness. These accounts invite a specialized investigation of positive anamnetic atavism, latent cerebral impressions, mnemonic reactivation, and the extraordinary phenomenology of recovered capacities.

Among Collyer's most singular contributions is his theory of vital photography, an ambitious attempt to account for the persistence and physical expression of nervous impressions. He considers the brain an extraordinarily sensitive recipient of experiential images and proposes that powerful impressions may influence the wider organization of living tissue. His examples include devotional stigmata, alleged maternal impressions, unusual congenital formations, animal resemblances, and bodily responses attributed to intense mental conviction. These materials belong to a historically important literature of psychosomatic morphology, teratology, cerebral imagery, reproductive speculation, and the relationship between imagination and physical embodiment. Their accompanying anatomical and physiological theories also expose the nineteenth-century search for causal correspondences between transient mental events and comparatively permanent organic structures.

The chapters concerning the creative function extend these questions into embryological development, anatomical differentiation, crystallographic analogies, and the successive transformations of animal life. Collyer's treatment of the developing ovum, the progressive formation of organs, and the metamorphosis of insects supplies a particularly rich foundation for examining what may be termed morphogenetic amplitude: the magnitude of structural transformation occurring between successive conditions of a living organism. His discussion of the punctum saliens, the initiating vital point, further connects embryological speculation with older natural-philosophical inquiries into the organization of matter and the emergence of articulated living forms.

The historical range of Collyer's investigations is equally remarkable. 

Ancient Egyptian initiation, the mysteries of Trophonius, Greek narcotic preparations, mandragorean anaesthesia, the mineral substance called Memphetis, medieval soporific sponges, Chinese medical traditions, and the pneumatic experiments of Humphry Davy enter a comprehensive account of induced insensibility. 

Particularly unusual is the association of ancient ritual preparations with surgical pharmacology, revealing an extensive field for investigating the transmission of obscure medicinal procedures through Greek, Latin, medieval, and early-modern literature. 

Collyer's documentary treatment of the nineteenth-century anaesthesia controversy also preserves valuable testimony concerning Horace Wells, William T. G. Morton, Charles T. Jackson, James Young Simpson, and the disputed chronology of inhalational discoveries.

Robert Hare's Experimental Investigation of the Spirit Manifestations introduces an entirely different experimental architecture. 

His elaborate spiritoscopic instruments, alphabetic indicators, rotating disks, pulley systems, spring balances, water-filled vessels, mechanical isolators, and weighted levers embody an attempt to subject purported invisible agency to physical measurement. 

The distinctive importance of these instruments lies in their translation of alleged extraordinary effects into observable displacements, symbolic communication, and calculable mechanical forces. Particularly striking are Hare's experiments involving the spring balance and unequal lever arms, through which a reported alteration of three pounds in the balance indication becomes an inferred eighteen-pound applied force. 

Such arrangements provide rare historical material for studying experimental control, instrumental sensitivity, static equilibrium, physical measurement, and nineteenth-century efforts to investigate extraordinary manifestations.

Hare's apparatus also introduces a curious form of mechanical information processing. His revolving alphabetic disks convert physical movement into readable characters, creating an unusual analogy with telegraphic communication. 

Visual screens, spherical supports, modified fulcrums, and arrangements intended to interrupt ordinary muscular influence reveal the experimental strategies employed to distinguish intentional mechanical interference from supposedly independent physical action. 

The resulting investigations occupy a distinctive position in the history of experimental spiritualism, anomalous instrumentation, mechanical communication, and the interpretation of phenomena attributed to invisible intelligences.

An especially important and comparatively neglected component of Hare's volume is its advanced discussion of electrical and molecular philosophy. 

His investigations of electro-ethereal polarization, ethereo-ponderable atomic constitution, electrical induction, galvanic reaction, molecular polarity, surface conduction, Leyden-jar discharge, magnetic effects, and electrical deflagration preserve a substantial technical vocabulary rarely associated with spiritualist literature. 

The discussions involving Faraday, Franklin, Ampère, and Mossotti situate Hare within major nineteenth-century controversies concerning the constitution of matter, the transmission of electrical action, and the theoretical relationship between ponderable substances and hypothetical ethereal media.

 These passages furnish an independent historical pathway into pre-electromagnetic-field theories of subtle matter, microscopic polarization, oscillatory electrical behaviour, and the proposed unification of seemingly dissimilar physical effects.

Beyond the laboratory, Hare develops an elaborate cosmography of post-mortem existence. 

Communications attributed to surviving intelligences describe graded celestial spheres, spiritual birth, continuing intellectual advancement, affinities between persons, rarefied forms of nourishment, and supposed agencies capable of operating upon terrestrial matter. These descriptions constitute an unusual system of progressive supernatural anthropology, in which personal identity, cognition, moral development, and the acquisition of knowledge are represented as continuing through successive conditions of existence. 

Their conceptual structure invites detailed comparison with biblical eschatology, ancient philosophical accounts of the soul, Swedenborgian cosmography, Neoplatonic gradations of being, and historical theories of spiritual substance.

Of particular significance is the fundamental disagreement between the two authors. 

Collyer frequently interprets extraordinary manifestations through the nervous capacities of embodied human beings, including cerebral imagery, concentrated volition, and the supposed projection of the vital principle. Hare increasingly attributes certain manifestations to independent surviving intelligences and constructs mechanical experiments intended to support that conclusion. 

Their conflicting interpretations preserve an exceptional historical problem concerning the identification of causal agency, the nature of consciousness, the persistence of personal identity, and the evidential relationship between observation and invisible explanation.

The combined works consequently establish an unusually extensive field for the investigation of;

positive atavistic phenomenology,

high-amplitude metamorphic transitions, 

ethereo-ponderable dynamics, 

electro-biological correspondences,

pneumatic physiology,

somatic image inscription, 

instrumental metaphysics,

latent cognitive organization,

molecular force transmission, 

& the dimensional gradation of conscious existence.

 These analytical categories extend the original historical terminology into a comparative framework for examining extraordinary transformations without confusing nineteenth-century theoretical constructions with subsequently established physical mechanisms.

Taken together, the volumes preserve a remarkable archive of obscure scientific language, experimental ingenuity, unconventional medical observation, anomalous physical testimony, philosophical speculation, and supernatural cosmography.

 Their most consequential scholarly contribution lies in the exceptional richness of the questions they preserve: how sensory awareness changes under unusual physiological conditions; how impressions become inaccessible and subsequently recoverable; how living organisms acquire their differentiated forms; how mechanical instruments register and transmit information; how electrical theories develop from observations of invisible action; and how nineteenth-century investigators attempted to describe the ultimate relations of matter, vitality, consciousness, and spiritual existence.

The resulting historical study offers a foundation for renewed investigation into the extraordinary boundaries of the living organism, the hidden constitution of physical processes, and the complex intellectual heritage through which natural philosophers, physicians, chemists, and investigators of spiritual phenomena sought to comprehend the transformations and continuities of existence.

6. William Robert Grove, On the Correlation of Physical Forces (London, 1846 and subsequent editions), for the nineteenth-century study of transformations among electrical, thermal, chemical, mechanical, and luminous phenomena.

“I’m Gonna Declare An Emergency For You!” ATC Steps In

A Beechcraft B200 Super King Air carrying three people declared an emergency over Texas on October 16, 2026, after part of its right engine cowling came loose during flight.

The aircraft, registered N92WC, was heading towards Conroe when the pilot explained that several cowling latches had released, allowing the rear section to lift into the airflow.

Only the front latches appeared to be holding it in place.

ATC offered a nearby airport, but the pilot chose to continue towards Conroe. The controller then took the unusual step of declaring an emergency on the pilot’s behalf.

“Just hoping it stays with us till we get there,” the pilot told ATC.

With three people aboard and 1,400 pounds of fuel remaining, the aircraft continued towards Conroe, where it landed safely.

text:
David Bowie sold over 140 million records. He invented three different musical personas that each defined an entire era. Rolling Stone called him the most influential artist of the 20th century. He turned down a knighthood from the Queen of England because he didn't think he deserved it.

In the mid-1970s he was also consuming so much cocaine that he later said he remembers almost nothing from that entire period. Not the albums. Not the tours. Not the interviews.

This is one of those interviews.

In the video below, the most creative mind in rock history sits across from a journalist and explains, completely unprompted, how to destroy a city.

Black noise, he says. A specific frequency that shatters everything it hits. Available in the French Patent Office until recently for about three or four dollars. A small device could kill four people in a room. A large one could level an entire city.

The interviewer stares at him.

Bowie moves on to Machiavelli. Then Diane Arbus. Then Frank Zappa naming his son Moon Unit. Then his own son Zowie. Then his wife Angela's thesis on everything. Then a book about the Trans-Siberian Express he may or may not be writing.

At one point he offers the interviewer a part in his next show.

This is the same man who wrote Heroes in a single afternoon. Who created Ziggy Stardust, Aladdin Sane, and the Thin White Duke from scratch. Who produced Iggy Pop's two greatest albums while barely sleeping.

He survived the decade. Cleaned up. Made ten more classic records.

The cocaine almost took all of it. The talent was just bigger than the damage.

Was he a genius who almost destroyed himself, or did the destruction make him the genius he became?

Today I visited Krishna Park on 3rd Parklands Avenue, where a group of enterprising young medics have opened a DKL Designated Service Partner (DSP) under the name Novaris Diagnostic.

They have managed to bring to life their idea of making DKL’s world-class laboratory services, at competitive rates and turnaround times, much more accessible to patients around Parklands, especially those who, after being seen by their doctors, would rather not navigate busy hospitals and medical plazas just to have laboratory tests done at much higher prices.

With the new DSP conveniently located at street level on 3rd Parklands Avenue, a patient can simply walk in, drive into Krishna Park or be dropped off at the ground-floor facility, have their samples collected and be on their way within minutes. Results are then delivered securely through the DKL mobile app or web portal once testing is completed.

Samples collected at Novaris in Parklands are transported to our state-of-the-art Class G, ISO-accredited laboratory at Real Towers in Upper Hill, with only about 30 minutes to one hour added for sample transit depending on the collection schedule.

For many patients and their doctors who wish to use DKL services, this is much more convenient than having patients travel all the way to Upper Hill after seeing their doctor, or having to arrange a home collection when they can have their samples collected almost immediately nearby. The centre will also be offering scheduled home sample collection for DKL clients within Parklands and the surrounding areas.

The onsite Novaris team supporting the laboratory services includes Ms Amran Adan Ibrahim and Mr Duke Otieno Awino, who warmly received us during the visit.

I was accompanied by Mathew Murage, our @DKLDrKalebiLabs LOH Operations Manager, who has been with our Client Relations team and is now overseeing the rollout and growth of this distributive DSP model under our dedicated partnership management subsidiary, Lab Owners Hub (LOH).

The DKL DSP model, which has already grown to more than 20 centres, is essentially a loose franchise model whereby independent medical centres and healthcare entrepreneurs establish convenient local patient-access and sample-collection points within the DKL service network, while the core laboratory testing, quality assurance, IT integrated insurance and billing, and digital reporting remain centralised under DKL. It allows us to extend our reach into more neighbourhoods without having to establish a full laboratory at every location.

This is a great move by these young medics at Novaris and one that will offer real convenience and bring immense value to the Parklands community, helping many patients and their doctors access DKL’s quality and advanced laboratory tests much closer to where they are.

text:
Washington school district that made kids hide Bibles in sealed envelopes must apologize and pay $275K | Fox News

A Washington state school district has agreed to publicly apologize, undergo religious liberty training and pay $275,000 in attorney’s fees after a lawsuit challenged policies that required elementary school students to keep Bibles concealed in sealed envelopes, according to a Christian education organization whose CEO says children felt pressured to hide their faith.

Joel Penton, founder and CEO of LifeWise Academy, told Fox News Digital in an interview Thursday that parents described the emotional toll of the Everett School District’s restrictions, which also included requiring families to submit permission slips every week for their children to attend voluntary, off-campus Bible instruction.

“I also heard from parents that their children felt like they were being told they had to hide their faith when they were told they had to put their Bibles and things in envelopes as though it was something to be ashamed of, and I know that was very hurtful as well,” Penton said.

LifeWise Academy, which provides privately funded Bible instruction to public school students during the school day with parental permission, filed suit after the Everett School District imposed restrictions that the organization argued unfairly targeted its program.

Penton said LifeWise had operated in Everett for several years, serving dozens of students and families, before the school board changed its policies.

“Then the school board changed some of their policies in some ways that were pretty transparently discriminatory and infringed on the religious liberty of our program there,” Penton said. “And some of those policy changes included requiring parents, instead of simply signing a permission slip one time for the entire semester, the entire year, they were requiring them to hand-bring in a permission slip each and every week, which was quite onerous.”

Penton said they were told they were not allowed to participate at some of the community fairs, which he claimed other student organizations were able to participate in.

“And then they also told students that if they received any worksheets or even a Bible at our program, when they came back to the school, that those had to come back in sealed envelopes so that other students wouldn’t be exposed to them,” Penton said.

He argued that the weekly permission requirement threatened the program’s ability to operate.

“We knew at least with the permission slip policy that it was meant to effectively shut down the program, that one of the reasons students, parents enroll their students is because of how practical and convenient it is for them to receive Bible education during school hours as part of their school day,” Penton said. “And now to tell them that they had to personally bring in a permission slip each and every week just made it really impractical for a lot of parents, and I know there are many who are frustrated about that.”

Penton said LifeWise initially attempted to resolve the dispute directly with school officials and later through an attorney before filing suit.

In April, a federal judge granted a preliminary injunction against the district, according to LifeWise.

The settlement announced Wednesday by LifeWise Academy requires changes to district policies, religious liberty training for school board members, a public written apology posted on the district’s website for six months and $275,000 in attorney’s fees, according to the organization.

The announcement of the settlement quoted a statement from the district which said, “The District recognizes that comments made at various Board meetings that concerned LifeWise, including by Directors, were offensive and hurtful to the families participating in LifeWise programming. For that, the District and its Board of Directors offer a sincere apology.”

In a statement posted on their website, Everett Public Schools said, “Parents and guardians have the right to choose to seek the release of their students during the school day for religious-related activities or instruction that occurs off school property for part of the school day pursuant to District Policy 2340 and Procedure 2340P. The policy and procedures align with both Washington State (RCW 28A.600.025) and federal law, with which the district is required to comply. The procedure allows students to be excused for a portion of the school day, provided the instruction is conducted off-site and does not disrupt their regular classroom instructional time.”

“Religious discrimination has no place in public schools,” Stephanie Taub, senior counsel at First Liberty Institute, told Fox News Digital. “We are grateful to have reached this settlement on behalf of LifeWise. This is a tremendous victory not only for our clients but for all religious release time programs.”

Fox News Digital reached out to the Everett School District for comment and was referred back to the district’s statement, with the school district saying, “There were no changes to the policy. The Student Release Guidelines have been updated to comply with the terms of the settlement.”

Weekend Agriculture
Publishing Date: October 17, 2026

As mid October advances across the nation's midsection, the 2026 row crop harvest is surging past its midpoint. The USDA's latest Crop Progress report confirmed that national corn harvest reached 47% complete, outpacing the five year average of 39%, while national soybean harvest advanced to 67% complete, well ahead of the 52% historical norm. Clear, dry weather across the Corn Belt and Plains provided optimal combine conditions, allowing producers to make rapid headway while dry topsoil profiles enabled uninterrupted field activity.

Grain and livestock boards closed Friday's session with active position adjustments as markets digested updated balance sheets following the October WASDE report. CME corn and soybean futures experienced two way trade as expanding harvest supplies were met by strong domestic processing demand and continuous foreign export sales. In livestock country, live cattle and feeder futures closed firmly, underpinned by historically tight fed cattle supplies and steady cash feedlot bids.

USDA AND POLICY DIGEST
The grain trade spent the week processing the latest USDA Crop Progress metrics alongside updated WASDE balance sheet figures, as field operations maintain a rapid pace across primary growing zones:

National corn harvest cleared 47% complete across 18 major reporting states, with maturity reaching 94% nationwide. Yield reports across the central Corn Belt continue to show strong baseline numbers on heavier soils, while dryland yields reflect midsummer moisture stress.

Soybean harvest leaped to 67% complete nationally, with leaf dropping virtually finalized at 95%. Processing demand remains robust, supporting interior crush values as new crop deliveries move into commercial storage and river terminals.

Winter wheat planting for the 2027 crop advanced to 64% complete nationally, while emergence reached 35%. Rain showers across portions of the Southern Plains provided much needed topsoil moisture for early establishing stands, though subsoil deficits persist across western districts.

On the policy and trade front, market focus centered on fall inland waterway logistics, with Mississippi River draft levels holding adequate for barge traffic during peak harvest movement. Private export reporting channels confirmed continuous sales of new crop soybeans to China and unknown destinations, alongside steady corn bookings to Latin American buyers.

WEATHER, SOIL AND FIELD REALITY
Weather conditions over the past week delivered near perfect harvesting conditions across the primary agricultural core:

In the Western Corn Belt and Plains, warm, low humidity conditions allowed growers in Nebraska, Kansas, and South Dakota to push corn and soybean cutting toward advanced stages. Dry conditions allowed farmers to minimize artificially applied heat drying, though hard dry topsoils are increasing power demands for fall tillage.

In the Central Corn Belt, clear skies allowed field operations across Iowa, Illinois, Minnesota, and Indiana to operate at full speed. Iowa soybean harvest cleared two thirds completion, with corn combining making rapid progress on mature fields.

In the Delta and Southeast, dry autumn weather enabled producers to wrap up soybean cutting and shift equipment into fall land prep and winter cover crop seeding.

Across regional production zones:
In the Western Plains, elevator operators managed heavy grain inflow by staging outdoor ground piles and coordinating unit train logistics.

In the Central Corn Belt, farm managers prioritized fields with stalk rot or lodging risks to minimize harvest shatter loss.

In the Northern Plains, custom harvest crews made rapid progress finishing sunflower and dryland row crop cutting.

In the Southern Plains, winter wheat drilling continued behind rain events as growers sought ideal seed depth moisture.

MARKET AND BOARD REVIEW
CME Group futures closed Friday, October 16, 2026, with active trade across grain, oilseed, and livestock contracts to round out the trading week.

Friday, October 16 CME closing settlements settled around these core baselines:

December CME Corn Futures (/ZCZ26): Settled Friday down 3 3/4 cents at $4.74 1/4 per bushel, facing seasonal harvest pressure against steady commercial processor buying.

November CME Soybean Futures (/SX26): Settled Friday down 1 3/4 cents at $12.61 1/4 per bushel (1261.25 cents/bu), maintaining solid footing on active domestic crush margins and export flash sales.

December CME SRW Wheat Futures (/ZWZ26): Settled Friday down 9 1/2 cents at $6.60 1/2 per bushel, balancing U.S. winter wheat seeding progress against global trade flow headlines.

November WTI Crude Oil: Settled up $3.44 at $101.41 per barrel, keeping operational fuel, transport, and commercial handling overhead elevated.

December CME Live Cattle Futures (/LCZ26): Settled Friday up $1.10 at $228.35 per hundredweight (October Live Cattle settled near $227.15), supported by tight cattle inventories and firm packer bids.

November CME Feeder Cattle Futures (/FCX26): Settled Friday down 5 cents at $341.90 per hundredweight, while December Lean Hogs settled up 35 cents at $66.92 per hundredweight.

Cash grain prices across the Corn Belt reflected competitive processor bids against heavy seasonal harvest throughput:

Corn Belt Cash Corn Bids: Country elevator bids posted between $4.45 and $4.65 per bushel, with interior country basis averaging 15 cents to 30 cents under the December contract. Ethanol processing facilities offered competitive local bids ranging from $4.68 to $4.85 per bushel.

Corn Belt Cash Soybean Bids: Country elevator bids ranged from $12.00 to $12.35 per bushel, while major crushing plants held firm bids near $12.45 to $12.80 per bushel to lock in harvest deliveries.

Corn Belt Cash Wheat Bids: Country bids across winter wheat zones held firm between $6.30 and $6.95 per bushel, with basis holding steady on milling quality.

In livestock markets, cash fed steer trade in the North occurred at $226.00 to $227.00 live and $350.00 to $355.00 dressed, supported by light market ready numbers, while packer bids in Texas and Kansas held near $228.00 per hundredweight.

TECHNICAL SPOTLIGHT, HISTORY AND HOMESTEAD

In agricultural technology, adoption of real time combine yield telemetry and automated moisture sensing enabled farm managers to optimize field logistics on the fly. By syncing combine yield maps directly with grain cart scale telemetry, operators are sorting grain by moisture content directly from the field to optimize aeration bin fan runtime.

Looking back at historical milestones, mid October marks the anniversary of the 1950s introduction of high capacity self propelled combines equipped with integrated corn heads across the Midwest. By eliminating multi pass harvesting and ear corn cribbing, self propelled combine harvesters revolutionized autumn field logistics and enabled the expansion of modern bulk grain handling.

On the homestead and in the field:
Fall Pasture Strategy: Livestock managers evaluated cool season pasture growth following recent rains, adjusting stocking density to protect root reserves prior to winter dormancy.

Fix It Corner: Daily harvest machinery checks remain essential, inspect combine cylinder/rotor clearances, check auger flighting for razor edges, monitor grain cart tire pressures, and blow out dust from combine engine compartments daily.

Producer Voice: "The weather gave us a great run this week, the corn is coming off dry and the trucks are rolling nonstop."

text:
🚨 €4.4 BILLION. The cost of treating obesity — or the cost of doing nothing?

Ireland is facing a major decision on Wegovy.

A new assessment says Novo Nordisk’s treatment could offer value for money, yet reimbursing everyone eligible under its licence could cost an estimated €4.4 billion over five years.

The NCPE recommends that the HSE consider reimbursement for eligible patients. The decision is still pending.

But here’s the bigger question:

Why do healthcare systems so often focus on the upfront cost of treatment without giving equal attention to the long-term cost of obesity and its complications?

Not everyone needs medication. Not everyone should receive it. And public budgets are finite.

But if effective treatment can improve health and prevent serious complications, shouldn’t we also calculate the cost of not treating people?

Obesity is expensive. The question is who pays — and when.

Source: Irish independent 17th oct.

text:
Supreme Court hands Trump midterm win in TV ad cash fight... as two liberal justices refuse to go along | Daily Mail

The Supreme Court handed Republicans a win in a fight over discounted political advertising rates, blocking a lower court order that gave federal regulators just 48 hours to rule on a Democratic challenge.

Democrats are contesting the FCC’s decision earlier this year to extend cheaper ad rates to political parties and joint fundraising committees.

Republicans have more money sitting in party committees, while Democrats have been stronger at raising money directly into candidates’ campaign accounts.

Extending the cheaper rates to party committees therefore makes the GOP’s cash go further, especially now as advertising skyrockets ahead of the midterm elections.

The 7-2 emergency decision allows the Federal Communications Commission to keep reviewing the challenge without the deadline imposed by the 4th Circuit US Court of Appeals.

Justices rebuked the lower court for trying to impose the deadline on the FCC despite its ongoing deliberations.

'Our system of separation of powers does not allow the Judiciary to meddle' in another branch’s workings .. in this manner,' justices wrote in the five-page majority opinion.

Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson said they would have denied the Trump administration's emergency request, though they declined to elaborate further.

The Supreme Court's emergency ruling is the second time that justices have sided with Republicans and the Trump administration the new FCC guidance in as many months.

The emergency ruling leaves in place the new FCC guidance, which grants political parties and joint fundraising committees the same 'lowest unit charge' advertising rates that broadcasters must offer to individual candidates, under federal election law, the final weeks of a campaign.

The FCC's decision to extend the favorable ad prices to parties and joint fundraisers, first announced in March, sparked outcry from some Democrats, who petitioned the FCC to review the changes.

They also sued in federal court to block the updates from taking force.

Three Democratic candidates running for Senate this cycle - including Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, former Senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio, and former North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper - argued that the changes were inconsistent with federal election law.

A divided panel of judges for the Fourth Circuit US Court of Appeals sided with the Democrats earlier this year.

That decision was halted by Supreme Court in September, which said the appeals court lacked jurisdiction to intervene, since the FCC had not yet ruled on the Democrats' petition.

US Solicitor General D John Sauer asked the Supreme Court to intervene a second time, arguing that the 4th Circuit appeals court had ‘seriously erred in trying to short-circuit the Commission’s deliberations.’

The National Republican Senatorial Committee and National Republican Congressional Committee also filed a separate emergency application on the same day, seeking to pause the lower court’s action.

The Supreme Court said Wednesday that the FCC must address applications for review but is under no obligation to do so within a particular timeframe.

They also said that forcing the FCC to make a final decision within the 48-hour period mandated by the lower court ‘irreparably harm’ the commission by requiring it to discard its own, ongoing deliberative process.

The FCC changes are seen as advantageous for Republicans, whose party committees have much more cash on hand than their Democratic counterparts, according to federal fundraising records.
