text:
Palmer Luckey’s argument—that China’s advantage in advanced technology stems from a series of deliberate policy choices rather than merely its large population—is supported by verifiable data. His core assessment is that China benefits from lower industrial electricity costs, a more efficient manufacturing ecosystem, and a more favorable regulatory environment for mineral processing. These advantages are reflected in 2026 data: China’s industrial electricity prices have been falling, while those in the U.S. have been rising; China controls approximately 90% of global rare-earth refining capacity; and U.S. manufacturing construction spending declined by about 22% year-over-year in 2026.

Luckey’s Claims vs. Verifiable Facts
Regarding energy costs: In an interview at the Reagan Library, Luckey stated, "They have extremely low energy costs. You can complain about their coal-fired power plants, but the net result is that their energy costs are very, very low." This assessment is borne out by 2026 electricity market data: in January 2026, China’s proxy electricity procurement prices fell by 10% year-over-year, with annual contract prices trending downward across key economic provinces such as Guangdong and Jiangsu. Meanwhile, in the U.S., capacity prices for PJM—the country’s largest grid operator—hit a regulatory cap of $333.40 per megawatt-day; absent these price controls, demand from data centers would have driven electricity prices up by nearly another 60%.

Regarding supply chains and logistics: Luckey described China’s "logistics and supply chain environment" as "very favorable." Quantitatively, this is underscored by the fact that China accounts for approximately 50% of global shipbuilding capacity, compared to less than 1% for the U.S.—with China’s annual output in terms of total vessel tonnage reaching 232 times that of the U.S. In the rare-earth sector, China controls roughly 90% of global refining capacity and 95% of magnet manufacturing.

Regarding the regulation of minerals and rare earths: Luckey noted that China has "very favorable laws" governing the extraction and processing of metals, minerals, and rare earths. Data from the Bank of Finland Institute for Emerging Economies (BOFIT) for August 2026 confirms that China accounts for 84% of the refining of rare earth elements used in permanent magnets and 59% of rare earth mining. Although its share of refining has declined from a previous high of over 90%, its dominant position remains firmly entrenched.

Regarding the labor market, Laki suggests that the United States "may need to loosen its labor laws." This observation comes against the backdrop of U.S. manufacturing construction spending, which stood at $169.8 billion in July 2026—a decline of approximately 21% from the $215.6 billion recorded during the same period the previous year. Despite 84 companies announcing over $900 billion in manufacturing investment commitments since January 2025, these pledges have yet to materialize into actual factory construction.

Laki’s Comprehensive Argumentative Framework
"Architect-Astronauts" vs. "Real Engineers." In his interview, Laki offers a sharper critique: American universities produce "architect-astronauts"—individuals who focus solely on high-level design while outsourcing the complex challenges of manufacturing. In contrast, China possesses "the world’s best battery, metallurgical, and optical engineers." He specifically points to Apple, noting that "most of the truly difficult work today is done by Chinese engineers."

A Tenfold Efficiency Gap. Laki asserts that if the Pentagon manages to spend even 50% of every dollar effectively, it is doing well; meanwhile, China operates with tenfold greater efficiency on comparable projects. He attributes this disparity not to cheap labor, but to China’s successful automation of labor-intensive processes.

"Queen Bees" vs. "Worker Bees." Laki acknowledges a structural characteristic of the Chinese education system: it excels at producing a vast number of deep-execution specialists ("worker bees") but yields fewer cross-disciplinary generalists ("queen bees"). His own career path—dropping out of school at 19 and leveraging capital-backed risk tolerance to launch ventures across different industries—is "extremely rare" in China.

Distinctions That Require Precision
The nature of Laki’s assessments is inherently shaped by his own background and identity. He is the founder of Anduril Industries—a company valued at $61 billion—which is currently building flexible production lines in Ohio, modeled after the approach seen in Shenzhen. His warnings serve a specific commercial and political agenda: to push for increased energy production, the easing of labor regulations, and the expansion of a confidential patent system in the United States. His assessments—most notably the claim that "China is ten times more efficient"—are estimates based on his personal experience rather than systematic academic research.

The assertion that "the U.S. needs to burn more fossil fuels" is a policy recommendation, not a statement of fact. It is verifiable that industrial electricity prices are falling in China while rising in the U.S.; however, attributing this price gap solely to a "coal versus natural gas" dichotomy overlooks critical variables such as grid structure, regulatory frameworks, and the pace at which renewable energy capacity is being installed. Analysis from Huatai Securities indicates that the "divergence" in electricity prices between the two nations since 2024 is fundamentally driven by the diverging costs of primary energy sources—specifically, a decline in coal prices in China contrasted with a rise in natural gas prices in the U.S.—with shifts in fuel costs accounting for 70% of the electricity price increase in the U.S.

The core reality is that the three structural advantages highlighted by Palmer Luckey—lower industrial electricity costs, an efficient manufacturing ecosystem, and a regulatory environment conducive to mineral processing—are all reflected in the data as of 2026. His conclusion—"You can't say, 'I want to win, but I'm not willing to do any of the things they’ve done'"—is an expression of a political choice, not a fact that can be empirically proven or disproven. Whether the United States is prepared to make the trade-offs he suggests regarding energy, labor, and regulatory policy is a political question, not a matter of data.

text:
Palmer Luckey explains why China is advancing so rapidly in technology and why the United States is struggling to keep up 🇺🇸🇨🇳

“The reason China is doing so well with advanced technology isn’t that they have a lot of people. It’s that they made a series of decisions that make high-tech companies much faster and much more effective.

They have very low-cost energy. You can complain about all of their coal plants, but the net output is that they have a very, very low cost of energy.

You have a really favorable labor environment. You have a very favorable logistics and supply chain world. You have very favorable laws regarding the extraction and processing of metals, minerals, and rare earths.

People ask me, ‘Palmer, what can we do to catch up with China?’

I say, ‘We need way more energy. We’re probably going to need to burn a lot more fossil fuels, and we’re probably going to need to relax labor laws.’

And they say, ‘I want to catch up with China, but I don’t want to do any of the things they’re doing to lead.’

You have to make a choice at some point. It’s not really possible to say, ‘I want to win, but I’m not willing to do anything to do that.’”

text:
The West is losing its children, its institutions, its courage – and its future. And it is paying for the privilege.

The media manufacture consent. Universities convert the next generation. Bureaucracies ration opportunity. Families raise their children for eighteen years, then pay to have them re-educated. And millions live in fear of stepping outside a system that needs them far less than they think.

Conservatism reproduces by birth. The left reproduces by conversion. We raise the children. They collect the harvest.

The diploma was meant to certify that you can think. It increasingly certifies that you think correctly. The media work the same way: they rarely need to invent facts. They choose which facts exist, which experts speak, and which questions may be asked. People trust institutions, not lone voices. That is their real advantage: they lie with a logo.

And communism? Lies plus an inability to see through them. AI is teaching us just how enormous differences in cognitive capacity can be. Add an ideology that puts its conclusions before the facts, and you get a system in which evidence becomes an enemy and failure is always somebody else’s fault.

We cannot defeat this with another thread. We must build institutions of our own.

But the problem goes deeper than institutions. We have taught people to fear losing their place in the system: their credentials, their networks, their meaningless jobs. Communism rationed meat. Its legacy rations belonging.

That fear is about to lose its foundation. An ageing society, shrinking generations and AI-driven abundance will increasingly need people to create value rather than beg for permission. The future belongs to those who can build, not those who sell tickets to the club.

But people need more than economic freedom. They need a reason to live, to have children, to inherit a civilization and pass it on. The left offers belonging and a cause. We too often offer rules and nostalgia.

We must become something worth being born into.

And we need a structure capable of protecting it.

Our nation-states were built for an age when Western countries competed against one another. Today, a family in Ohio may share more with a family in Warsaw or Milan than with the managerial class ruling its own capital. Brussels offers the wrong answer: more bureaucracy, more centralization, more distance from reality.

We need something older and wiser: a Council of Western Civilization. Not a superstate, not another government. A framework for guidance, coordination and identity – a family of nations protecting a shared inheritance without abolishing their differences.

The Greeks had no single state. They had Homer, Delphi and the Olympic Games. They knew who they were.

We can do the same. Build institutions that expose manipulation, map networks of influence, publish evidence and become trusted references. Build educational alternatives that reward competence rather than conformity. Build communities in which families, children, courage and productive work are valued.

And above all, stop being afraid.

The left converts. We must convince. The left monopolizes institutions. We must build our own. The left offers a future in exchange for obedience. We must offer a future worth inheriting.

Tell the truth. Have courage. Build.

The West does not need to be managed into survival. It needs to remember what it is – and organize itself accordingly.

text:
We all know here that the mainstream media are professionals of lying and manipulation in the service of global leftism – the enemy of Western Civilization, Our Civilization.

The question is how to explain it to everyone else.

Because "everyone else" doesn’t read threads on X. They read the headline, watch the evening news, and trust the man in the suit who says "experts agree." People trust institutions, not lone voices on X. That is the media’s real power: not that they lie, but that they lie with a logo.

And they rarely need to invent anything. They choose which facts exist. The story told, and the story ignored. The word that frames it. The expert invited, and the one never called. The "fact-checker" who checks the framing, not the facts. And all the same way: the same story, the same angle, often the same words, in every outlet on the same morning.

Everyone has had the experience: you read an article about your own field and see it’s full of errors and falsehoods. Then you turn the page and believe the next one. That reflex is what keeps the whole machine running. While obviously they all lie the same way – it’s just that you don’t notice it outside of your area of expertise.

So the answer cannot be one more thread. It has to be a visible structure – something people can point to, cite and trust. The other side has universities, foundations, fact-checking networks and prizes. We have brilliant individuals and millions of followers – and almost nothing in between.

I suggest the Council of Western Civilization, for a start. Public and transparent – everything the other side is not. A place that names the methods, gives people the vocabulary, maps who funds whom, and shows the receipts. Not one more opinion. A reference.

Lies with a logo can only be beaten by truth with an address.

Let’s build it.

text:
Willi Münzenberg – The Man Who Wrote the NGO Playbook.

You have never heard of him. That was the point.

Gramsci explained why culture had to be conquered. Münzenberg showed how – and built the machine that still runs today.

1. Born in 1889 in Thuringia, the son of a poor innkeeper. During the First World War he met Lenin in Zurich. He became one of the founders of the German Communist Party and sat in the Reichstag. But his real talent was something else: he understood that most people will never join a revolution – and can still be made to work for one.

2. In 1921, famine struck Soviet Russia, and Lenin asked him to raise help from abroad. Münzenberg created Workers International Relief – and discovered that a humanitarian cause attracts people who would never join a communist party. The aid was real. So was the propaganda. The first modern NGO used as a front.

3. Then he built an empire. Newspapers, an illustrated magazine read by hundreds of thousands, publishing houses, book clubs, film studios. Germans called him the Red Millionaire. It was the media group of the Comintern – and almost nobody reading it knew.

4. His masterpiece was what he privately called the Innocents’ Clubs: committees for peace, against war, against fascism, against imperialism. Causes every decent person supports. Famous writers and scientists on the letterhead, congresses in grand halls – and a few communists in the back office deciding everything. The cause was the bait. The network was the catch.

5. When the Reichstag burned in 1933, he struck back with a book of accusations and a mock "counter-trial" in London, staged with eminent lawyers – and won world opinion before any real court had ruled. Trial by narrative. The template of every media tribunal since.

6. He didn’t need intellectuals to join the party. Only to lend their names. The fellow traveler – the professor, the actor, the novelist who signs the petition and never asks who drafted it – was his invention as much as anyone’s. Arthur Koestler worked for him in Paris and later described the whole system from the inside.

7. In the end he broke with Stalin, over the purges and then the Hitler–Stalin pact. In 1939 he published an open attack titled "The traitor, Stalin, is you." A year later, in France, he was found hanging from a tree in a forest. Suicide or murder – it was never solved. The machine outlived its builder.

Now look around. The "coalition" of NGOs. The open letter signed by a hundred celebrities on the same morning. The "civil society" platform funded by governments. The tribunal of public opinion that convicts before any court. The cause sounds always noble. The network is always the same.

Münzenberg would recognize all of it. He wrote the playbook.

Next time a hundred famous names sign the same letter on the same day, ask the one question nobody asks: who drafted it?

text:
New "Biological Data Center" Uses Millions Of Living Human Brain Cells To Process Information | IFLScience

In a very on-brand move for the 2020s, Singapore is building a “Biological Data Center” that uses millions of living human brain cells to compute information.

Human neurons meet silicon chips

The project is a collaboration between the School of Medicine at the National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine), data center developer DayOne, and Melbourne-based startup Cortical Labs.

The latter is one of the world’s only companies that is developing commercial biological computers. Their flagship product is called CL1, a system that uses “wetware” – AKA living biological neurons derived from stem cells – and conventional silicon chips to process data.

In August 2026, NUS Life Sciences Institute received 20 of these units as part of what they called a “Biological Data Center.” Each CL1 contains hundreds of thousands of living human-derived neurons (the true number has been reported as 200,000 or 800,000 by different outlets), which equates to millions of brain cells that will be working away in the lab.

“By growing living human neurons from stem cells and pairing them with rigorous engineering, we’re not only building a more efficient alternative to silicon; we’re creating a platform that can help us understand learning and adaptation at their biological source,” Professor Rickie Patani, director of the neurobiology programme at NUS Medicine, said in a statement.

“That dual promise is what makes this collaboration sustainable and scientifically generative. It gives us a real route to accelerate drug discovery and neurological disease research, turning laboratory insight into real-world impact far faster than we could before,” he added.

The neuron-driven data center is the first of its kind outside Australia, where a facility in Melbourne houses 120 CL1 units. Each unit contains a "life-support system" designed to keep the neurons alive for up to six months, according to Cortical Labs.

This technology is still in its infancy, but the idea is that biological systems could potentially be more efficient at processing data with a fraction of the power required by digital computers. Cortical says its devices are "low power, to the extreme" and require "a fraction of energy other technologies use", but as of yet it's unclear how that translates into actual numbers.

NUS Medicine suggests the biological data center will be used to “supplement AI in areas where data is sparse,” such as drug discovery, robotics, cybersecurity, and fraud detection. For now, however, it is essentially a prototype that will be used to explore how the technology can be scaled.

To Pong or not to Pong

In 2021, scientists at Cortical Labs published a peer-reviewed paper in the journal Neuron describing how they had developed a computer system interlaced with 800,000 brain cells that could play the video game Pong.

In the paper, they proposed that the human and mouse-derived brain cells were coaxed into playing the game because of the “free energy principle,” which posits that any self-organizing system, like a brain, will always attempt to minimize surprise and unpredictability in its environment.

In the context of Pong, a miss resets the game, resulting in the ball heading in a random direction and increasing unpredictability. A hit, on the other hand, sends the ball in a more predictable direction. The researchers suggest the cells are incentivized to minimize unpredictability in feedback signals from the game, which is why they become better at controlling the paddle, thus preventing the ball from hitting the edge of the screen.

It's not yet proven that this is really what is going on, but that hasn't stopped Cortical Labs from building on their success. Earlier this year, the team demonstrated that an array of CL1 chips was able to play the classic first-person shooter game DOOM.

It's worth saying, however, that it was the silicon side of things that rendered the game's graphics and ran its logic; Cortical are only claiming that the neurons processed the inputs and outputted commands to the player character.

For the moment, conventional computers with good-old-fashioned silicon chips are far, far better at general computer tasks. However, Cortical Labs has lofty hopes for the technology.

Musing in the book Science for a Better Tomorrow, the team write that natural neural systems could offer a way to develop better and more efficient AI.

“Since biological brains operate with power and data efficiencies otherwise unparalleled, along with the capability for rapid real-time adaptation, it may be beneficial to reconsider neural systems in the current search for AI,” they write.

Bioethical conundrums

Brain organoids are becoming increasingly common in scientific research, but they pose a conundrum for bioethicists over the theoretical risk of consciousness. If a network of neurons becomes sophisticated enough to compute complex problems, is it capable of experiencing pain and suffering?

At this point, no one would seriously claim the neurons in Singapore's prototype computer are sentient, and bioethicists overwhelmingly say these things are a long way off from that level of sophistication. But, presumably, if biological data centers do scale up as their advocates wish, there could come a time when questions of consciousness look a little less farcical.

Two examples, admittedly from different titles of US Code but still revealing: 

28 U.S.C. § 3002(15) (Federal Debt Collection Procedures Act only):
“‘United States’ means—(A) a Federal corporation; (B) an agency, department, commission, board, or other entity of the United States; or (C) an instrumentality of the United States.”

42 U.S.C. § 659(i)(1) (certain child-support enforcement/garnishment provisions):
“United States” includes departments, agencies, or instrumentalities of the legislative, judicial, or executive branches, the United States Postal Service, the Postal Regulatory Commission, any Federal corporation wholly owned by the Federal Government, and the governments of the territories and possessions. 

28 USC 3002 (above) says United States is a corporation or one of the many depts and agencies of United States. 

42 USC 659 (above) says as well that United States is the departments, agencies, etc. Meaning it's the government, not the 50 states.

Boris Johnson’s article in the Daily Mail raises a fundamental question: what is Europe’s plan to bring this terrible war in Ukraine to an end?
He condemns Vladimir Putin’s strategy, criticises Donald Trump’s decisions and challenges a Europe that too often seems to react to events rather than shape them.
But beyond indignation, one essential question remains: what is our actual strategy for achieving peace?
Supporting Ukraine in its defence is one thing. Defining the conditions for a lasting peace is another. Europe cannot simply continue funding the war, issuing statements and waiting for events to determine its future.
It must defend Ukraine’s sovereignty, safeguard the security of the continent and, at the same time, work seriously towards the conditions for credible negotiations.
Peace does not mean surrendering to an aggressor. But neither can it be reduced to hoping for a military victory without a clearly defined endgame.
Indignation is not a strategy. War must not become a political horizon. And peace cannot simply be declared: it must be prepared, negotiated and secured.
Can Europe still offer a genuine vision for peace, independent of political changes in Washington, or is it condemned to follow decisions made by others?
It is time for our leaders to answer that question.

IT’S JANUARY 2029. TRUMP IS GONE. AMERICA WANTS A FRESH START.

A new president offers to lift tariffs, end the threats and rebuild trust with America’s allies.

But the world has moved on.

Canada has found new customers and built new trade relationships. Other countries have reconsidered their dependence on Washington. Those investments and partnerships won’t vanish with a change of president.

And the consequences extend far beyond lost exports.

Consider Stelco.

In 2024, Cleveland-Cliffs acquired the Canadian steelmaker with binding employment commitments. Two years later, hundreds of jobs are threatened, with U.S. tariffs among the reasons cited. Ottawa is examining enforcement options.

What happens when the next American company wants to acquire a strategically important Canadian business? Will promises suffice, or will governments demand stronger guarantees—or refuse the sale?

And why would that scrutiny stop at Canada’s border?

Around the world, uncertainty about American commitments could carry a price:

• Higher required returns.
• Stronger contractual guarantees.
• Tougher foreign acquisition reviews.
• More diversified supply chains.
• Lost customers and investment opportunities.

Not necessarily because countries oppose America. Because uncertainty creates risk, and risk has a cost.

Here’s the problem for Trump’s successor.

A president can lift tariffs, withdraw threats and sign new agreements.

But they cannot compel customers to return, reverse investments made elsewhere or guarantee what the next administration will do.

Canada and America will always be neighbours. Cooperation can recover without restoring Canada’s former dependence.

Ending a confrontation is one thing. Recovering the economic advantages of being a trusted partner is another.

What will America have to offer the world to make its commitments worth trusting again?

text:
For Trump, the Iran War Is Stuck Between Combat and Genuine Peace https://t.co/BGTcgCh7CP 

Iran Holds the Key to Trump’s Political Future

President Trump’s MAGA legacy is being undermined by the Iran war, and he seems unable to find a way out. Poor advice from his own advisers has compounded his errors in judgment. Yet one option could help him salvage his political future: bring the Iran war to an end.

The first step is to acknowledge how this disastrous war began. At the urging of Israel’s Netanyahu, Trump chose to attack Iran, apparently hoping to topple its theocratic regime, gain access to its oil wealth and seize its nuclear materials. His fundamental mistake was assuming Iran would surrender without a fight. He and his advisers ignored the lessons of America’s past five decades of warfare. In Korea, Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan, America won battles but failed to achieve its broader objectives. Iran threatens to become another such debacle.

Trump’s second error was choosing the wrong mediator. Pakistan was a questionable choice for negotiations of such magnitude, given its complicated and often conflicting relationship with Washington. Critics raised doubts from the outset, but Trump ignored them. The failed ceasefire effort was hardly surprising, and Trump must accept much of the blame.

His third mistake was repeatedly rejecting opportunities to end the war. The consequences were predictable: Iran obstructed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while America imposed a naval blockade to restrict Iran’s imports and oil exports. Oil prices surged, gasoline and diesel became more expensive, and American consumers paid the price. Public opposition to the war grew.

Trump’s hope that Iran will surrender and meekly accept American demands is unrealistic. Even threats to send Iran back to the Stone Age are unlikely to break its resistance.

The way out is not another threat, but a change of strategy.
Trump should signal America’s willingness to withdraw and begin moving some of its threatening naval forces away from the Persian Gulf. In return, Iran should agree to stop attacks on commercial shipping. Both sides must then cooperate to remove naval mines and restore safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz. This process could take weeks, but it is essential to restoring normal oil shipments.
Next, Washington should consider lifting sanctions in stages, releasing frozen Iranian assets and allowing trade to resume. Years of sanctions have inflicted considerable pain on Iran. Renewed trade would benefit Iran, oil-importing countries and American businesses alike.

Only after military threats recede should negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme resume. Iran must accept meaningful inspection arrangements and restrictions on further uranium enrichment. Expecting Tehran simply to surrender its reported stockpile of 600 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% is unrealistic. The priority should be preventing further enrichment and negotiating verifiable limits.

The 2015 Kerry-era nuclear agreement offers a starting point. A new deal may take months, but negotiations can proceed without an outside mediator if both sides demonstrate genuine commitment.

Trump still has a choice: continue a costly war with uncertain results or pursue a negotiated exit. Ending the Iran war could be his best chance to rescue his MAGA legacy—and his political future.

Did you know Japan has its own ancient Thanksgiving? ⛩️🌾

Every October 17, Japan celebrates Kannamesai, a sacred Shinto ritual at Ise Grand Shrine.

Freshly harvested rice is offered to Amaterasu, the sun goddess and ancestral deity of Japan’s Imperial Family.

Dating back to the 7th century, this tradition reflects a time when rice was life itself.

Unlike America’s Thanksgiving, there are no turkey dinners—just quiet gratitude for nature’s blessings.

Japan has long cherished one simple belief: Never take food for granted. 🇯🇵❤️

text:
The Infrastructure of Finance | Storage Technologies of the Past
No. 2: The scrolls that were burned to survive

My friends and especially my family know well that I have more than a few odd obsessions besides #TheInfrastructureOfFinance: old books, libraries, the history of classical Greece and Rome, more old books... And those obsessions happily came together earlier this year in news of another of the world's oldest storage technologies, papyrus scrolls.

When Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, it buried a grand villa outside Herculaneum, along with its library of papyrus scrolls. The heat didn't destroy them. It turned them into something like charcoal briquettes, and then sealed them under a thick layer of volcanic rock for seventeen centuries. Like the clay tablets in No. 1 of this series, which lasted because the cities around them burned and baked them hard, the Herculaneum scrolls survived because of the fire, which is not a disaster-recovery plan I would recommend to any of our customers.The workmen who found them in the 1750s weren't sure what they were, and some were reportedly mistaken for lumps of coal and thrown away. About 1,800 scrolls and fragments were eventually recovered, most now in the National Library in Naples. Then came the hard part. A priest named Antonio Piaggio built a machine that unrolled them with silk threads, at a rate of millimeters a day, and the scrolls that it didn't destroy came apart in flakes. For two and a half centuries, every attempt to read them risked destroying them.

The answer came from data science. Brent Seales at the University of Kentucky spent two decades developing "virtual unwrapping": scan the rolled scroll with X-rays at a particle accelerator, build a 3D model, trace each layer of papyrus through it and flatten it into a readable sheet. The catch was that the carbon ink barely shows up on X-ray. So in 2023 the Vesuvius Challenge offered prize money to anyone who could find it, and a group of young researchers trained machine-learning models to spot ink their own eyes couldn't see. The first word, in October 2023, was "purple." By February 2024 the winning team had read more than 2,000 characters, probably Philodemus on pleasure. In 2025 a team recovered a scroll's title, "On Vices," and this June one scroll was virtually unwrapped and read from end to end for the first https://t.co/NGJz2D6hcO's what strikes me. 

These scrolls have been readable, in principle, for two thousand years; it took us that long to build the drive. Meanwhile the National Archives recommends copying video tape older than five years, and NASA had to rebuild obsolete tape machines to recover its own 1960s images of the moon. Carbon ink on papyrus is a remarkably good storage medium. It just had a very slow read head.

Coming up in this series: what happened when the scroll became a book.

text:
Happy birthday to former Millwood, Oklahoma State University and NFL receiver Rashaun Woods, born on this day in 1980 in Oklahoma City.

Woods was an All-State selection as a senior as a defensive back after intercepting seven passes. On offense, he had 58 catches for 1,129 yards an 11 touchdowns.

Woods chose Oklahoma State over several other offers and went on to have one of the most prolific collegiate careers.

He was a two-time First-Team All-Big 12 selection, consensus All-American in 2002 and First-Team All-American in 2003. When he completed his OSU career, he held Big 12 career records for receptions (293), yards (4,414) and touchdowns (42).

Seven of his touchdowns came in a win over SMU in 2003, which is also an NCAA record.

He had some of his most memorable moments against rival Oklahoma. In 2001, he made the winning touchdown catch in the Cowboys' Bedlam victory and a year later he had three touchdowns as the Cowboys made it back-to-back victories in the series for just the fifth time.

In 2004, Woods was selected by the San Francisco 49ers with the 31st overall pick in the NFL Draft. He had seven catches for 160 yards and a touchdown as a rookie, but spent the entire 2005 season on injured reserve.

He was later traded to the San Diego Chargers, but was released prior to the season.

Woods later played in NFL Europe for the Frankfurt Galaxy.

After his playing career, Woods returned to Oklahoma where he became an assistant with his alma mater Millwood and also at Star-Spencer.

In 2013, he was hired as head coach at John Marshall, helping lead the Bears to the state championship in 2017. In 2019, he accepted the head coaching position at Enid, coaching the Plainsmen for four seasons.

In 2023, Woods became head coach and athletic director in Tyler, Texas.

text:
From post on Facebook 

“Hello, I am Palestinian. 🇵🇸
And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.

1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three noes. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.

Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.

Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.

Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.

I am Palestinian.
I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.

And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit."

So, I visited a childhood friend recently. While I was there, her gas cylinder ran out, and when I offered to change it, she and her daughter freaked out! They preferred calling a male neighbour instead.

I smiled. For me, it was the simplest thing in the world. 

And then it struck me. Years of living in separated family quarters, raising children and handling every little crisis while our husbands served miles away on field postings had taught us so much.

We Army wives don’t even realise how beautifully this life shapes us into strong, capable and independent women.

The Indian Army doesn’t just groom its soldiers. It quietly grooms their wives too.

And what immense pride I feel in having been part of this wonderful institution! ♥️🇮🇳♥️

text:
Dear Brigadier General Dikko, our mothers did not raise their sons for Borno

Dear Brigadier General Dikko,

1. You lamented that Abia State could not produce even 100 recruits for the Nigerian Army. 

2. You wondered how you would explain this failure to your superiors.

3. But General, perhaps you are asking the wrong question.

4. What exactly is the Nigerian Army desperately seeking in Igbo youths that the NNPC, FIRS, EFCC, Customs and Immigration are not equally desperate to find?

5. Why must southeastern inclusion become urgent only when rifles are involved?

6. Nigeria fought a devastating war to prevent the Igbo people from leaving. 

7. Perhaps Nigeria should concentrate on protecting the people it fought to retain, rather than lamenting their reluctance to become its protectors.

8. Times are changing, General.

9. A generation is emerging that understands that patriotism is not measured by willingness to die.

10. A farmer feeds civilisation.

11. A doctor preserves life. 

12. An engineer builds nations.

13. An entrepreneur creates prosperity.

14. These are also forms of national service.

15. Some warn that without military recruitment today, the Southeast may have no generals in thirty years.

16. But General, perhaps in thirty years, these young people will own hospitals, industries, farms and technological empires.

17. Tinubu never became a general to command the protection of generals.

18. The military exists to protect citizens, not merely those who enlist.

19. And before you recruit another mother's son to fight insurgents in the never ending Borno war, remember that his life is not a statistic.

20. His mother cannot embrace a military medal.

21. His children cannot eat a posthumous citation.

22. If fewer than 100 youths volunteered, perhaps you should investigate why public confidence has diminished, rather than lament their absence.

23. Help these young people find other meaningful opportunities.

24. General, the Igbo youth is not a recruitment quota. His life is not expendable.

25. A generation that chooses to build rather than fight has not necessarily lost its courage.

26. Perhaps it has finally discovered the value of its future.

27. If you still need soldiers, ask Soludo, Rochas, OUK, TA Orji to send their sons.

text:
ZELENSKYY WAS ASKED WHO HIS HERO IS. HIS ANSWER SAYS EVERYTHING. 🇺🇦❤️

For nearly five years, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has lived with the responsibilities of leading a country at war. But in a deeply personal exchange with Reuters, the Ukrainian president revealed what he misses most about the life he left behind.

Asked whether he missed being an actor, Zelenskyy replied:

“I miss being a good father.”

The conversation then turned to his children.

When they were younger, what did he tell them?

“I love you.”

And now that they are older?

“I miss you.”

Three words that capture the personal cost of a presidency consumed by war. Behind the speeches, negotiations and constant demands of leadership is a father who misses spending time with his children.

Then came a question about heroism.

“Are you a hero?”

“No.”

When asked whom he considers his heroes, Zelenskyy answered:

“My children, our army, and the Ukrainian people. I am part of our nation. I think our nation is absolutely heroic.”

He was given the opportunity to describe himself as a hero. Instead, he spoke about his family, the soldiers defending Ukraine and the people enduring the war.

For all the attention surrounding Zelenskyy as a wartime president, this exchange offered a much more personal glimpse of the man behind the office.

And perhaps the most moving words were not about courage or leadership at all.

“I miss you.”

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE: Hudson River Museum acquires Maya Lin sculpture

PRESS RELEASE: The Hudson River Museum (HRM) in Yonkers announced on October 16, 2026, the acquisition of The Hudson Bight by acclaimed artist, architectural designer, and environmental advocate Maya Lin, recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, and the National Medal of Arts.

YONKERS, NY: Originally created as the site-specific centerpiece of HRM’s acclaimed 2018-19 solo exhibition Maya Lin: A River Is a Drawing, The Hudson Bight transforms scientific data into a single monumental hanging sculpture that reveals the hidden underwater landscape connecting the Hudson River to the Atlantic Ocean.

QUOTE: “My work has always been finding the art in the natural world and my focus on rivers is because, from an environmental view, they are our lifeblood; without them we couldn’t survive,” Lin said.

“I’m trying to get people to see things that are quite literally under their feet but they had no idea were there. Having The Hudson Bight find its home at the Hudson River Museum is the perfect continuum for the work we began with my exhibition A River Is a Drawing, for which The Hudson Bight was originally erected and to which it has now returned as part of the Museum’s permanent collection.”

The Hudson Bight, which Lin conceived as a “drawing in space,” has been suspended dramatically in the Museum’s Atrium, with the wire-mesh sculpture cascading into the galleries below, translating advanced topographic imaging and sonar mapping into an immersive work of art.

Inspired by a 2018 U.S. Geological Survey expedition, the artworkmaps an underwater plateau that extends more than 100 miles offshore before descending into the Hudson Canyon.

“Throughout her career, Lin has inspired people to experience the world differently, revealing the connections between history, place, and the environment,” Masha Turchinsky (@masha_tee), HRM’s Anita K. Hersh Director and CEO, said.

“While the Hudson Canyon is a natural wonder that exists below the surface of water, Maya Lin’s work exemplifies the power of art to make the invisible visible, inspiring curiosity, wonder, and a deeper understanding of our relationship to the natural world.”

About Maya Lin

Maya Lin (American, b. 1959) is internationally renowned for her environmental artworks, architectural works, and memorial designs. Her singular career has defied disciplinary boundaries, combining art, architecture, science, and ecology to explore humanity’s relationship with the natural world.

First emerging in the public eye through her award-winning Vietnam Veterans Memorial, Lin has created landmark works including the Civil Rights Memorial and the ongoing environmental project What Is Missing?

Her work has been exhibited worldwide and is held in the collections of The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Museum of Modern Art, the National Gallery of Art, the Smithsonian Institution, and the Obama Presidential Center. 

In recognition of her extraordinary contributions to American culture, Lin received the National Medal of Arts in 2009 and the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016. She is a member of both the American Academy of Arts and Letters and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

About the Hudson River Museum

The Hudson River Museum is a preeminent, award-winning cultural institution in Westchester County and the New York metropolitan area. 

Situated on the banks of the Hudson River in Yonkers, New York, the Museum’s mission is to engage, inspire, and connect diverse communities through the power of the arts, sciences, and history.

The HRM offers engaging experiences for every age and interest, with an ever-evolving collection of American art and dynamic exhibitions that range from nineteenth-century paintings to contemporary art installations. 

The campus, which recently expanded to include a West Wing with stunning exhibition galleries and sweeping views of the Hudson River, features Glenview, an 1877 house on the National Register of Historic Places; a state-of-the-art planetarium; an environmental teaching gallery; and an outdoor amphitheater.

The Museum is dedicated to collecting, preserving, exhibiting, and interpreting its multidisciplinary offerings, which are complemented by an array of public and educational programs that encourage creative expression, collaboration, and artistic and scientific discovery. 

The Museum is accredited by the American Alliance of Museums (AAM), an honor awarded to only 3% of museums nationwide.

Museum Hours: The Hudson River Museum is open to the public Wednesday–Friday, from 12–5pm, and Saturday–Sunday, from 11am–5pm. On Free First Fridays, the Museum is open and admission is free on the first Friday of the month, from 5–8pm. The Museum is accessible by Metro-North (Hudson Line—Yonkers and Glenview stations), by Bee-Line Bus Route #1, by car, and by bike.

General Admission: Adults $15; Youth (3–18) $8; Seniors (65+) $9; Students (with valid ID) $9; Veterans $9; Children (under 3) FREE; Members FREE; Museums for All* $2, *SNAP/EBT card with photo ID (up to 4 people). New! free general admission for all Westchester County high school students on Saturdays and Sundays.

Planetarium Tickets: Adults $8; Youth (3–18) $6; Seniors (65+) $7; Students (with valid ID) $7; Veterans $7; Children (under 3) Free.

Glenview Tours: Adults $8; Youth (3–18) $6; Seniors (65+) $7; Students (with valid ID) $7; Veterans $7; Children (under 3) Free.

text:
Global Biofuels – Advanced Bioproducts: Industrial Competition – Feedstock Security and the Future of Renewable Diesel - The central finding is that the strategic scarcity in advanced liquid biofuels is shifting from refinery conversion capability towards sustainably available feedstocks, credible lifecycle carbon performance, access to mandated markets and the financial resilience needed to sustain production through volatile margins. Seven conclusions are particularly material.

1. Global demand is expanding, but not uniformly. The International Energy Agency forecasts global sustainable aviation fuel consumption rising from approximately 1 billion litres in 2024 to 9 billion litres in 2030. Its accelerated-policy scenario places total global liquid biofuel demand at 310 billion litres annually in 2030, approximately 30% above its main case. These forecasts are conditional on policy execution and do not represent guaranteed industrial demand. Renewables 2025: Renewable Transport — IEA — October 2025.

2. ENI–Enilive possesses a credible industrial platform, but its announced expansion is not yet equivalent to realised production. Enilive reported biorefining capacity of 1.65 million tonnes annually in 2025 and targets approximately 5 million tonnes by 2030, alongside potential SAF production exceeding 2 million tonnes annually. Its operating industrial base includes Gela, Porto Marghera and the St. Bernard Renewables operation in Louisiana. The strategic challenge is to convert nominal capacity, processing flexibility and waste-based procurement claims into sustained, independently auditable output and commercial margins. Eni’s Position on Biomass — Eni; Enilive Sustainability Report and Financial Statements Announcement — Eni — May 2026.

3. Neste establishes a demanding competitive benchmark. The Finnish company reports approximately 5.5 million tonnes of annual renewable-products nameplate capacity across its manufacturing system, including its Martinez joint operation, and projects 6.8 million tonnes following completion of its Rotterdam expansion in 2027. Enilive’s planned growth therefore has to be assessed against larger existing competitors, their feedstock procurement systems, product optimisation capabilities and project execution, rather than against European demand growth alone. Who We Are — Neste.

4. The feedstock supply chain is the critical vulnerability. Used cooking oils, animal fats, vegetable-oil processing residues and other recoverable lipids are simultaneously demanded by renewable diesel producers and HEFA aviation-fuel suppliers. The United Kingdom has explicitly recognised the finite nature of these resources in its SAF policy design. Consequently, replacing fossil diesel with HVO does not automatically establish additional carbon savings if feedstock sourcing displaces existing users, generates land-use pressures or depends on poorly verified waste classifications. SAF Mandate: Crop-Derived Sustainable Aviation Fuel — UK Department for Transport — 2026.

5. Fiscal policy can create markets without guaranteeing economically efficient decarbonisation. The European Union combines renewable-energy targets and sectoral fuel mandates; the United Kingdom imposes a SAF supply obligation; and the United States supports qualifying domestic production through Section 45Z, as modified by 2025 legislation and subsequent guidance. Different incentive structures can produce materially different outcomes for the same physical feedstock and conversion technology. Biofuels — European Commission; Section 45Z Guidance — Internal Revenue Service — September 2026.

6. Industrial improvement must concentrate on a limited number of high-impact interventions. The most consequential candidates are increased feedstock acceptance through pretreatment, improved conversion yields and selective hydrocracking, lower-carbon hydrogen integration, heat and hydrogen recovery, and better allocation between HVO diesel and SAF. Their relative value must be determined at plant level, since higher jet-fuel yields can impose additional hydrogen consumption and processing costs. Eni’s modifications at Gela demonstrate the commercial relevance of product-slate flexibility. Enilive Begins SAF Production at Gela — Eni — January 2025.

7. The priority for governments is verifiable additional emissions abatement, not aggregate installed capacity. Policy should distinguish existing and incremental waste recovery, genuine non-food feedstocks, lifecycle emissions and competing claims on the same materials. Investment support should be conditional on auditable physical output, traceability, measurable carbon performance and exposure to feedstock-price stress. The EU Union Database offers a regulatory foundation, but its effectiveness depends on comprehensive participation, upstream verification and enforcement. Union Database for Renewable and Recycled Carbon Fuels — European Commission.

The overall assessment is that ENI has significant strategic options, particularly through the conversion of existing refining assets and the integration of fuel production with distribution and customers, but its competitive position in 2030–2035 will depend less on the quantity of projects announced than on verified feedstock access, product yields, effective carbon intensity, realised returns on capital and the capacity to serve aviation without undermining the economics of renewable diesel.

The Biofuels Paradox: Europe Is Building Refineries Faster Than It Can Secure Sustainable Feedstocks
Europe is committing industrial capital to renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel while the availability of verifiably sustainable biological feedstocks remains the unresolved constraint on production. Eni, Neste and TotalEnergies are expanding or converting refining infrastructure under regulatory frameworks that create demand but do not guarantee profitable manufacturing. The European Union requires sustainable aviation fuel to represent 6% of eligible aviation fuel supplied in 2030 and 20% in 2035, while Enilive aims to triple its reported biorefining capacity to approximately 5 million tonnes annually by 2030. The contradiction is consequential for industrial policy, public finance and energy security: Europe can increase its capacity to manufacture renewable hydrocarbons without securing the raw materials, margins or additional emissions reductions needed to justify the investment. The decisive test is no longer the number of refineries converted, but the economic and environmental value of what they actually produce.

Capacity Is Expanding Faster Than the Evidence of Profitable Production
The industry’s investment cycle reveals a widening distinction between manufacturing capability and commercial performance. Enilive reported 1.65 million tonnes of annual biorefining capacity in 2025, compared with 1.157 million tonnes of biological feedstock throughput. Its separately disclosed average refinery utilisation indicator was 78%, while a simple division of reported throughput by capacity produces approximately 70.1%. The figures follow different accounting definitions and cannot be reconciled without additional operational information. That difference matters because nominal processing capacity is not finished-fuel production, and neither establishes profitability.

The international comparison reinforces the point. Neste reports approximately 5.5 million tonnes of renewable-products nameplate capacity, with an objective of 6.8 million tonnes following its Rotterdam expansion. Diamond Green Diesel, associated with Valero and Darling Ingredients, reports approximately 1.2 billion US gallons of annual renewable diesel capacity, including the ability to upgrade part of its production into sustainable aviation fuel. These figures cannot form a reliable market-share ranking without adjustment for product definitions, ownership and operating utilisation.

The United States illustrates the financial exposure behind industrial scale. Its Energy Information Administration recorded 324,000 barrels per day of renewable diesel and other biofuels manufacturing capacity on 1 January 2026, alongside 128,000 barrels per day of conventional biodiesel capacity. Yet the International Energy Agency reported severe pressure on American producers during 2025, forecasting a nearly 15% contraction in combined biodiesel and renewable diesel production amid weak regulatory-credit values, feedstock costs and policy uncertainty.

Shell’s September 2025 decision not to restart construction of its Rotterdam biofuels facility supplies the clearest industrial counterpoint. A major integrated energy company abandoned additional manufacturing capacity after reassessing completion costs and market competitiveness. The existence of future renewable-fuel obligations was insufficient to justify completing the investment.

Eni’s Industrial Conversion Is a Test of Italian Competitiveness
Enilive’s programme is important for Italy because it transforms existing refining infrastructure rather than relying exclusively on new industrial construction. Porto Marghera began biorefining in 2014 and Gela in 2019, using Ecofining technology developed by Eni and Honeywell UOP. Gela’s sustainable aviation fuel unit, commissioned in January 2025, has a declared nameplate capacity of 400,000 tonnes annually.

The next investment phase extends the industrial model. Sannazzaro de’ Burgondi has an announced feedstock-processing capacity of approximately 550,000 tonnes annually; Priolo is planned at approximately 500,000 tonnes; and the international portfolio includes a 650,000-tonne project in Malaysia and a 400,000-tonne development in South Korea. Construction status, commissioning schedules and ownership interests differ. Treating these projects as already operating would exaggerate present supply.

The financial exposure is tangible. Eni and the European Investment Bank announced two financing arrangements of €500 million each for the Livorno and Sannazzaro conversion programmes. These are financing commitments, not €1 billion of non-repayable public grants, but their scale illustrates the capital committed to transforming Italian downstream manufacturing.

Italy’s industrial interest extends beyond renewable-fuel volumes. Converting refineries can preserve technical employment, utilities, port connections, storage infrastructure and specialised engineering capabilities. Nevertheless, these benefits do not establish that the resulting plants will obtain sufficient qualifying feedstocks at prices compatible with commercial operation. A refinery manufacturing fuel in Italy from imported recovered oils strengthens domestic conversion capability while retaining significant external supply dependence.

Enilive’s advantage lies in integrating processing technology, existing infrastructure and fuel distribution. Its principal test will be whether additional capital improves certified production, operating margins and resilience rather than simply increasing the capacity recorded in corporate reporting.

The Scarce Commodity Is Not Refining Technology but Eligible Carbon
Hydrotreated vegetable oil and hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids convert oils and fats into hydrocarbon fuels using hydrogen and catalytic processing. Their industrial maturity supports large-scale production, but their biological inputs are constrained by the activities that generate them. Used cooking oil comes from food preparation; animal fats from livestock processing; and agricultural oils from crop cultivation and crushing.

These feedstocks respond differently to demand. Higher collection prices can increase recovery of cooking oil, but they cannot indefinitely increase the quantity physically generated. Animal-fat production remains connected to slaughtering and rendering, while expansion of cultivated vegetable oils can affect agricultural prices, land use and competing food or industrial demand.

The International Energy Agency’s December 2022 feedstock assessment projected that demand for vegetable oils, waste oils and fats used in biofuel production could increase by 56%, reaching approximately 79 million tonnes during its 2022–2027 forecast horizon. The projection was not an observed 2026 supply figure; it identified the structural problem of expanding demand against finite recovered-material streams.

Indonesia illustrates the geopolitical transmission mechanism. Its B40 biodiesel programme in 2025 supported domestic palm-based fuel consumption, while the government announced a further B50 objective in June 2026. Brazilian policy moved to B15 biodiesel blending on 1 August 2025, after an earlier postponement associated with food-price concerns. Domestic blending decisions in major agricultural economies can reduce exportable feedstock availability and alter costs for European refiners.

Certification adds another layer of scarcity. Material classified as qualifying waste can command a different commercial value from chemically similar material without that status. In July 2025, the European Commission reported systemic weaknesses in certification audits concerning investigated Chinese biofuel imports, while stating that the evidence did not establish fraud in the consignments examined. The distinction matters: weak verification can distort compliance markets even where misconduct by an individual supplier has not been legally established.

Europe’s Union Database for renewable and recycled carbon fuels addresses traceability, but documentary compliance must ultimately correspond to physical waste generation, material transfers and refinery intake.

Aviation Mandates Create Demand, Not Guaranteed Industrial Returns
The European Union’s ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation requires sustainable aviation fuel to account for 2% of eligible aviation fuel supplied in 2025, 6% in 2030 and 20% in 2035. The 2035 obligation includes a 5% synthetic aviation-fuel requirement. This distinction limits the assumption that the expansion of conventional lipid-based HEFA production alone can satisfy Europe’s longer-term aviation transition.

The United Kingdom operates a separate mandate, rising from 2% in 2025 to 10% in 2030 and 22% in 2040, while introducing specific requirements for power-to-liquid fuels. Its proposed revenue-certainty arrangements recognise a fundamental financing problem: regulatory demand does not automatically produce predictable manufacturing revenue, particularly for technologies requiring substantial initial capital investment.

For refiners, aviation creates an additional commercial choice. Producing more jet-range hydrocarbons from lipid feedstocks may require further hydrocracking, isomerisation, hydrogen and separation, potentially reducing output of other valuable products. The relevant calculation is the additional net margin from aviation fuel, not the difference between quoted aviation and diesel prices alone.

France’s TotalEnergies faces this problem through its Grandpuits development and SAF production activities at La Mède. Germany approaches the market through its greenhouse-gas reduction obligations, chemical engineering and fuel-compliance system. Italy’s Enilive combines domestic refinery conversion with aviation-fuel capability and international manufacturing projects. These national positions differ enough that a uniform European subsidy for refinery capacity would not produce uniform economic or environmental returns.

Public Incentives Can Transfer Value Without Creating Additional Fuel
The fiscal problem is illustrated by the differences between European mandates, Britain’s certificate-based system and the United States’ Section 45Z clean fuel production credit. The American mechanism ties qualifying production benefits to prescribed emissions calculations, while European obligations primarily create regulated demand and associated compliance costs. California’s Low Carbon Fuel Standard adds another system in which the value of lower-carbon fuels depends on recognised lifecycle carbon intensity and tradable credits.

These instruments influence commercial behaviour, but their benefits are not necessarily retained by refiners. Where recovered biological feedstock supply is relatively inelastic, higher fuel incentives can increase the prices paid to collectors and commodity suppliers. Part of the financial value created by climate policy can therefore migrate upstream without generating equivalent additional material.

The dossier’s illustrative fiscal model makes the problem measurable. A programme supporting 1 billion litres annually at €0.20 per litre costs €200 million. If it delivers 1.5 million tonnes of genuinely additional carbon-dioxide-equivalent avoidance, gross expenditure is approximately €133 per tonne. If only half the assumed emissions benefit is additional, the effective figure increases to approximately €267 per tonne.

These calculations are hypothetical, but the mechanism is decisive. A government purchasing additional emissions reductions should distinguish them from fuel production that would have occurred without support. Financing a refinery, supporting a feedstock collector and rewarding the same fuel’s environmental attributes may serve different objectives, but their combined cost must be assessed before declaring the intervention economically efficient.

The Next Investment Cycle Will Separate Production from Industrial Survival
Over the next 12–24 months, the decisive indicators will be commissioning performance, verified feedstock procurement, operating utilisation, product yields and the commercial returns of facilities entering service.
