Lecture: 
Chaos, 
Contingency, 
and Disposable Labor 
in the Carceral State 
– The 2014 San Quentin Termination 
as Interdisciplinary Case Study

Students of 
Law, 
Political Science, 
Psychiatry, 
and Social Anthropology: 
the episode from San Quentin State Prison 
in 2014 
is not an anecdote of personal inconvenience. 

It is a concentrated illustration 
of how large-scale organizations 
absorb and redistribute risk. 

On October 17, 2014, 
a contractor
 sat in San Francisco International Airport 
with coffee and near-sighted glasses, 
recording a mundane post. 

The contract had ended abruptly 
amid simultaneous shifts 
across multiple California state agencies a
nd federal oversight structures 
that converged on San Quentin. 

The individual experience 
registered as annoyance and surprise. 

The structural consequences
—disrupted continuity 
for health-care employees 
whose careers were affected 
even if they were 
not direct contractors
—were invisible to the person 
whose work had just been severed.

This is the operational fact set. 

We examine it through 
five interlocking frameworks,
 read against the operational practice 
of minimalist management: 
deliberate strategies 
that minimize fixed labor costs 
by treating personnel 
as interchangeable inputs 
rather than carriers of 
institutional knowledge, 
relationships, 
and capacity.

Chaos Theory and Sensitive Dependence.

Complex organizations 
are not linear machines. 

In systems 
with many interacting agents
—California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, 
California Correctional Health Care Services, f
ederal receivership structures 
established under constitutional litigation, 
and contracted service providers
—small changes in 
policy, 
funding, 
or leadership 
can produce large, 
non-proportional effects. 

The multi-agency flux of 2014 
functioned as a perturbation. 

A contractor termination 
that appeared local and limited 
was the visible tip 
of a cascade 
that reconfigured staffing 
for health-care delivery. 

Chaos theory 
does not require mystical indeterminacy; 
it requires 
recognition 
that the prison’s 
operational environment 
already contained 
high degrees of coupling. 

When agencies 
reconfigure simultaneously, 
the butterfly 
is not a single decision 
but the intersection itself.

Murphy’s Law as Organizational Default.

Murphy’s Law 
is frequently dismissed as folk wisdom. 

In institutional settings 
it describes the interaction 
between incomplete information 
and high consequence. 

The individual believed 
only contractors were affected. 

That belief was reasonable 
under ordinary contracting assumptions 
yet false 
under the actual interdependencies. 

Anything that could go wrong
—loss of continuity 
for non-contractor staff, 
interruption of care protocols, 
secondary effects 
on recruitment and retention
—did go wrong, 
not because of malice 
but because 
the system contained 
latent pathways for those outcomes. 

Minimalist management 
amplifies this:
 by keeping permanent staff lean
 and relying on contingent labor, 
organizations reduce buffer capacity. 

The result is 
that ordinary administrative adjustments 
become high-impact events.

Pandora’s Box and 
Unintended Release.

Opening processes of reform or realignment
—whether driven by court orders, 
budget cycles, 
or internal reorganization
—releases consequences 
that cannot be fully anticipated 
or contained. 

The “box” 
in this case 
was the simultaneous 
reconfiguration of state and federal actors 
at a single facility already 
under long-term constitutional scrutiny 
for medical care. 

What emerged 
was not only the expected contractual adjustment
 but effects on employees 
who were not parties to the contract. 

Once released, 
those effects 
travel through professional networks, 
licensing pathways, 
and individual career trajectories. 

The organization 
that opens the box 
rarely retains responsibility 
for every released consequence; 
minimalist structures 
are designed 
to limit residual liability.

Self-Organizing Systems.

Large organizations 
do not require constant central direction 
to produce patterned outcomes. 

Rules of cost minimization, 
risk externalization, 
and compliance 
with overlapping mandates 
generate emergent order. 

At San Quentin 
the intersection of agencies 
self-organized around 
the imperative 
to control personnel costs. 

Contractors supply flexibility; 
permanent staff supply continuity. 

When pressure rises, 
the system preferentially 
sheds the former 
and redistributes residual work 
onto the latter, 
or simply reduces capacity. 

This is not a conspiracy; 
it is an attractor state 
produced by the incentives 
embedded in public-sector budgeting 
and procurement. 

Self-organization here 
favors disposability.

The Dichotomy of Lived Experience 
and Structural Organization.

The individual narrative 
is temporally compressed 
and affectively bounded: 
annoyance, 
unexpectedness, 
a coffee at the airport. 

The structural narrative 
is temporally extended 
and distributed: 
careers altered, 
institutional knowledge lost,
 continuity of care 
for a high-need population 
compromised. 

Social anthropology 
insists on recovering 
the thick description of both. 

Psychiatry 
examines the downstream effects
—job loss as a stressor, 
moral injury among remaining staff, 
potential degradation 
of mental-health services 
inside a total institution. 

Law and political science 
examine the formal architecture: 
at-will or limited-term contracts, 
multi-level principal-agent problems, 
and the weak accountability mechanisms 
that exist 
when federal, state, 
and contracted actors interact. 

The dichotomy 
is not a failure of perception alone; 
it is produced 
by the scale 
and opacity 
of the organization. 

Minimalist management 
widens the gap by design: 
it reduces 
the number of people 
who possess both long-term stake 
and deep local knowledge.

The Minimalist Management Lens.

Across these frameworks 
the consistent practice 
is the treatment of labor 
as a variable cost 
rather than a valued asset. 

Contractors lower fixed obligations 
and simplify termination. 

When multi-agency turbulence occurs, 
the cheapest 
and most readily available adjustment 
is to end contingent relationships. 

The short-term fiscal benefit is real. 

The longer-term costs
—recruitment churn, 
loss of tacit knowledge 
about complex patient populations, 
reduced continuity of care, 
secondary impacts 
on non-contractor staff
—are externalized. 

In a carceral health-care setting 
those externalized costs 
are borne 
by both workers 
and the people in custody 
whose constitutional right 
to adequate care 
is already 
under judicial supervision.

For law students 
the case raises 
questions of 
contract interpretation, 
constructive discharge, 
and the interaction 
between procurement rules 
and constitutional minima. 

For political scientists 
it illustrates bureaucratic fragmentation 
and the difficulty 
of coherent policy implementation 
across overlapping jurisdictions. 

For psychiatry students 
it underscores 
how organizational instability 
becomes a clinical variable: 
staff discontinuity 
affects both provider mental health
 and the reliability of services 
delivered to incarcerated patients. 

For social anthropologists 
it offers a site 
for examining 
how total institutions 
reproduce precarity 
among those who work inside them, 
and how official narratives 
of “operational adjustment” 
erase lived disruption.

The 2014 termination was not anomalous. 

It was a predictable output 
of systems organized 
to minimize standing labor commitments 
while navigating 
chronic 
legal, 
fiscal, 
and political constraint. 

Recognizing the pattern 
does not require 
attributing bad faith 
to every actor. 

It requires 
observing that the structures 
currently in place 
systematically convert 
individual contracts 
into disposable inputs 
and convert institutional turbulence 
into distributed personal cost.

No One to Depend On 
(San Quentin, 2014)
Ain’t got no contract 
that I can depend on

Ain’t got no agency 
that I can depend on
Ain’t got nobody t
hat I can depend on

Coffee at the airport, 
glasses off to type

Twelve years later the same light
Chaos moving through the gates
Murphy waiting in the dates

Opened the box of changes
State and federal ranges
Out came the terminations
Careers left in the stations

Self-organizing toward the cheap
Labor light, the costs they keep
Individual story short and neat
Structural story incomplete

Ain’t got no buffer 
that I can depend on
Ain’t got no continuity 
that I can depend on

No tengo a nadie 
that I can depend on
Health-care workers felt the cut
I thought the contractors only, 

but
The lived and the organized
Never fully synchronized

Minimalist hand on the lever
Assets become whatever
You can end without a letter

Tomorrow’s problem, 
someone better
Ain’t got nobody that I can depend on

Ain’t got nobody that I can depend on
In the intersection of the rules
No one to depend on
—that’s the school.

The federal lawsuit, filed in the Central District of California on October 15, requests an order preventing the tabulation of ballots belonging to individuals identified as likely noncitizens until their citizenship can be determined.

Under California law, registered active voters are automatically mailed ballots. That practice has become central to the DOJ’s concerns about individuals who may be improperly registered.

The Justice Department says Homeland Security Investigations and federal partners examined voter-registration records and conducted additional verification work to identify potential noncitizens.

In its official announcement, the DOJ confirmed it is asking the court to require California to set aside the disputed ballots, rather than automatically cancel them.

The letter from Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter, dated October 13, 2026, lays out the facts with devastating clarity. Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections.

The Supreme Court has long held that states may not induce or encourage private persons to do what the Constitution forbids.

On July 16, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin warned Weber that large numbers of noncitizens were registered to vote in California. Weber’s response the following week did not deny it. She simply asked for more information.

The Trump administration provided that information. text:
The harshest realities of life nobody wants to accept:

1. Nobody is coming to save you. The people you are waiting for might never show up.

2. Poverty will teach you lessons that money can never explain.

3. Some people love you more when you are useful to them than when you need them.

4. Being a good person doesn't guarantee that people will treat you well.

5. You can give someone your last, and they can still abandon you when you have nothing.

6. Life doesn't stop because you are hurting. You still have to wake up and face another day.

7. Sometimes, the people you call family will treat you worse than strangers.

8. People may celebrate your success without caring about the suffering you endured to achieve it.

9. Nobody truly understands your struggle until they experience something similar.

10. Love without respect will slowly destroy your self-worth.

11. You can pray, cry, work hard, and still face difficult seasons. Life isn't always fair.

12. The world is often kinder to people who have something to offer than to those who have nothing.

13. Some apologies come only because someone has lost access to you, not because they regret hurting you.

14. Your sacrifices will not always be appreciated. Sometimes, people will even act as though you did nothing.

15. The hardest truth? You can be struggling to survive, and the same people who know your situation may still sleep peacefully without checking on you.

💔 And perhaps the most painful reality of all: you can spend your whole life being there for everybody, only to discover that when you finally need somebody, you are standing alone.

But remember this: being abandoned does not mean you are worthless, and having nothing today does not mean you will have nothing tomorrow.

text:
THE PRICE OF BLACK OWNERSHIP: WHO GETS TO CONTROL M&F BANK?

A Black bank can get bigger and still lose something.

Its name. Its headquarters. Its charter. Its connection to the community that built it.

That's the decision facing shareholders of Durham-based M&F Bank, one of the country's historic Black financial institutions.

And two competing deals offer two very different answers to a question that doesn't appear on a balance sheet:

When a Black institution changes hands, who actually inherits the power?

THE DEALS

On July 22, M&F Bancorp agreed to merge with South Carolina-based Optus Financial in a transaction expected to create the largest Black-owned bank in America.

Bigger balance sheet. Greater lending capacity. A larger regional footprint.

But there's a catch.

Under the Optus agreement, M&F Bank would be absorbed into the combined institution. Its headquarters would move to Columbia, South Carolina. Its independent charter would disappear. And after a transition, so would the M&F name.

More scale. Less institutional continuity.

Then came another offer.

On October 15, Greensboro-based Triad Business Bank publicly identified itself as the competing bidder and released its fourth proposal.

Triad wants a common holding company overseeing both banks while preserving M&F's separate charter, Durham headquarters and historic name.

The financial terms also deserve attention.

TRIAD'S OFFER:

$53.50 cash per share for up to 25% of M&F shares.
Alternatively, 1.25 shares in the combined company for each M&F share.
OPTUS AGREEMENT:

Up to $46.57 per share at closing.
Up to another $6.73 per share, contingent on specified preferred-share payments.
Those figures aren't directly interchangeable. The deals distribute cash, equity and conditional value differently.

M&F's board continues to recommend Optus and has not determined that Triad's competing proposal is superior.

Shareholders are scheduled to vote October 20.

THE PART THEY DON'T PUT IN THE HEADLINE

The Optus deal comes wrapped in an attractive headline:

America's largest Black-owned bank.

That matters. Black-owned financial institutions have historically operated with far less capital than their competitors. Scale can expand lending capacity, improve technology and strengthen a bank's ability to survive.

But size isn't the same thing as control.

And preserving a historic name isn't the same thing as protecting a historic mission.

Triad promises to keep M&F's identity and charter intact. That's meaningful. But a separate charter under a common parent doesn't automatically guarantee independent decisions.

Who appoints the directors?

Who controls lending standards?

Who decides which neighborhoods receive capital?

Who controls the deposits, customer relationships and institutional data?

And when profitability conflicts with community investment, who wins?

Those answers matter more than the lettering above the bank's front door.

FOLLOW THE POWER, NOT THE PLAQUE

Black banking institutions weren't created because America had an abundance of financial opportunity waiting for Black depositors.

They emerged in a system that routinely excluded Black people from credit, ownership and capital.

Their importance was never merely symbolic.

They represented a measure of economic decision-making power in communities denied access to it elsewhere.

That's what makes this transaction worth examining.

One proposal would consolidate two Black-owned institutions into a potentially more powerful regional bank while ending M&F's independent institutional identity.

The other would preserve that identity while shifting ultimate authority to a new holding company.

Neither structure automatically guarantees that Black communities retain meaningful control over the capital those institutions manage.

A bigger Black bank isn't automatically a stronger Black community. And a preserved Black brand isn't automatically Black economic independence.

Both claims have to survive scrutiny of the governance documents, shareholder rights, lending commitments and actual decision-making authority.

The October 20 vote will determine more than which offer M&F shareholders accept. It will help decide what happens to a piece of Black financial infrastructure that took generations to build.

The winning bidder may inherit the assets.

The shareholders may capture the financial value.

But what happens to the institutional power?

That's the question the merger announcements can't answer by themselves.

Because Black ownership isn't just about whose name is on the building.

It's about who controls the money when the doors close.

On this day in 1814 – U.S. Sailors and Marines landed on Grand Terre Island, Louisiana, to punish pirates. 

Pirate leader, Jean Lafitte’s activities threatened to monopolize the city’s import trade. New Orleans merchants goaded the new American governor of Louisiana, William C. C. Claiborne, into accusing him of piracy and posting a $500 reward. 

Lafitte made Claiborne a laughingstock with his own offer of $1500 for Claiborne’s capture, and to rub it in he hired District Attorney John R. Grymes as his counselor (for a reported $10,000). 

Lafitte would not be bought, bribed, or intimidated. In 1814 the British offered him $30,000 and a Royal Navy commission to help them capture New Orleans. 

The buccaneer turned them down and informed Claiborne of his wish to become a citizen and to give Claiborne his support, if his privateer followers were pardoned for all past crimes. 

Claiborne was ready to relent when the American Navy swooped down on the Grand Terre base and destroyed it. Fortunately for the infant United States, General Andrew Jackson sought out the buccaneer and agreed to honor his request.

On December 17, 1814, Gov. Claiborne announced a pardon for Baratarians who volunteered their service. Pierre and Jean Lafitte, multiple Baratarian captains, and 300-400 others took the deal.

What Happened to Jean Lafitte and the Baratarians?
After the war, President James Madison granted the promised pardons in February 1815. This created an interesting business opportunity for Lafitte and the Baratarians. With Presidential pardons, they were able to reclaim nearly half a million dollars in goods from the U.S. Navy.
 
The ships and goods captured during the 1814 September attack on Grande Terre were meant to be prizes. The strategic victory of the Barataria Bay turned into a financial let down.
 
Many of the Baratarians settled in New Orleans or in the Barataria area. Some of their descendants still live there today. Lafitte later went back to smuggling on Galveston Island in Spanish Texas. His business there continued until he was kicked out by the U.S. Navy in 1820.
 
Jean Lafitte's exact whereabouts after that are unknown. His life and death remain as mysterious as any myth from the swamps and bayous of South Louisiana.

text:
A bigger sample doesn’t fix a bad poll.

I joined fellow pollster John McLaughlin (@jmclghln) on @NEWSMAX’s National Report to explain why the most important question isn’t simply how many people answered a poll. It’s how they conducted the poll, who answered, AND who was missed.

McLaughlin offered a striking example: A Texas survey had far more respondents recalling voting for Kamala Harris than actually did, in a state that strongly backed Trump.

That’s why good reporters need to start examining the methodology, not just write a headline.

I explained why American Pulse uses multiple ways to reach people: live telephone interviews, text surveys, and other modes. Someone who ignores a call may answer a text. Different methods help reach different people.

Then look underneath the numbers: Are they surveying likely voters? Are postgraduate respondents overrepresented—a common problem? And most importantly, does the sample’s recalled 2024 presidential vote reasonably reflect what actually happened?

For pollsters whose livelihoods depend on getting it right, those aren’t academic questions. They’re essential checks and should be for reporters too.

Getting it right is a very different incentive from producing cheap, drive-by media polls to grab headlines.

Before trusting a poll’s take on the next election, let’s look at what it says happened in the last one.

Thanks to anchors @E_D_Hill and @KyleLowder, @jmclghln, @NEWSMAX, and the excellent National Report team for the opportunity to pull back the curtain on what good polls actually look like.

This was rare, next-level news coverage. Kudos.

text:
Buffalo Bill Cody carried the same Remington .44 from 1863 until 1906. When he finally gave it to his ranch foreman, his handwritten note said, "It never failed me."

The New Model Army had a feature most revolvers of its day lacked: small safety slots milled between the chambers. Rest the hammer in one and it sat clear of every cap, so a dropped gun was far less likely to go off.

In 1861 Samuel Remington offered the government his revolvers at $15 each, $10 less than Colt was charging. Then Colt's factory burned in 1864, and large Remington orders followed.

Cap and ball, solid frame, six shots. Would you have trusted one for 43 years?

text:
The Power Watch Is the New Power Move for Women at Work

As women embrace watch collecting, they’re finding that their expertise can be an unexpected professional asset

Julianna Wanner, a partner manager in advertising sales, was trying to win over a prospective client at dinner last October when she noticed the Rolex on his wrist. “Cool Datejust,” she said.

The remark prompted a wide-ranging conversation about their shared passion for watches. Exchanging stories, he told her that he bought the timepiece to commemorate reaching $1 million in revenue for the business he built. She landed the client, and the deal helped her exceed her quarterly revenue goal. She credits the watch talk with helping build the rapport that closed the deal.

Wanner, 31, is among a growing number of women who say that becoming a watch enthusiast has become an unexpected workplace advantage, giving them an entree into conversations traditionally dominated by men. Watches are a hobby worn on the wrist, making enthusiasts easy to spot. A comment about a timepiece can open the door to stories about a milestone purchase, a family heirloom or a passion for collecting.

“It’s a male-dominated hobby,” said Wanner, who lives in Los Angeles. “When a woman says ‘I love your [Omega] Speedmaster,’ it raises eyebrows.”

Last year, she marked her 30th birthday and career milestones with a large Cartier Tank Française, automatic movement, which cost $6,750.

Entry-level luxury watches can go for a couple thousand dollars, while the most coveted models can cost upward of $60,000 and be hard to get, with long wait lists at some dealers.

“It establishes social status, peer-to-peer status and signals that I’m not a tiny woman in the back who doesn’t know how I got into the room,” said Nicole Cost, an executive at Bank of America in Greenwich, Conn., who works with high-net-worth individuals on trusts and estate planning. “It builds trust.”

Cost became interested in watch collecting while attending watch events with her husband, where she found herself drawn to vintage pieces. She wears three watches in rotation: a $7,500 Hermès H08 in brushed titanium; a Rolex Datejust with blue Roman numeral dial from 1984, which she said cost about $6,000; and a Rolex Oysterdate Precision from the 1950s, which she said cost about $4,750.

She once noticed one of her clients wearing a Breitling Emergency, a $17,650 to $22,400 technical watch with a built-in locator that can transmit distress signals for search-and-rescue teams. Knowing it’s often worn by skiers, she used it as an opening to talk to him about the sport.

Cost said that she’s still one of few women at watch events. But women’s interest in watches has risen in recent years.

Sales of women’s watches in the U.S. have more than doubled in the last three years and more than quadrupled in the last six on Chrono24, a global luxury-watch marketplace, according to company spokesman Johannes Förster. Cartier has the highest share of women’s-watch spending on the site, he said, and that share continues to grow.

Dimepiece, an online media platform dedicated to women who love watches, launched in 2020 and now has around 62,000 followers on Instagram and around 1,200 subscribers on Substack. Its founder, Brynn Wallner, said she had discovered “watches are cool” working at her previous job in editorial at Sotheby’s.

“I was about to turn 30 and felt like the watch industry missed me as a consumer,” she said. “Why aren’t there websites or Instagram [accounts] for me?” Her site offers information for first-time buyers and seasoned collectors as well as celebrity watch sightings and interviews with influencers about their first watch.

These women are already in the rooms they’ve historically been left out of. Now, their watch hobby is helping them build connections and be taken more seriously, said Laurie Henneborn, vice president of research, insights and solutions at Catalyst, an organization that studies women at work.

“That’s about much more than watches,” she said. “It’s about social capital and who gets access.”Erica Eckes, 29, a director of strategy at a tech company living in Charlotte, N.C., bought her “gateway drug,” a $6,795 Cartier Panthère, to celebrate a promotion. When she later became a director, she purchased a Rolex Datejust model that retails for $18,000.

At a dinner with her leadership team in a previous job, she noticed her boss’s boss—the company’s new chief revenue officer—wearing a Breitling Navitimer, which can go for as much as $54,000 for solid gold or limited-edition variants. He told her the timepiece was a gift from his wife and kids, and they compared notes on watches and the stories behind their collections.

For her next watch, Eckes is torn between an A. Lange & Söhne 1815 Up/Down, priced at about $40,000, or a vintage Piaget stone-dial dress-watch, which costs from $5,000 to $30,000.She’s turning 30 soon, a milestone birthday. “There’s potential for either scenario,” she said.

Tara Weiss is a contributor to The Wall Street Journal.

text:
BRANDIN COOKS: SNEAKY PLAY 👀🏈

Every year, there’s a veteran WR who seems to come out of nowhere, gets his opportunity, and suddenly reminds everyone he can still play. 

It’s like momentary Lightning in a Bottle! 

Think Jamison Crowder. The guy nobody wants on his roster until he drops 20 fantasy points out of nowhere.

This year, that guy could be Brandin Cooks. 👀

The 49ers are running dangerously thin at WR, and with Deebo Samuel expected to miss multiple weeks with a hamstring injury, somebody has to step up.

Enter the old dude.

He’s barely seen the field this season, but when Deebo went down in Week 5, Cooks stepped in and scored on a 7-yard TD. That’s not a huge stat line, but it was a glimpse of what he could offer if his role expands.

Kyle Shanahan has been a fan for 10 years. When San Francisco signed him, Shanahan praised his veteran experience and long track record of production. He also gave Cooks a chance to compete for snaps.

Now that opportunity could be here.

WEEK 6 PROJECTION vs. COMMANDERS (MNF) 🏈

📈 6–9 PPR points

A modest projection, with upside if the targets come. If you’re scrambling at WR because of injuries or bye weeks, Cooks is worth a look.

And if you’ve got Mike Evans on your roster, you know how quickly a hamstring issue can turn your lineup upside down. Having a cheap contingency plan on the waiver wire isn’t a bad idea.

This isn’t a long-term dynasty investment. When Deebo returns, Cooks’ role will shrink again.

But for now? He’s a veteran with an opportunity in a depleted WR room, and that makes him an intriguing short-term play.

Depth Wins Championships 🏆

“When I was in my early twenties, I was going to college and working evenings at a gas station. Even then, I felt a calling to do something more—something that mattered, something that helped people in moments when they needed it most. One evening, an officer stopped for gas and suggested I apply to the local police department as a 911 Telecommunicator. That small moment of encouragement changed the course of my life.
 
I soon applied to both the local police department and the sheriff’s department for a 911 Telecommunicator/Matron position. After interviewing with both agencies, I felt a growing excitement about the possibility of joining law enforcement and serving the community that raised me. I accepted a position with the sheriff’s department and stepped into the role of a 911 Telecommunicator at a time when the entire system was still new to our small community. It was a period of transformation—computers were just being introduced, pen and paper systems were fading, and communities were transitioning to standardized 911 addresses. Change was constant, and I loved being part of something that was evolving to better protect and serve people.
 
As technology grew, so did my desire to learn more, to do more, and to challenge myself. That drive led me to apply for a Telecommunicator position with the Illinois State Police. I began my ISP career in January 2000, and from the very start, I knew I had found my purpose. Through intensive training, strong mentorship, and continued professional development, I became a certified Telecommunicator and discovered just how impactful this career could be.
 
At ISP, technology quickly advanced Computer Aided Dispatch, statewide land mobile radio systems, touch screen operations, and more. The responsibilities grew as well. Being an ISP Telecommunicator means managing multiple emergencies at once, tracking officer locations, coordinating with countless partners, and answering both emergency and non emergency calls from the public. It is demanding work, but it is deeply meaningful. It is a career built on courage, compassion, and the unwavering commitment to help others, even on their hardest days.
 
Not everyone is called to this type of work, but for those who are, it becomes more than a job. It becomes a purpose, a passion, and a second family. This career also offers meaningful pathways for advancement; something reflected in my own journey. Over the years, dedication, continued learning, and a commitment to service led me to where I am today as the Deputy Director of the Division of Statewide 9 1 1. It is a reminder that the opportunities within this field are wide ranging for those who choose to pursue them.
 
If you have drive, strong multitasking abilities, and the desire to work in a career that brings growth, accomplishment, and community, I encourage you to explore the Illinois State Police Telecommunicator positions listed below and apply today. You will never regret the opportunities you seize, only the ones you walk away from.” - Cher Clodfelter, Division of Statewide 911 Deputy Director
 
Join the ISP team as a Telecommunicator and step into a career that will challenge you, shape you, and reward you in ways you never expected. It will push your limits, strengthen your skills, and bring moments of emotion, pride, and fulfillment that stay with you forever.
 
Most of all, it will give you the honor of saying, “I am an Illinois State Police Telecommunicator, and I am here to help you.”

text:
How COVID reshaped college grading | Indiana University

Twenty-three Indiana University undergraduates are co-authors on a new study examining how the pandemic reshaped college grading, the result of a semester-long research seminar that took them from a classroom question to a published paper in a national academic journal.

The students conducted the research, "The Shock That Stayed: The COVID Pandemic and Its Impact on Assessment," published in the journal Social Science Quarterly, as part of the Indiana Political Analytics Workshop (IPAW), an undergraduate training program led by William Bianco, professor of political science in the College of Arts and Sciences at Indiana University Bloomington and a recipient of a 2026 Fulbright Distinguished Scholar Award in American Studies.

"These students built the entire research design themselves, argued through the statistics and worked to generate a publishable result," Bianco said. "That's the kind of experience that usually happens in graduate school, and every one of them earned their place on this paper. It is an important and new finding about the impact of COVID on undergraduate education."

The undergraduate co-authors are Zoe Bogan, Juntao Chi, Olivia Cutka, Gabe Codada, Janani Eswaran, Nathan Fang, Ralph David Fernando, Nick Foxworthy, Avalin Hess, Ranit Kar, Jennifer Karakash, Warren Kim, Violet Lamptey, Adam Longstreth, Sydney Machado, Riley Odier, Thomas Pigott, David Rasmussen, Sophia Richason, Faith Shands, David Tashjian, Ariana Wagner and Jianhan Yin.

The paper was first submitted in December 2025 and accepted in July 2026 after revisions based on feedback from outside reviewers, the same review process any professional researcher submitting to the journal would face.

At the center of the students' analysis was what they called the asymmetry hypothesis, the idea that the pandemic's effect on grades wouldn't be the same in every class. The students reasoned that courses that already had high average grades before COVID had little room left to climb before hitting the 4.0 ceiling, while courses that started with lower average grades had much more room to rise.

The study drew on publicly available grade records for more than 82,000 undergraduate classes taught in the College of Arts and Sciences between 2004 and 2025, then focused on roughly 4,300 courses per year taught just before and after the pandemic.

To measure the pandemic's specific effects, the students worked in small groups to build a statistical model that matched the same courses, and in many cases the same instructors, across different years, isolating how much of the increase was tied to the pandemic itself, against the backdrop of a longer-running national trend toward higher grades.

The students found that their hypothesis held. Grades rose the most in courses that started lower, particularly introductory and STEM classes, and rose only modestly in classes like advanced seminars. Different groups wrote sections of the paper and edited each other's work.

The findings are consistent with trends documented across higher education during and after the pandemic. The paper notes that changes in grading patterns observed at IU are similar to those reported at colleges and universities nationwide.

For many of the students, the seminar offered a rare undergraduate opportunity to see a research question from a classroom discussion to a finished, peer-reviewed publication, the kind of full research arc that shapes how students think about pursuing further research, teaching or other work after graduation.

"They did a great job, and I am very proud of what they accomplished. This is exactly what IPAW was created to do," said Bianco.

Tampa Bay Lightning vs Vancouver Canucks — a perfect home record against a struggling road side

Preview · NHL · Regular season · Saturday 17 October 2026

Tampa Bay finished far above Vancouver last season, are 4-0-0 at home and face a Canucks side that is 1-4-1 on the road and has conceded 41 goals in nine games. The one caution is last season's split series. The Lightning are the pick at medium confidence.

THE MATCHUP

Tampa Bay finished 2025-26 on 106 points at 50-26-6, second in the Atlantic, before losing 3-4 to Montréal in the first round. Vancouver were last in the league on 58 points at 25-49-8.

Nikita Kucherov had 44 goals and 130 points for Tampa Bay last season, with Jake Guentzel on 88 and Brandon Hagel on 74. Hagel leads them this season with six goals and 10 points in seven games; Kucherov has eight points and Guentzel seven.

Vancouver's leading scorer last season was Elias Pettersson with 51 points. He has nine points in nine games this season, and Paul Cotter has four goals.

FORM & CONTEXT

Tampa Bay are 5-2-0, 21 goals for and 19 against, and 4-0-0 at Benchmark International Arena: 3-1 over Washington, 4-1 over Philadelphia, 3-2 over Minnesota and 4-3 in overtime over Seattle on Thursday. Both defeats came on the road against the Rangers, 1-5 and 1-4.

Vancouver are 2-6-1, with 28 goals for and 41 against, and 1-4-1 on the road. Their last win was 4-1 at home to Calgary on 3 October. Since then: a 2-3 home loss to Vegas, then 2-7 at Carolina, 1-4 at New Jersey, 2-6 at the Rangers, 2-3 at the Islanders and 2-3 in overtime at Florida on Thursday.

Both teams last played on Thursday, so rest is level.

THE DECIDING FACTOR

Vancouver's goals against. Kevin Lankinen has a .786 save percentage over five starts. Leevi Meriläinen has been far better at .925 over four starts, but the defence in front of both has leaked goals. Andrei Vasilevskiy has started six for Tampa Bay at .886, below his .912 of last season, which is the main reason this is not a stronger call.

The head-to-head is the counterweight. Vancouver won 6-2 in Tampa on 16 November; Tampa Bay replied with a 6-2 win in Vancouver on 19 March. One apiece by the same score, so it offers no lean.

THE CALL

Last season's table, the current form and the home-and-road records all point to Tampa Bay. The split series and Vasilevskiy's slow start keep it at medium.

Tampa Bay Lightning to win, medium confidence.

text:
Stéphane Ratel, the founder and CEO of the SRO Motorsports Group, on Portimão being a one-off and on Max Verstappen making his GT World Challenge Europe powered by AWS debut this weekend.

The Autódromo Internacional do Algarve is hosting a GT World Challenge round for the first time since 2015, but next year it's already off the calendar. The series will visit the Hungaroring instead with a Sprint Cup round.

"The biggest change [the last couple of years] has been the spectators", says Ratel. "We really started having a spectator attendance and it's growing and it's growing fast. We went from being a championship organising company with one event we promoted, Spa, to now promoting [multiple] events. And to promote an event, of course, you need to go to the same place, preferably at the same time [year after year]. I'm upset we can't go to Monza next year and we have to go to Imola, because Monza became our biggest event after Spa in terms of spectator attendance." Monza will undergo major infrastructure improvements with among others a new pit building, so GT World Challenge plan om going back from 2028 onwards.

"But we wanted to offer a bit of diversity", he continues. "We have many drivers and many teams here in Europe, and it's good to have one rotating event that is different every year. That's why we decided: 'We went to Valencia, now we're coming here [in Portimão] and next year we'll go to Budapest, and the year after we'll go somewhere else.'"

Ratel did not seem satisfied with the ticket sales at the Algarve circuit before the announcement of Max Verstappen joining the grid. "It's true that here, without Max, we would have had a very, very small spectator attendance. What you see here, it's probably - well, not even probably - it is the result of Max. Because up until the moment his entry was announced, the ticket sales were slow at the beginning. But it finally picked up in the last couple of days and now we have a good attendance and a good atmosphere. To go to a circuit with nobody there is not something I'm keen on doing. And Budapest is a big city and [the Hungaroring] is probably one of the tracks that is closest to a capital city."

He is excited to have Verstappen competing in the GT World Challenge this weekend. "I had many dreams coming true. If you told me some years ago that one day I will have the driver of his generation, the F1 driver of his generation, and Valentino [Rossi] here... We would've said: 'Maybe in another life'. But it's happening in this life."

text:
Background: the Treaty Ports. Under the 1921 Anglo-Irish Treaty, Britain had kept three naval bases in the new Irish state: Berehaven and Queenstown (Cobh) in the south, and Lough Swilly in the north. In the 1938 Anglo-Irish Agreement, Neville Chamberlain’s government handed them back to Éamon de Valera’s government. Winston Churchill bitterly opposed this at the time, and the return was what made neutrality practical. As long as Britain held bases on Irish soil, Ireland could hardly claim to stand apart from a British war.

The Irish position. When war broke out in 1939, de Valera argued that a small country only recently independent could not let a former occupying power use its territory. He believed that allowing access would make Ireland a target for German bombing, split Irish opinion, and undermine the sovereignty that had just been won. He also tied the question to partition: Ireland would not join a British-led war while Northern Ireland remained under British rule. In June 1940 Britain floated a vague offer to move toward Irish unity in exchange for entering the war, including use of the ports. De Valera rejected it as unreliable, partly because it depended on Ulster unionists agreeing.

Consequences. The ports would have extended Allied escort range far into the Atlantic, and Churchill blamed their loss for higher shipping casualties in the Battle of the Atlantic. Britain considered seizing them by force but never did. Instead it relied on bases in Northern Ireland, especially Derry/Londonderry and Lough Erne. In practice Irish neutrality leaned toward the Allies. Ireland secretly allowed RAF flying boats from Lough Erne to cross Donegal (the “Donegal Corridor”), shared weather reports (including the Blacksod Point forecast that shaped the timing of D-Day), and usually released Allied airmen while interning Germans. The tension came out openly after the war. In his VE Day broadcast Churchill condemned Ireland’s refusal over the ports, and de Valera replied with a widely praised radio address defending a small nation’s right to stay out of the war.

On the other side, Ireland gave quiet help that a truly neutral state wouldn’t have: the Donegal Corridor for RAF flying boats, weather reporting (including the D-Day forecast), intelligence cooperation between Irish military intelligence (G2) and British security services against German agents, and the release of most Allied airmen while German airmen stayed interned. Tens of thousands of Irish citizens also volunteered for the British forces, and many more worked in British war industries.

The fairest bottom line is probably this: Ireland’s refusal on the ports was a real but temporary setback during the most dangerous phase of the Atlantic war, and its covert cooperation offset much of that. Churchill saw it as a betrayal, while many later historians describe it as “benevolent neutrality” that served Allied interests better than open hostility to Britain, or a forced occupation, would have.

The Houthis are using imitative communications deception in an attempt to disrupt Yemeni government-aligned forces’ command and control and hinder government efforts to defend Taiz City.

Imitative communications deception is a mode of military deception in which a military force introduces false but plausible messages into an adversary’s communications network to induce the adversary to react in a manner contrary to its own objectives.

Yemeni military sources told a Marib-based Yemeni journalist on October 15 that the Houthis infiltrated and broadcasted false evacuation orders on government-aligned force commanders’ radio communication channels during a Houthi ground attack on Jabal Han, immediately west of Taiz City.

Yemeni government-aligned forces and commanders refused to withdraw from Jabal Han despite the Houthis’ false withdrawal orders and reports that friendly forces’ withdrew, however.

The Houthis are supplementing their kinetic efforts to capture Jabal Han with imitative communications deception because the group’s ground attacks have repeatedly failed in recent days.

Successful military deception enables a military force to achieve discrete objectives, such as capturing advantageous terrain on a frontline, with less force than the operational environment would otherwise require.

The Houthis previously used imitative communications deception to successfully disrupt government-aligned forces’ coordination during the Houthi Red Sea coastal plain offensive between September 9 and 11.

Yemeni government-aligned forces’ apparent refusal to withdraw from Jabal Han indicates that these forces have likely strengthened their command-and-control networks and learned from the coastal plain offensive in order to adapt to Houthi deception efforts.

Yemeni government-aligned forces have previously demonstrated their ability to mount successful urban warfare operations against the Houthis, such as in Aden in 2015.

Lean Hog Futures Weekly Outlook: October 12 to 16, 2026

Top News Story: December Hogs Stabilize Near Contract Lows as Strong Wholesale Rebound Cushions Cash Pressure
The lean hog complex closed out mid October trading on a steadying note, with deferred active contracts mounting a Friday bounce to stabilize following earlier multi month low extensions. With the spot October contract reaching expiration, market attention shifted fully to the December contract, which managed a fractional gain into Friday's CME close despite ongoing fundamental pressure from the cash index.

The primary highlight of Friday's session was a sharp upside bounce in wholesale carcass cutout values, which surged back toward the $82.50 to $80.55 per cwt band in USDA updates. Driven by broad based strength across primal cuts, the carcass value uptick provided much needed relief to packer margins and offered immediate short covering incentive for speculative traders holding net short positions in front month paper.

However, near term gains remain capped by a persistently soft physical cash backdrop. The CME Lean Hog Index slipped down to $75.09 mid week, continuing its seasonal slide as heavy autumn processing schedules keep spot hog availability elevated across major growing regions.

Market Notes
The CME Lean Hog Index continued its seasonal glide downward, dropping 66 cents to settle at $75.09 as of October 14. Negotiated cash procurement reflected this softer tone, keeping country bids anchored near mid $70's levels.

Wholesale carcass values staged a solid late week recovery. The USDA Friday carcass cutout value rebounded significantly to $80.55 per cwt (up $3.00 on the day), led by firm strength in primal loins at $81.10 and steady support across butts and hams.

Federally inspected slaughter runs remained heavy, with daily processing paces hovering around 485,000 head as packers maintain high capacity utilization to process peak autumn swine supplies.

Price Summary and Recent Movements
Futures prices executed a modest Friday bounce off lower daily bounds, allowing winter contracts to construct a temporary support floor. Performance metrics at the CME close on Friday, October 16, 2026:

December 2026 (HEZ26): 66.925, up +0.350 (Daily), stabilizing above recent contract lows.

February 2027 (HEG27): 69.150, up +0.275 (Daily), consolidating within lower winter frames.

April 2027 (HEJ27): 74.050, up +0.200 (Daily), tracking long term seasonal spreads.

Cash Trade: Friday morning national base price near $73.50; Friday afternoon pork carcass cutout value at $80.55.

Key Market Factors
Supply: Heavy daily slaughter runs near 485,000 head reflect seasonal marketings, maintaining plentiful wholesale pork availability across distribution channels.

Demand: Export movement offers a solid foundation, with USDA Weekly Export Sales reporting 36,287 MT of pork sold for 2026 shipment, while actual weekly shipments totaled 32,225 MT led by Mexico.

External: Firmness in feeder cattle futures and stable grain markets provided mild spillover support, helping cushion downside momentum across the livestock complex.

Technicals: December hogs defended daily support near $66.30 before pushing back to settle at 66.925. Initial overhead resistance remains established near its 20 day moving average at $68.50.

Upcoming USDA Reports Expectations
With the October contract officially exiting the board, market attention pivots toward post holiday retail features and weekly export shipment velocity. Traders will closely audit daily negotiated cash bids and morning cutout trends to see if packers can maintain wholesale pork pricing strength into late October.

Funds Activity
Managed money accounts maintained a defensive orientation overall, though Friday's price action reflected light short covering. Commitments of Traders data indicates speculative funds remain net short, keeping market rallies vulnerable to technical resistance until a clear cash index bottom is established.

Outlook for the Week Ahead
The near term trajectory remains neutral to cautious as the market searches for a seasonal cash floor. A sustained move above $68.50 in December hogs is needed to signal a meaningful short term bottom, while a failure to hold $66.00 would re-open technical downside risks toward new contract lows.

Risks: A breakdown below $66.00 in December hogs or renewed weakness in primal cutout values below $78.00.

Strategy: Neutral to cautious. Maintain disciplined risk management on long positions until technical indicators confirm a clear daily reversal above intermediate moving averages.

Iraq's greatest obstacle to economic development is not a lack of opportunity, but the political and security challenges preventing that opportunity from being realised.

In an interview with Rudaw, NAMEA Group CEO Dr. Norman Ricklefs discusses Iraq's economic prospects, the challenges posed by armed groups operating outside state control, and the country's potential to emerge as a centre of regional stability and international investment.

Several important issues stand out:

Security and economic reform are inseparable. Bringing armed groups under effective state authority is essential to unlocking investment, privatisation, and economic diversification.
Iraq remains an attractive investment destination. Despite significant challenges, the presence of major international companies demonstrates considerable confidence in the country's long-term potential.
Kurdistan's neutrality and political unity are vital. Closer cooperation between Erbil, Sulaimani, and Baghdad will be increasingly important amid regional instability.
*A federal oil and gas law is long overdue.* A durable legal framework is essential to resolving recurring disputes between Baghdad and Erbil.
Iraq can become a regional mediator rather than a battleground. Its relationships with both Washington and Tehran offer opportunities for constructive diplomacy.

text:
EUROPE’S NEW SECURITY COMPACT

A 10-Point Grand Bargain for Peace in Ukraine and European Strategic Independence

#EuropeanIndependence #UkrainePeace #NewSecurityOrder

1. #EuropeMustStandAlone — Strategic Independence

Europe must never again tie its security to American elections. Build a European-led defence system independent of Washington, while remaining open to American cooperation.

2. #EuropeanSecurityFirst — Redefining NATO

Negotiate a phased US military withdrawal, while building independent European command, intelligence, conventional and nuclear deterrence. Any transition must respect existing treaties and national sovereignty.

3. #BeijingPeaceInitiative — A New Diplomatic Partnership

Europe proposes an economic and diplomatic agreement with China. Beijing uses its influence over Moscow to support a durable Ukrainian ceasefire. In exchange, Europe offers a conditional, decade-long programme of economic normalization.

4. #FifteenYearsOfPeace — Freeze the Front Lines

Establish a 15-year ceasefire along mutually agreed, internationally verified lines inside Ukraine. The arrangement constitutes neither Ukrainian recognition of Russian annexations nor the permanent surrender of Ukrainian territory. Ukraine must consent to the deal.

5. #NeutralPeacekeepers — International Monitoring

Deploy an internationally mandated monitoring force drawn from mutually acceptable non-NATO countries. Its mission would include ceasefire verification, observation of demilitarized areas, investigation of violations and protection of agreed monitoring arrangements.

6. #ChinaHasLeverage — Make Beijing Responsible for Its Commitments

China formally undertakes to respond to serious, independently verified Russian violations. Agreed enforcement measures could include restrictions on sensitive industrial exports, financial transactions and economic cooperation with designated Russian entities.

7. #TenYearEconomicDeal — Reward Chinese Cooperation

Over ten years, Europe gradually relaxes selected restrictions affecting Chinese civilian technology, investment and trade, subject to EU and national laws. Each stage depends on verified implementation of the agreement. Critical military and security-sensitive technologies remain protected.

8. #PeaceHasConsequences — Automatic Enforcement

Establish independent compliance reviews every six months. Russian violations trigger agreed corrective measures. If Beijing fails to implement its enforcement obligations, the next European economic concessions are suspended, with predefined mechanisms for reversing eligible benefits.

9. #UkrainianSovereignty — No Peace Without Kyiv

Ukraine retains its internationally recognized sovereignty, right of self-defence and freedom to determine its political future. No settlement may be imposed on Ukraine by Moscow, Beijing or European capitals. Security guarantees and continued Ukrainian military capabilities remain essential.

10. #AStableEurasia — A New European Security Order

Build a durable European security system based on military self-reliance, enforceable agreements and diversified international partnerships. Maintain constructive relations with the United States, establish a conditional economic partnership with China and make renewed Russian aggression carry substantial consequences.

⸻

THE CENTRAL PROPOSITION

Europe offers China ten years of conditional economic opportunity in exchange for meaningful, enforceable Chinese cooperation in securing fifteen years of peace in Ukraine.

Europe simultaneously develops the military capabilities necessary to guarantee its own security, independently of changes in American political leadership.

The bargain is not built on trusting Moscow or Beijing. It is built on verification, conditional economic benefits, credible deterrence and measurable consequences for violations.

text:
Washington Capitals vs New Jersey Devils — level records, different goaltending

Preview · NHL · Regular season · Saturday 17 October 2026

There is almost nothing between these two on paper. Both sit at 4-3-0, both have a goal difference close to zero, and last season's four meetings were split two apiece. Washington get the nod on home ice, an extra day of rest and steadier goaltending, but this is a low-confidence call.

THE MATCHUP

Washington finished 2025-26 on 95 points at 43-30-9, fourth in the Metropolitan. New Jersey ended on 87 points at 42-37-3, seventh in the division. Neither made the playoffs.

The Capitals' scoring last season ran through Alex Ovechkin (32 goals, 64 points), Tom Wilson (30 goals, 62 points) and Jakob Chychrun (26 goals, 60 points). This season Alex Tuch leads them with five goals and six points in seven games, with Ryan Leonard also on six points.

For the Devils, Jack Hughes had 77 points in 61 games last season, Jesper Bratt 71 and Nico Hischier 66 with 28 goals. Hughes has nine points in seven games so far, Bratt seven, and Hischier has four goals.

FORM & CONTEXT

Washington are 4-3-0, 24 goals for and 22 against, and 3-1-0 at home. Their last two at Capital One Arena brought a 3-5 defeat to Seattle and then a 5-4 win over Montréal on Wednesday, in between a 2-4 loss at Carolina. They finished last season 8-2-0 over their final ten games.

New Jersey are also 4-3-0, with 23 goals for and 23 against, 3-2-0 at home and 1-1-0 on the road. They arrive on two straight wins: 5-4 in overtime at Detroit on Tuesday and 7-1 at home to the Rangers on Thursday. Earlier in the month they lost 0-6 at the Islanders and 3-5 at home to Utah, beat Vancouver 4-1 at home, then lost 1-4 at home to Ottawa.

Washington last played on Wednesday, New Jersey on Thursday, so the hosts have the extra day of rest.

THE DECIDING FACTOR

The crease. Logan Thompson has a .904 save percentage over five starts for Washington, after .912 across 58 starts last season. New Jersey's Jake Allen is at .885 over four starts and Nico Daws .857 over three. Neither starter is confirmed, but the Capitals' numbers are the more reliable.

Last season's series offers no lean. New Jersey won 3-2 in a shootout in Washington on 15 November; Washington won 4-3 in overtime in New Jersey on 27 December and 2-1 at home on 20 March; the Devils won the most recent meeting 7-3 at home on 2 April.

THE CALL

Washington have home ice, more rest and the better save percentages, and that is enough to pick them. Last season's points difference is small, the current records are identical and the Devils come in scoring freely, which is why it stays low.

Washington Capitals to win, low confidence.

text:
Peptides could become one of the most interesting opportunities in consumer health in my opinion.

Here's why I'm watching $HIMS and $ENHA:

Something potentially significant is happening in Washington.

On October 15, Reuters reported that the FDA had submitted a proposed policy change to the White House that could ease restrictions on pharmacy compounding of certain peptides.

The proposal follows a July advisory committee recommendation to expand access to six compounds, including BPC-157 and TB-500.

Importantly, this is NOT FDA approval of these substances. Their safety and effectiveness remain insufficiently established, and the specific scope of the proposed policy has not yet been disclosed.

Nevertheless, a clearer regulatory pathway could help shift demand away from the largely unregulated gray market toward licensed pharmacies, physician supervision, and more reliable supply chains.

So where do $HIMS and $ENHA come in?

1. $HIMS: The established distribution platform

Hims & Hers already has nearly 2.9 million subscribers and generated approximately $753 million in revenue in Q2 2026, representing 38% year-over-year growth.

The company has invested heavily in pharmaceutical infrastructure and is preparing for a potential expansion into peptides, including domestic ingredient manufacturing and clinical protocols.

Its biggest advantage is scale.

HIMS wouldn't need to build an entirely new customer base to introduce these products. It already has the infrastructure, distribution channels, and established consumer relationships.

A larger peptide offering could create opportunities for cross-selling, higher customer spending, and recurring revenue.

2. $ENHA: The more speculative opportunity

Enhanced Group approaches this market from a fundamentally different angle.

Through its Live Enhanced platform, the company already offers sermorelin and has outlined plans to introduce additional peptide-based protocols if regulations permit.

But its most interesting competitive advantage could be its brand.

Enhanced combines elite athletic competition, performance medicine, and consumer products within a single ecosystem.

The Enhanced Games generate attention. The Live Enhanced platform aims to convert that attention into paying customers.

If the company can successfully commercialize this model, peptide treatments could become an important component of its recurring revenue strategy.

Unlike $HIMS, however, $ENHA remains an early-stage business with substantial execution risk.

Its $17.7 million in Q2 revenue came primarily from sponsorships, not an established consumer healthcare business.

3. The bigger picture

I believe the opportunity extends beyond individual products.

Consumer healthcare is becoming increasingly personalized, digital, and focused on prevention, longevity, and performance.

Both companies are positioning themselves around aspects of that trend, but through very different business models.

There are significant risks: uncertain clinical evidence, regulatory restrictions, competition, liability exposure, and the possibility that actual consumer demand falls short of expectations.

And expanding legal access does not automatically translate into commercial success.

My takeaway:

$HIMS is the established, scalable telehealth play.

$ENHA is the smaller, substantially riskier bet on building a recognizable performance medicine brand.

Both could benefit from a more favorable regulatory environment, but the eventual winners will be determined by execution, customer retention, and sustainable profitability.

The regulatory developments are worth watching closely.

Disclosure: I am a $ENHA shareholder. NFA.

Trump says US is talking to Russia and China about denuclearisation | Carl Deconinck, Brussels Signal

US President Donald Trump has said Washington is holding talks with Moscow and Beijing aimed at reducing the nuclear arsenals of the countries with the largest stockpiles.

Speaking in an interview with Newsmax broadcast on October 15, Trump said: “The whole thing is a shame, because I’d love to denuclearise if possible, but we’re actually talking to Russia about that, and we’re talking to China about that denuclearisation.”

He added that he expects China to “catch up” with the United States within the next five years, though he said Beijing remained “substantially behind” and was “probably less inclined” to negotiate because its arsenal is smaller.

Asked whether the discussions involved Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin directly, Trump said they did but gave no further detail.

Trump also said the United States might launch another strike against Iran’s nuclear facilities, including a heavily fortified site known as Pickaxe Mountain. “We may have to go there,” he said, adding that Washington would “knock it out fast”.

The site, Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La in Persian, sits south of the Natanz enrichment plant and is thought to run at least 100 metres beneath the mountain. Its main tunnel complex was not among the targets hit in June 2025, according to the Institute for Science and International Security.

He added that he was considering using the “mother of all bombs” against Iran, the GBU-43 conventional munition. “The mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” he said, calling it “just an extremely large bomb”. Asked whether he would use nuclear weapons, he said: “No, I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to.” He also ruled out sending ground troops.

CNN, citing unnamed sources, reported that the administration was weighing such a strike, possibly after the midterm elections of November 3.

According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), Russia holds the largest number of stored nuclear warheads, followed by the United States and China.

Russia also keeps slightly more deployed warheads than the United States — 1,796 against 1,770 as of January 2026, SIPRI estimates. Russia’s total inventory stands at 5,420 warheads, the United States’ at 5,042 and China’s at 620.

SIPRI’s latest figures put the global total at around 12,187 warheads as of January 2026, with Russia and the United States accounting for the large majority of those in military stockpiles. The institute counts 9,745 warheads in military stockpiles worldwide and 4,012 deployed with missiles and aircraft.

Trump’s comments come months after the New START treaty expired on February 5, 2026.

The 2010 agreement, which limited strategic nuclear weapons between the United States and Russia, had been extended once for five years under former president Joe Biden and Putin. It capped each side at 1,550 deployed strategic warheads and 700 deployed missiles and bombers.

No further formal extension was possible.

Russia has said it will continue to observe the treaty’s numerical limits as long as the United States does the same, while Trump previously indicated he preferred a new agreement rather than a simple extension and has long expressed interest in involving China in arms-control discussions.

Putin made that offer on September 22, 2025 and Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the Russian parliament on February 11 that Moscow was abiding by the ceilings. On the day the treaty lapsed Trump said Washington would seek a “modernized Treaty” lasting well into the future.

No detailed timetable or formal proposals have been made public. China has previously resisted trilateral arms-control talks on the grounds that its arsenal remains substantially smaller than those of the United States and Russia. Its disarmament ambassador, Shen Jian, said on February 6 that Beijing would not join nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage.

The exchanges follow Trump’s instruction to the Department of War, issued on October 30, 2025, to begin testing nuclear weapons “on an equal basis” with Russia and China. The United States has not carried out an explosive nuclear test since 1992.

**With trades**
- **sports-v1:** buys underdogs priced 5¢ to 20¢ late in games (basketball Q4 or OT within about 6 minutes and 10 points, soccer after the 65th minute within 1 goal, plus football, hockey and baseball rules). It sells at 2x, with no stop-loss. Max 2 open at a time.
- **sports-v2:** the same entries for basketball only. It holds to the final result with no cash-out.
- **btc-v1:** bets on BTC 15-minute and 1-hour up/down windows when its model sees at least a 7¢ edge, with 30 seconds to 7.5 minutes left. Since Oct 16 it only buys at 60¢ to 90¢. It holds to settlement.
- **mm:** a market maker on the top 40 US markets with mids of 20¢ to 80¢. It posts bids and offers, takes at most $20 of inventory per market, and closes positions after an hour.
- **updown_mm:** a market maker on 15-minute BTC up/down windows. It quotes 2.5¢ either side of its fair price and pulls quotes in the last 25 seconds. Since Oct 16 it only quotes prices of 50¢ to 95¢.
- **sports_maker:** a maker on live two-team moneylines.
- **weather:** bets on US daily temperature markets (NYC, Chicago, Miami, Philadelphia, LA, SF) when its forecast model shows an edge of at least 8¢.
- **mm (Kalshi):** the same market-making idea on Kalshi. It's being paused with the new guard.
- **weather (Kalshi):** the same weather model on Kalshi.

**Why three have 0 trades on Day 6**
- **btc-v2:** it only bets in the last 5 to 30 seconds of a window, at asks of 85¢ to 98¢. By then the likely winner usually has no asks, only bids, so there's nothing to buy. Only 5 of 82 past windows had one.
- **longshot:** it only buys outcomes priced 8¢ or less, on markets ending within 14 days with at least $5,000 volume. I'd guess very few US markets pass all three, but I haven't confirmed that.
- **crypto_range:** it needs a 98.5% or higher chance on BTC above/below markets that end in 15 minutes to 36 hours, bids of 95¢ to 99¢, and a 1¢ edge. That's very rare.

text:
There is something revealing about the argument that keeping Nasir El-Rufai in detention could weaken the African Democratic Congress. It raises a fundamental question about the relationship between political power, individual liberty and the strength of democratic institutions.

Hon. Bello El-Rufai has offered a striking explanation of what he believes is driving the political controversy surrounding his father.

“There’s this fear about Mal. Nasir El-Rufai, because even his enemies will never say he’s not intelligent, he’s hardworking, he’s bold, he’s fearless.”

Bello further suggests that some political actors believe keeping El-Rufai detained would prevent the ADC from functioning effectively.

That is a serious allegation. It deserves examination, not automatic acceptance.

Nasir El-Rufai is an experienced political figure who served as Minister of the Federal Capital Territory and Governor of Kaduna State. His years in public office have made him a prominent and often controversial participant in Nigeria's political debates.

His supporters admire what they describe as his administrative discipline, willingness to take difficult decisions and readiness to confront powerful interests.

His critics have also raised important questions about aspects of his record in government. Both perspectives belong in any serious assessment of his political legacy.

But the immediate issue is bigger than whether Nigerians admire or oppose El-Rufai.

No political figure should be detained merely because of their influence, political associations or capacity to challenge an incumbent administration.

Equally, political prominence must never confer immunity from legitimate investigation or prosecution.

The distinction is essential.

Where criminal allegations exist, investigators must act within the law, disclose the applicable grounds for detention and respect judicial oversight. The accused must have a meaningful opportunity to challenge the allegations and defend themselves.

Where allegations of political interference arise, they should be examined through credible evidence rather than speculation.

The ADC, like every opposition party, must be free to organise, recruit members, develop policies and compete in elections without unlawful obstruction.

Its institutional strength should also depend on more than one personality.

Bello El-Rufai's remarks therefore raise questions worth asking: What are the legal grounds for his father's continued detention? Have applicable court orders been respected? And what evidence, if any, supports the allegation that detention is being used to undermine opposition activity?

These questions deserve clear, verifiable answers.

Nigeria's democracy is strengthened when political competition remains open, criminal justice remains independent and citizens can distinguish legitimate law enforcement from political persecution.

The test is not whether El-Rufai is feared, admired or criticised. It is whether the same constitutional protections apply to him as to every other Nigerian. https://t.co/B5SnNN7GkI

text:
In December 2016, Northshore Kalo LLC—a shell company controlled by Mark Zuckerberg—filed eight "quiet title" lawsuits concerning 14 *kuleana* parcels (small plots of land granted to Native Hawaiians in the mid-19th century) located within his 700-acre estate on the north shore of Kauai, Hawaii. The lawsuits sought to have the court confirm ownership and mandate a forced sale of the land. In January 2017, following intense public backlash, Zuckerberg published an op-ed in *The Garden Island* newspaper announcing the withdrawal of the lawsuits, acknowledging, "We made a mistake."

Verified Facts
Regarding the "$800" inquiry: One woman named in the lawsuits recounted to BBC Mundo that when a lawyer for Northshore Kalo first contacted her, they asked: "How would it feel to receive $800 for a piece of land you didn't even know you owned?" At the time, she assumed the buyer was a taro farm—as "kalo" means "taro" in the Hawaiian language. Upon learning from news reports that the buyer was actually Zuckerberg, she canceled the transaction.

Testimony of Shannon Buckner: According to a sworn declaration submitted to the court in 2019, Buckner—who held a 0.026% interest in one of the parcels—was contacted multiple times by a lawyer for Northshore Kalo in January 2017. The lawyer asked her, "How would you feel about receiving money for a piece of land you never knew you owned?" The lawyer initially offered $400, later increasing it to $500, while warning that she would face "hundreds of thousands of dollars in legal fees" if she refused to sell. In her testimony, Buckner stated that the lawyer claimed Northshore Kalo was a "locally owned taro farm," but later admitted that he had been "instructed not to disclose the true identity of the buyer."

Testimony of Teri Ferreira-Ige: In a sworn declaration, she further alleged that Northshore Kalo’s attorneys “misrepresented the ownership and nature of the company” and threatened her with a “long and expensive legal process,” as well as decades of unpaid property taxes on the land.

Zuckerberg’s apology and the withdrawal of his lawsuit. On January 26, 2017, Zuckerberg published an op-ed in *The Garden Island* newspaper, writing: “Upon reflection, I regret that I did not take the time to fully understand the ‘quiet title’ process and its history before moving forward. Now that I have a better understanding of these issues, it is clear that we made a mistake.” He pledged to “engage with the community to find a better path forward.” Hawaii State Representative Kaniela Ing hailed this as “a victory,” noting that “it’s not every day that you can go up against one of the world’s most influential billionaires—backed by top-tier PR and legal teams—and come out on top.”

The situation following the withdrawal. While Zuckerberg dropped his own lawsuit, he continued to support a “quiet title” action initiated by retired professor Carlos Andrade regarding his family’s parcels. In 2019, a judge ordered a public auction for these lands. Descendants of the Rapoza family—including Shannon Buckner—continued to resist, though they acknowledged that their chances of success were “slim to none.” Buckner stated, “This belonged to a grandfather I never knew; I don’t want it to disappear. I want my children to be able to enjoy it. Even if we lose, I will fight to the very end.”

The core facts are as follows: Zuckerberg’s shell company, operating under the guise of a “taro farm,” reached out to the descendants of Native Hawaiians—asking how they felt about the prospect of selling off land they hadn’t even realized they owned—before filing lawsuits to force a public auction. Under public pressure, Zuckerberg withdrew his own suit and issued an apology; however, he continued to back others in pursuing the same “quiet title” process, which ultimately led to a public auction. Even though Teri Ferreira-Ige declared, “I wouldn’t accept $100,000 from him,” her stance proved insufficient to prevent the transfer of the land through the auction process. #TheWorldCorrespondent #Zuckerberg #Kauai #Hawaii #Kuleana #LandRights #QuietTitle

text:
My time in Hawaii has been instructive and compelled a schizo-rant.

The Big Island offers genuine landscape variety and a population that behaves like other American communities. Oahu does not. It has absorbed a disproportionate share of mainland chronic homelessness through deliberate transfers from Democratic jurisdictions seeking to reduce their own visible burdens. California and New York have externalized the costs of their housing and social policies onto Hawaii. Presented as humanitarian, the arrangement is a fiscal and social subsidy that preserves those states’ political viability at Hawaii’s expense.

Native Hawaiians occupy a peculiar position. Claims of historical dispossession are routinely advanced, yet outcomes do not support the narrative of systemic exclusion. Substantial fractions receive means-tested assistance, and ancestry-based preferences operate in education and certain land and program rules. These preferences have not produced competitive results; they have coincided with persistent underperformance relative to other groups. An attitude of entitlement toward non-natives is nevertheless widespread. Preferential treatment, high transfer dependency, and middling achievements are difficult to reconcile with the rhetoric of grievance.

Day-to-day economic activity is sustained largely by labor from the Philippines and Japan. English proficiency is frequently limited to basic transactional vocabulary, raising coordination costs. Parallel to this has been a deliberate revival of the Hawaiian language in official signage, advertising, and institutional branding. The practical effect reduces the functional domain of English and aligns with foreign commercial actors who benefit from a population less fully integrated into U.S. norms.

The treasonous slogan “Hawaiian lands in Hawaiian hands” illustrates the point. Advanced by networks that include Japanese commercial interests and Southeast Asian intermediaries, it demands that ancestry supersede title rather than calling for ordinary market transactions or enforcement of existing property rights. The logic is familiar from jurisdictions where political majorities have subordinated private property to ethnic claims. South Africa and Zimbabwe supply recent examples in which such rhetoric preceded measurable declines in investment and institutional reliability. In Hawaii the same principle threatens ordinary expectations of ownership.

Labor preferences reinforce the pattern. Non-military white workers are steered toward the outer islands, while Oahu opportunities are allocated preferentially to Filipino and Japanese workers whose qualifications are often lower than available domestic alternatives. Some lack lawful status. Ancestry and foreign origin function as positive selection criteria; American citizenship and English fluency do not.

A concrete manifestation appears in state vehicle procurement. Across more than thirty other states, government fleets rely predominantly on American nameplates. Assembly in Mexico does not erase that Ford, Chevrolet, and Ram are American firms. Hawaii is the exception. Procurement documents repeatedly designate Toyota models as the primary specification, with “or equivalent” language that functions more as formality than open competition. American vehicles are typically available at lower cost, yet the state systematically bypasses them. Taxpayer resources are directed toward a Japanese manufacturer rather than American producers. The practice extends the same preference for foreign economic partners visible in labor policy and land rhetoric.

Taken together, preferential treatment by ancestry, importation of dependent populations, linguistic fragmentation, selective labor recruitment, and procurement bias toward a foreign automaker weaken ordinary expectations of equal citizenship, private property, and economic reciprocity. Outcomes are measurable in dependency rates, language barriers, and the destination of public funds.
