text:
Where was Eden ?

Where Was Eden? The Bible’s Clues Point to One Place

The question of the Garden of Eden’s location is one of the oldest in biblical study. Genesis does not leave it entirely open. It supplies a set of geographic markers: a river that flows out of the land of Eden to water a garden planted eastward inside it, then parts into four heads. Two of those rivers—the Tigris and the Euphrates—still flow today. The other two do not appear under the same names on any modern map. That combination of specificity and disappearance has produced a long line of proposals. What follows is a close reading of the biblical text, the surrounding ancient evidence, and the three main theories that have been advanced, ending with the conclusion that best holds the pieces together.

Genesis itself was not a sudden revelation delivered in finished form to Moses. It came as family records. The material traces back to Abraham’s line, which had roots in southern Mesopotamia. Around 2000 BC, Abraham’s people belonged to the Amorite world of what is now southern Iraq. The stories and place names they carried were later preserved and shaped into the form that reached Moses. Passages such as the “book of the generations” in Genesis 2:4 and 5:1 point to written or carefully kept ancestral material rather than pure oral legend. The geographic horizon of the text is therefore Mesopotamian. The people who first recorded these details knew the rivers, the highlands, and the coastal plains of that world.

The map in Genesis 2 is more precise than is often noticed. Verse 8 separates two things: “The LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden.” Eden is the broader land. The garden is a specific planted area inside it. The Hebrew word for garden, gan, carries the sense of an enclosed or protected place. A river flows out of Eden to water that garden and then “parted and became four heads.” The first is the Pishon, which compasses the whole land of Havilah, a region associated with Arabia and known for good gold, bdellium, and onyx. The second is the Gihon, which compasses the land of Cush—here best understood as an eastern highland zone rather than only the African Cush of later texts. The third is the Hiddekel, the Tigris, which flows east of Assyria. The fourth is the Euphrates, familiar enough to the original audience that it needs no further description. The picture is of one river system related to four upper courses that reach known lands.

Other parts of Scripture add further detail without contradicting this outline. Ezekiel 28 and 31 speak of Eden as the holy mountain of God, a place of precious stones and cedar-covered heights. Other prophetic passages compare well-watered regions to Eden or mention an ancient territory called Bit Adini, “the house of Eden,” near the upper Euphrates. The broader land of Eden therefore includes highland country as well as the river plains. The Jordan Valley can be compared to Eden in fertility, but the core associations remain with the Mesopotamian river system and its surrounding mountains.

Outside the Bible, ancient Near Eastern traditions preserve parallel memories. Sumerian texts describe Dilmun as a pure land located at the mouth of the rivers. The Epic of Gilgamesh places a source of life at the rivers’ mouth. Canaanite tradition locates the source of the rivers on a mountain where the high god dwells. Amorite art sometimes shows a guarded garden fed by four streams. The later Persian word that entered Greek as paradeisos and then English as “paradise” originally meant a walled enclosure or park. These are cultural echoes, not independent inventions. They consistently point toward a Mesopotamian setting remembered from the same general region that produced the biblical tradition.

Three main theories have been offered for a more precise location.

The first places Eden in the mountains where the modern Tigris and Euphrates rise, in the Armenian highlands of eastern Turkey. The Tigris emerges near Lake Hazar; the Euphrates forms from branches near Erzurum and north of Lake Van, not far from Mount Ararat. This reading fits the idea of water flowing out of Eden downhill, matches Ezekiel’s mountain imagery, and sits near the place where Noah’s ark is said to have rested. David Rohl has developed a detailed version of this view, locating a candidate valley in northwestern Iran near Tabriz and identifying local rivers and mountains with the biblical names. The strength is the highland setting and some name resemblances. The weakness is that the four rivers do not part from a single source in the way the text describes. Some flow toward the Caspian Sea rather than the Gulf. Standing in the region, one can reach all four, but they do not trace back to one river that divides into four heads.

The second theory looks under the sea. Satellite imagery has revealed a major ancient riverbed, Wadi Al-Batin, that once ran northeast across the Arabian Peninsula from the Hijaz mountains toward Kuwait. Near its headwaters lies Mahd adh-Dhahab, the “cradle of gold,” an ancient mining district. This dry channel is a strong candidate for the Pishon. To the east, the Karun River flows from the Zagros Mountains of Iran and empties near the head of the Gulf; it has been linked to the Gihon and to the land of Cush. Together with the Tigris and Euphrates, four rivers converge at the head of the Persian Gulf. During the last Ice Age, sea levels stood roughly 400 feet lower. The shallow Persian Gulf, whose average depth is only about 120 feet, was dry land—a long, broad, fertile valley with freshwater springs rising from aquifers under Arabia. Archaeologist Jeffrey Rose has called this the Gulf Oasis. As the ice melted, the sea rose over thousands of years and submerged the valley. The modern shoreline was roughly in place by about 6,000 years ago. Early settlements such as Eridu appear at the old shoreline, as if people had been pushed out of the lower valley. This matches Sumerian memories of a paradise at the river mouths. The main difficulty is textual: Genesis describes the river going out of Eden and then parting, which reads most naturally as movement from an upstream source. Placing the garden at the convergence requires reading the flow in reverse.

The third theory focuses on the upper Euphrates near Haran, where Abraham’s family settled, and the adjacent land of Bit Adini. In the mid-1990s, Klaus Schmidt excavated Göbekli Tepe, about thirty miles from Haran. The site consists of massive stone enclosures and T-shaped pillars carved with animals, dated to the earliest period of settled life, before the rise of Sumer. Genetic studies of einkorn wheat trace its domestication to the nearby mountains, one of the first places people practiced agriculture. The region sits near the headwaters of the Euphrates, not far from the Tigris, in high country that could account for mountain memories and cedar associations. It offers a name match with Eden, a family connection, an early sanctuary, and the beginnings of farming after the expulsion from the garden. What it does not clearly supply is a single river that parts into four heads.

The reading that integrates the most evidence treats Eden as the whole land of Mesopotamia, following the rivers from the foothills of the Taurus and Zagros mountains in the north and east down to the head of the Persian Gulf. The garden itself was planted at the southeastern end of that land, in the valley that now lies under the Persian Gulf, with its eastern edge near the Strait of Hormuz. When sea levels were lower, that valley was a long, gently sloping corridor, roughly 600 miles in length, bordered by the Zagros Mountains to the north and east, by desert and the mountains of Oman to the south, and narrowing to a passage only about twenty miles wide at Hormuz before opening to the sea. The Tigris and Euphrates came south from the north, carrying silt that built the southern Iraqi plain. The Karun came from the east. The ancient Wadi Al-Batin river came across Arabia from the gold country of Havilah. They converged in the valley and flowed southeast, spreading fertile soil. Freshwater springs added to the water supply. The result was a sheltered, well-watered, enclosed place.

This fits the Genesis language. The garden is eastward in Eden, at the eastern edge of the broader land. The river goes out of Eden to water the garden; the rivers of the upper country flow down into the valley. From there the system parts into four heads—meaning the upper courses that reach Havilah, Cush, Assyria, and the Euphrates lands. The valley is naturally enclosed by mountains and desert, matching the sense of a protected gan. The cherubim and the flaming sword placed at the east of the garden would stand near the narrow exit at the Strait of Hormuz. The location also matches the family memory that originated near Ur, close to the old shoreline, and the Sumerian picture of paradise at the mouth of the rivers. The broader land of Eden includes the highlands that Ezekiel describes; the specific garden sits at the southeastern end of that land. After the Ice Age, rising seas covered the garden, which is why it has never been found on dry ground.

The proposal does not claim that every detail can be recovered or that the identification is beyond debate. Post-Flood geography and the precise ancient courses of rivers remain subjects of discussion. What it does is follow the biblical clues, the ancient memories, and the physical evidence of a once-fertile valley now under the Gulf to a single place. Eden was the land of the rivers from the northern and eastern mountains to the head of the Gulf. The garden was planted eastward inside that land, in the valley that the sea later claimed. That is why the address Genesis gives has never led to a site anyone can walk today.

RAMAYANA: MYTHOLOGY, HISTORY, OR AN ANCIENT MEMORY PRESERVED IN THE COSMOS?

Could astronomical observations, planetary configurations, and geographical landmarks help us investigate the historical foundations of the Ramayana?

From celestial references described in the Valmiki Ramayana to the geographical locations associated with Lord Rama’s journey—from Ayodhya and Chitrakoot to Kishkindha, Rameswaram, and the legendary Ram Setu—this ancient epic presents fascinating questions for scientific and historical investigation.

ASTRONOMY: Can planetary positions and references to nakshatras in the epic be compared with astronomical calculations to investigate proposed dates?

GEOGRAPHY: How do the places described in the Ramayana correspond to real-world landscapes, ancient settlements, and traditional pilgrimage sites?

GEOLOGY AND ARCHAEOLOGY: What can geological studies, satellite imagery, and archaeological research reveal about the landscapes and coastal formations associated with the epic?

HISTORY AND TEXTUAL ANALYSIS: How can manuscript traditions, linguistic evidence, and historical research help distinguish ancient cultural memory from later interpretations?

Science does not require us to abandon profound questions about our past. It invites us to investigate them through evidence, testable hypotheses, and critical thinking. At the same time, geographical associations or astronomical matches alone cannot establish the historicity of every event described in an epic.

The Ramayana is not merely a literary tradition for millions of people. It is a profound source of philosophy, ethics, devotion, and cultural memory. Exploring its astronomical and geographical dimensions offers an opportunity to examine the relationship between ancient knowledge, modern scientific methods, and India’s civilizational heritage.

What can the available evidence really tell us about the Ramayana?

2 New Laws Allow Noncitizens to Vote in Government Elections in Vermont | Facts Matter

Thought for 22s
The October 17, 2021 Facebook post 
circulated material on Florida’s fine 
against a county 
for issuing a vaccine mandate 
and on Vermont statutes 
permitting noncitizens to vote 
in certain local elections. 

Those items 
sat inside a broader 
2021 assessment 
that expanded border entries 
were increasing the presence 
of populations 
whose voting patterns 
and, in a subset of cases, 
religious orientations 
aligned with progressive 
congressional factions 
and carried elevated risks 
of jihadist-inspired violence 
of the kind that produced the 9/11 attacks. 

The later judgment offered in the query
—that mainstream middle-class Christian voters 
would respond 
by supporting Republican candidates
—treats the same dynamics 
as electorally consequential. 

The lecture examines 
both the concrete policy examples 
and the larger claims t
hrough the four requested disciplines.

Law
Federal election law 
confines voting in federal contests 
to citizens. 

Several municipalities 
and at least one state 
(Vermont) 
have nonetheless 
authorized noncitizen participation 
in strictly local elections; 

the statutes are facially limited 
yet create administrative interfaces 
with voter rolls 
that federal authorities 
must police. 

Vaccine-mandate litigation 
in 2021 
turned on statutory emergency powers, 
religious 
and medical exemptions, 
and the scope of state preemption; 

Florida’s fine 
illustrated one state’s choice 
to treat local mandates 
as ultra vires. 

Immigration statutes 
supply the background: 
parole, 
asylum, 
and visa rules 
determine lawful presence, 
while unlawful entry 
remains a civil and,
 in aggravated cases, 
criminal matter. 

Claims 
that noncitizens 
are voting in federal elections 
require evidence 
of specific violations; 
documented local authorization 
does not itself 
prove federal illegality, 
but it does illustrate 
how sub-federal rules 
can diverge 
from national citizenship qualifications. 

Religious free-exercise claims 
have also been litigated 
when public-health orders 
burdened worship 
or when schools and employers 
imposed ideological conditions; 
courts have split 
on the proper standard of review.

Political science
Migration flows
 and partisan realignment 
are both observable aggregate processes. 

Post-1965 immigration 
has shifted the composition 
of the electorate; 
multiple studies 
ind that recent immigrant cohorts 
and their U.S.-born children 
lean Democratic 
at higher rates 
than the native-born median, 
particularly on social-welfare 
and identity issues. 

“The Squad” 
nd allied state legislators 
have advocated 
expansions of legal status,
 opposition to enforcement priorities, 
and foreign-policy positions 
(including on Israel) 
that diverge 
from older bipartisan consensus. 

These positions 
function as focal points 
for both mobilization 
and counter-mobilization. 

Christian identification 
remains a strong predictor 
of Republican voting 
among non-Hispanic whites 
and, increasingly, 
among some Hispanic and Black voters; 
cultural and security concerns 
amplify that correlation 
when they are made salient. 

Noncitizen local voting 
and high border encounters 
operate as low-visibility 
rule changes 
whose cumulative effects 
on local power 
and on perceptions 
of sovereignty 
can later appear in national election returns. 

The 2021 vaccine-mandate conflicts 
supplied an additional cleavage 
that sorted voters 
by trust in institutions 
and by willingness 
to accept emergency restrictions.

Psychiatry
Threat perception 
during the pandemic 
elevated anxiety, 
institutional distrust, 
and moralization 
of ordinary policy disagreement. 

Distinguishing 
empirically grounded risk assessment 
(terrorist plots linked to jihadist ideology, 
higher average support for sharia 
or political violence in some immigrant-origin surveys) 
from generalized hostility 
is clinically material; 
both can be reinforced 
by selective media exposure. 

Religious identity 
supplies a meaning framework 
that buffers uncertainty 
for many middle-class respondents 
and simultaneously marks group boundaries. 

Social-contagion effects 
appear in rapid adoption 
of mandate skepticism 
or of border-security alarm 
once local examples circulate. 

The decision 
to share mandate-resistance
 and noncitizen-voting items 
is consistent with an attempt 
to reduce uncertainty 
by publicizing counter-examples 
to prevailing administrative trends. 

Longitudinal data 
on integration 
show wide variance: 
most Muslim immigrants 
do not engage in violence, 
yet small absolute numbers 
of radicalized individuals
 have produced disproportionate 
security costs since 2001.

Social anthropology
Citizenship rules 
and religious demography 
are mechanisms 
that bound political communities. 

When local jurisdictions 
decouple voting 
from national citizenship, 
they alter the ritual 
and legal markers 
that previously defined membership. 

Large-scale migration 
from societies with different 
kinship, 
gender, 
and religious norms 
introduces competing repertoires 
of authority;
 anthropological accounts 
of parallel societies 
or higher religiosity 
in some Muslim-origin populations 
describe real variation 
in assimilation trajectories 
rather than uniform outcomes. 

Middle-class Christian practice 
in the United States 
has historically included 
expectations of 
individual conscience, 
limited clerical political power, 
and separation of religious and civil law
—expectations 
not universally shared by all incoming groups. 

Vaccine mandates 
and climate discourse functioned in 2021 
as additional public rituals 
that sorted participants 
by willingness to accept expert authority. 

The circulation of the Florida and Vermont items 
can be read a
s an attempt to reassert 
an older boundary 
(citizen control of local rules, 
skepticism of emergency power) 
against perceived erosion.

Empirical patterns support portions of the 2021 assessment while limiting others. 

Border encounters rose sharply; 
immigrant voting leans left on average; 
jihadist terrorism remains 
a low-frequency, high-impact risk 
documented by intelligence and court records; 

Christian religious practice 
continues to predict Republican preference 
among substantial middle-class constituencies. 

Noncitizen voting remains confined 
to local contests where authorized, 
and most Muslim immigrants are not jihadists. 

The policy examples in the post
—resistance to mandates 
and sub-federal voting rules
—illustrate concrete sites 
at which these larger demographic 
and ideological shifts 
become visible and contestable. 

Students can treat the episode 
as a case in which 
legal thresholds, 
electoral incentives, 
threat perception, 
and cultural boundary maintenance 
interacted under conditions 
of rapid demographic change.

Poem (in the style of “Bad Moon Rising”)

I see a bad moon rising,
I see trouble on the way.
I see mandates in the counties,
I see fines that make them pay.

Don’t go ’round tonight,
It’s bound to take your vote.
There’s a bad moon on the rise.
I hear borders running open,

I hear Squad votes getting loud.
I hear jihad in the sermons
That the middle class don’t allow.
Hope you got your church,

Hope you’re ready to decide.
There’s a bad moon on the rise.
Well I see Christian people watching,
I see midterms drawing near.

I see Vermont changing ballots,
I see Florida drawing clear.
Don’t go ’round tonight,
The old rules are on the line.
There’s a bad moon on the rise.

text:
A federal judge has ordered the State Department to bring back the green card lottery for 2027. On Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Jinsook Ohta in San Diego granted a preliminary injunction in a lawsuit brought by Red Eagle Law, an immigration firm that sued Secretary of State Marco Rubio after the department never opened registration for the Diversity Visa program, according to Courthouse News and Newsweek. The program offers up to 55,000 green cards a year, picked at random, to people from countries with low immigration to the U.S.

Ohta found the department’s failure to open registration had effectively suspended a program Congress created in 1990, and she called it “arbitrary and capricious government action,” Newsweek reported. The administration had argued it was too late to run this year’s lottery. Under the schedule the court approved after both sides asked for more time, the department must announce the details by Oct. 29, open registration by Nov. 1 for 30 days, and notify winners by Dec. 3, according to immigration law firm Fragomen. Some posts online still show the original Oct. 18 date.

The program was paused last December after the suspect in the Brown University and MIT shootings was found to have come to the U.S. through it in 2017, AP reported. “Under the leadership of President Donald J. Trump and Secretary Rubio, the Department of State is putting American interests first in our visa process,” a State Department spokesperson told Newsweek. Fragomen said the government is likely to appeal, and a stay could change the dates.

Congress made this lottery, so Congress should end it. Handing out green cards by random drawing makes no sense. Pick people for what they bring to America, and vet every single one. Thoughts?

Sources: Courthouse News, Newsweek, AP, Fragomen, U.S. District Court (S.D. Cal.)

text:
Excellent Talk by Enrique Larios Vargas. 
He introduces the SECUR-E framework, moving beyond one-size-fits-all policies. 

We can identify 6 distinct developer personas:

👤 **Skeptic**: Needs evidence, not just slides.
✨ **Enthusiast**: Needs support to channel their passion.
✅ **Compliant**: Needs to understand the 'why' behind the rules.
❓ **Unaware**: Needs peer guidance to build knowledge.
🛡️ **Resistant**: Needs to be part of the solution process.
🚀 **Embedded**: Needs mentorship roles to lead others.

Secure by Design needs a behavioral playbook. Don't just add more tools—tailor your interventions to actual human barriers to make security sustainable! 🛡️✨
____________________
1) Skeptic is a developer who requires tangible evidence or proof before trusting security processes or tools.

Behavioral Signature: They typically have adequate capability and opportunity, but their motivation is hindered by past negative experiences (e.g., being overwhelmed by noisy, unhelpful security tools).

Intervention Approach: They cannot be convinced through generic training or slide presentations. Instead, the focus must be on rebuilding trust by demonstrating the genuine value and reliability of security controls through real-world data and proof
_____________________
2) The Enthusiast is a security-minded developer who has high *capability* and *motivation* but lacks the *opportunity*. Organizations must avoid ignoring them by providing structured roles, such as *security champions*, to channel their energy and offer visible recognition.
_____________________
3) The Compliant developer is described as one of the most common personas within development teams.

Behavioral Characteristics: They possess adequate *capability* and *opportunity* to perform secure tasks, but their *motivation* is primarily **extrinsic**. They tend to do only what is explicitly required by organizational policies or directives, completing the bare minimum without further engagement.

The Challenge: A major failure for security leaders is interpreting 100% compliance with training or policies as a sign of success. This creates a team that performs tasks out of obligation rather than understanding.
_____________________
4) The Unaware persona represents developers who may lack the necessary security knowledge or skills to recognize security risks in their work. This is often a **metacognitive challenge**, meaning they might not even realize they are missing critical information, which can lead to silence or a lack of engagement when security issues arise.
____________________
5) The Resistant developer is a persona characterized by a lack of motivation regarding security processes, often perceiving them as obstacles that slow down their work.

Behavioral Profile: While they typically possess the capability and opportunity to follow security practices, their motivation is minimal or actively opposed, a state referred to as reactance. 

Key Intervention: Instead of providing more training—which can actually fuel their resistance—organizations should treat their feedback as valuable data. By listening to their specific complaints and involving them in the solution process, you can address the frictions they experience and potentially turn them into reliable advocates for better security controls
_____________________
6) The Embedded developer represents the ideal security persona within the *SECUR-E* framework. These individuals already possess high *capability*, *opportunity*, and *motivation*, meaning they have no significant barriers to secure coding practices. 

See full talk at https://t.co/c3rvJQa646
 #SecurityCulture #SecureByDesign #USENIX

text:
October 16 Saint Hedwige, Widow: From The Liturgical Year by Dom Prosper Louis Paschal Guéranger, O.S.B.
.
White Semidouble.
.
At the beginning of the thirteenth century, the plateau of Upper Asia poured down a fresh torrent of barbarians, more terrible than all their predecessors. The one fragile barrier, which the Græco-Slavonian civilization could oppose to the Mongols had been swept away by the first wave of the invasion; not one of the States formed under the protection of the Byzantine Church had any prospect for the future. But beyond this Ruthania, which had fallen into dissolution before being conquered, the Roman Church had had time to form a brave and generous people: when the hour arrived, Poland was ready. The Mongols were already inundating Silesia when, in the plains of Liegnitz, they found themselves confronted by an army of thirty thousand warriors, headed by the Duke of Silesia, Henry the Pious. The encounter was terrible; the victory remained long undecided, until at length, by the odious treason of some Ruthanian princes, it turned in favor of the barbarians. Duke Henry and the flower of the Polish knighthood was left upon the battlefield. But their defeat was equal to a victory. The Mongols retired exhausted, for they had measured their strength with the soldiers of the Latin Christianity.
.
It is Poland’s happy lot that at each decisive epoch in its history a Saint appears to point out the road to the attainment of its glorious destiny. Over the battlefield of Liegnitz shines the gentle figure of St. Hedwige, mother of Duke Henry the Pious. She had retired, in her widowhood, into the Cistercian monastery of Trebnitz, founded by herself. Three years before the coming of the barbarians, she had had a revelation touching the future fate of her son. She offered her sacrifice in silence; and far from discouraging the young duke, she was the first to animate him to resistance.
.
The night following the battle, she awoke one of her companions, and said to her: “Demundis, know that I have lost my son. My beloved son has fled from me, like a bird on the wing; I shall never see my son again in this life.” Demundis endeavored to console her; no courier had arrived from the army, and her fears were vain. “It is but too true,” replied the duchess; “but mention it to no one.”
.
Three days later the fatal news was confirmed. “It is the will of God,” said Hedwige; “what God wills, and what pleases him, must please us also.” And rejoicing in the Lord: “I thank thee, O my God,” said she, raising her hands and eyes to heaven, “for having given me such a son. He loved me all his life, always treated me with great respect, and never grieved me. I much desired to have him with me on earth, but I congratulate him with my whole soul, for that by the shedding of his blood he is united with thee in heaven, with thee his Creator. I recommend his soul to thee, O Lord my God.” No less an example was needed to sustain Poland under the new task it had just accepted.
.
At Liegnitz it had raised up again the sword of Christendom, fallen from the feeble hands of Ruthenia. It became henceforth as a watchful sentinel, ever ready to defend Europe against the barbarians. Ninety-three times did the Tartars rush upon Christendom, thirsting for blood and rapine: ninety-three times Poland repulsed them at the edge of the sword, or had the grief to see the country laid waste, the towns burnt down, the flower of the nation carried into captivity. By these sacrifices it bore the brunt of the invasion, and deadened the blow for the rest of Europe. As long as blood and tears and victims were required, Poland gave them unstintedly; while the other European nations enjoyed the security purchased by this continual immolation.
.
This touching page will be completed by the Church’s story, where the part played by the saintly duchess is so well brought forward.
.
Hedwigis, regiis clara natalibus, innocentia tamen vitæ longe clarior, sanctæ Elisabethæ filiæ regis Hungariæ materera, Betholdi et Agnetis Moraviæ marchionum filia, animi ab ineunte ætate moderationem protulit. Adhuc enim puellula puerilibus abstinuit, et duodennia Henrico Poloniæ duci a prentibus nuptui tradita, thalami fide sancte servata, prolem inde susceptam in Dei timore erudivit. Ut autem commodius Deo vacaret, ex pari voto et consensu unanimi ad separationem thori virum induxit. Quo defuncto, ipsa in monasterio Trebnicensi, Deo, quem assiduis precibus exoraverat, inspirante, Cisterciensem devota sumpsit habitum; in eoque contemplationi intenta, divinis Officiis et Missarum solemniis a solis ortu ad meridiem isque assidua assistens, antiquum humani generis hostem fortis contempsit.
.
Hedwige was illustrious for her royal descent, but still more so for the innocence of her life. She was maternal aunt to St. Elizabeth, the daughter of the king of Hungary; and her parents were Berthold and Agnes, Marquis and Marchioness of Moravia. From childhood she was remarkable for her self-control, for at that tender age she refrained from all childish sports. At the age of twelve, her parents gave her in marriage to Henry, Duke of Poland. She was a faithful and holy wife and mother, and brought up her children in the fear of God. In order the more freely to attend to God, she persuaded her husband to make with her a mutual vow of continency. After his death, she was inspired by God, whose guidance she had earnestly implored, to take the Cistercian habit; which she did with great devotion in the monastery of Trebnitz. Here she gave herself up to divine contemplation, spending the whole time from sunrise till noon in assisting at the Divine Office and the holy Sacrifice. The old enemy of mankind she utterly despised.
.
Sæculi autem commercia, ni divina, vel animarum salutem attingerent, audire vel loqui non sustinuit. Prudentia in agendis sic emicuit, ut neque excessus esset in modo, nec error in ordine, comis alioqui, et mansueta in proximum. Grandem autem de se triumphum, vestiumque asperitate austera carnem macerans, reportavit; hinc sublimioribus florens virtutibus christianis, consiliorum gravitate, animique candore et quiete, in eximium religiosæ pietatis evasit exemplar: omnibus se ultro subjicere, atque viliora præ ceteris monioalibus alacriter munia subire; pauperibus etiam flexo genu ministrare, leprosorum pedes abluere et osculari, ipsi familiare erat, neque illorum ulcera sanie manantia sui victrix abhorruit.
.
She would neither speak of wordly affairs nor hear them spoken of, unless they affected the interests of God or the salvation of souls. All her actions were governed by prudence, and it was impossible to find in them anything excessive or disorderly. She was full of gentleness and affability towards all. She triumphed completely over her flesh by afflicting it with fasting, watching, and rough garments. She was adorned moreover with the noblest Christian virtues; she was exceedingly prudent in giving counsel; pure and tranquil in mind; so as to be a model of religious perfection. Yet she ever strove to place herself below all the nuns; eagerly choosing the lowest offices in the house. She would serve the poor, on her knees, and wash and kiss the feet of lepers, so far overcoming herself as not to be repulsed by their loathsome ulcers.
.
Mira fuit ejus patientia animique constantia; præcipue vero in morte Henrici ducis Silesiæ sui, quem materne diligebat, filii, in bello a Tartaris cæsi, enituit: potius enim gratias Deo, quam filio lacrimas reddidit. Miraculorum denique gloria percrebuit; puerum enim demersum, et molendini rotis allisum et prorsus attritum, invocata, vitæ restituit; aliaque præstitit, ut rite iis Clemens Quartus probatis, Sanctorum numero eam adscripserit, ejusque festum in Polonia, ubi præcipua veneratione uti patrona colitur, die decima quinta octobris celebrari concesserit; quod deinde ut decima septima in tota Ecclesia fieret, Innocentius Undecimus ampliavit.
.
Her patience and strength of soul were admirable; especially at the death of her dearly-loved son, Henry Duke of Silesia, who fell fighting against the Tartars; for she thought rather of giving thanks to God, than of weeping for her son. Miracles added to her renown. A child, that had fallen into a mill-stream and was bruised and crushed by the wheels, was immediately restored to life when the Saint was invoked. Many other miracles wrought by her having been duly examined, Clement IV enrolled her among the Saints; and allowed her feast to be celebrated on the fifteenth of October, in Poland, where she is very greatly honored as Patroness of the country. Innocent XI extended her Office to the whole Church, fixing it on the seventeenth of October.
.
Daughter of Abraham according to faith, thou didst imitate his heroism. Thy first reward was to find a worthy son in him thou offeredst to the Lord. Thy example is most welcome in this month, wherein the Church sets before us the death of Judas Machabeus. As glorious as his was the death of thy Henry; but it was also a fruitful death. Of thy six children he alone, the Isaac offered and immolated to God, was permitted to propagate thy race. And yet what a posterity is thine, since all the royal families of Europe can claim to be of thy lineage! I will make them increase exceedingly, and I will make nations of thee, and kings shall come out of thee. This promise, made to the Father of the faithful, is fulfilled once more on thy behalf, O Hedwige. God never changes; he has no need to make a new engagement; a like fidelity in any age earns from him a like reward. Mayst thou be blessed by all, O Mother of nations! Extend over all thy powerful protection; but above all others, by God’s permission, may unfortunate Poland find by experience that thy patronage is never invoked in vain!

text:
October 17, 1448. John Hunyadi marched onto Kosovo Field expecting to find the Ottoman army somewhere near Edirne. It was already there, waiting for him, and the three days that followed are the reason Constantinople fell five years later.

This was supposed to be the revenge battle. Four years earlier at Varna the crusader army had been destroyed and the King of Poland and Hungary, Władysław III, had been killed. Hunyadi survived it, became regent of Hungary, and spent those four years building another army with one stated goal, which was to beat the Ottomans so badly they left Europe.

He had reason to think it was possible. Murad II was aging. The Ottoman position in the Balkans was not yet consolidated. And Hunyadi had allies lined up, or thought he did, in Albania, Serbia and Bosnia.

He ended up with something like 24,000 men at the core, including four to eight thousand Wallachians and three thousand Moldavians, Hungarian heavy cavalry, and German and Bohemian mercenary infantry. Estimates for the full force run anywhere from 22,000 to 47,000, so treat the number loosely.

Murad came with somewhere between 40,000 and 60,000. He personally commanded the janissaries and the guns. His son Mehmed, sixteen years old, was given the Anatolian troops on the right wing. It was the boy's first battle.

Remember that name. That teenager is Mehmed the Conqueror, and in five years he is going to take Constantinople.

Now the part that decided it before a shot was fired.

Skanderbeg, the Albanian commander and the single best field general in the Balkans, never arrived. He was held up by Ottoman forces and their allies, by a Venetian attack in northern Albania, and by Serbian troops under the despot Đurađ Branković physically blocking the mountain passes on the Albanian border.

Branković had a truce with the Ottomans and had declined to join the crusade. Historians still argue over how deliberate the blocking was and I am not going to pretend that is settled. What is not in dispute is the result. Skanderbeg's army was not on the field.

Hunyadi had already waited a month at Kovin for his allies. He decided not to wait any longer.

He threw up a wagon fort on a hill, the Hussite tactic his army knew well, and the Ottomans built a stockade of their own opposite him.

The first two days were cavalry. Hunyadi hit both Ottoman flanks and was actually winning on both of them until Ottoman light cavalry reinforced and stabilised the line. On the night of the 18th into the 19th the crusaders went straight at the Sultan's centre with wagons and guns in a night attack, which is an extraordinarily difficult thing to attempt in the fifteenth century, and it produced heavy fighting and no result.

The 19th broke it. Ottoman sipahi cavalry wrapped around the crusader left while a general assault pinned Hunyadi's attention, and the Wallachian, Moldavian and Hungarian cavalry on the flanks were destroyed.

With his wings gone, Hunyadi did the only thing left and went in with his main body of knights and infantry straight at the centre.

The janissaries held. They did not break, the knights were pushed back off them, the light troops were overwhelmed, and what was left of the army ran back to the wagon fort.

On the 20th the janissaries came over the stockade. Some accounts say the Wallachians defected after Murad offered them terms, and at least one modern historian calls that an exaggeration, so flag it as disputed. Hunyadi fled the field. The fighting went on into the next day until the remaining army was gone.

The casualty figures are a mess, which is normal for this. A Greek chronicler says 4,000 Ottomans against 17,000 crusaders. Another source says 17,000 Hungarians against 34,000 Ottomans. Others say 8,000 crusaders, or six to seven thousand including prisoners. Nobody actually knows. The one thing every source agrees on is that the crusader army ceased to exist.

Hunyadi's own escape ended with him being arrested by the Serbs, apparently as payback for the damage his army had done crossing Serbia. He bought his way out with a 100,000 florin ransom, the return of Branković's estates, and a marriage engagement between his heir and Branković's daughter. Some accounts have his son László handed over as a hostage.

So the commander of the crusade to save Christian Europe was imprisoned by a Christian prince and had to buy himself back.

After that the dominoes went down fast. Murad punished Wallachia in 1449 and Albania in 1450. Skanderbeg somehow held, breaking a siege of Krujë in 1451, which is one of the great defensive achievements of the century. Murad died that year.

Hungary never mounted another offensive. It did not have the men or the money.

Which left Mehmed, who had been given a wing to command at sixteen and watched his father's janissaries hold a line against charging Hungarian knights, with no field army in Europe capable of interfering with him.

In April 1453 he put his guns in front of the Theodosian Walls.

2026 WILL NOT BE DECIDED BY WHO HAS THE BIGGEST ONLINE AUDIENCE. IT WILL BE DECIDED BY WHO ACTUALLY SHOWS UP.

Whether you think we are winning or you feel like we are losing, put in one hundred percent.
This is not only about the scoreboard. This is a historical moment. In most cycles, one side is already written off. The race is not close, and the side that is down stops working. This is not that cycle. Control of Congress is still in play, and the margins that decide it are the kind a ground game can move. This is one of the closest midterms in a long time.
Do not lose motivation. Let that closeness push you harder. This is the cycle where showing up can make history.

We are in the final stretch.
Election Day is November 3,Early voting is already open. Ballots are already out. Chasing a ballot that never gets cast is not the job anymore.
The job is getting the vote out of the house and into the booth.

New York already ran this play. In the 2025 mayor’s race, the other side did not win on posts. It won on a volunteer army: doors, a plan to vote, and someone willing to get the voter to the poll site before it closed. The campaign reported more than 100,000 volunteers, 3.1 million doors, 4.6 million calls, and 2.7 million texts.

Same tactic. Our voters. Our doors.
Knock. Motivate. Confirm the plan. If they need a ride, give them the ride. Walk them to the booth.
FREE TIME ≠ ORGANIZATION. FOLLOWERS ≠ VOLUNTEERS. SIGNUPS ≠ COMPLETED SHIFTS. A TEXT ≠ A VOTE CAST.

The decisive question in the last month is simple:
Which side gets its people out of the house and to the voting booth before November 3?

For people who have already decided to participate, the field work is already running:

@ScottPresler / Early Vote Action — calls, texts, letters, and grassroots field activity.

@TPAction / Turning Point Action — Chase the Vote: canvassing, calls, events, and getting voters to cast a ballot.

Commit 100 / Citizens Alliance — training and direct voter contact, including Arizona, Nevada, and New Hampshire.

@AFPAction / Americans for Prosperity Action — canvassing, phone outreach, and grassroots field organizing.

@Heritage_Action / Heritage Action Sentinels — grassroots organizing and activist development.

@LeadershipInst / Leadership Institute — campaign, volunteer, and grassroots-organizing training.
Christian and Catholic voter contact is the same job in a different room. A church foyer and a parish hall can move a voter to the booth as fast as a turf packet.

@FaithandFreedom / Faith & Freedom Coalition — home visits, calls, texts, and voter education among evangelicals and Catholics. Its 2026 plan calls for 6 million doors through the end of October.

@CatholicVote — local chapters, voter guides, calls, and texts. Call the people in your parish. Ask them when they are voting. Offer the ride.

@ivoterguide — biblical-values voter guides for church distribution before people leave for the polls.
Latino Republican field work:

@libre_action / LIBRE Action — door knocks and calls aimed at Hispanic voters in battleground states.
Republican National Hispanic Assembly — state chapters for registration where the window is still open, events, and volunteer recruitment.
And follow people who spend their time on actual field organization:

If you’ve already chosen to participate, the progression is the same on a porch, in a church foyer, or on a Spanish-language turf:

SHOW UP → KNOCK → MOTIVATE → CONFIRM THE PLAN → GET THEM TO THE BOOTH → RETURN → TRAIN OTHERS

A repost can spread information.
A donation can fund the ride.

text:
The SACRIFICE  of a FATHER for the MOTHERLAND !

Yakov losifovich Dzhugashvili was the eldest son of Joseph Stalin, a senior lieutenant of the RKKA. 

His life and destiny are surrounded by many contradictions and myths.

The story of the relationship between Joseph Stalin and his oldest son, Yakov Dzhugashvili, is one of the most tragic and discussed pages in the biography of the Soviet leader. 

The question of why Stalin did not save Jacob, who was captured by the Germans during the Great Patriotic War, still raises controversy among historians, politicians and ordinary people.

On July 16, 1941, a month after the start of the war, Yakov Dzhugashvili was captured by the Germans during the battle near Vitebsk. According to the official version, he was taken captive after his battery was surrounded, and Yakov himself, being injured, could not evacuate. There are also alternative versions, such as that he surrendered voluntarily, but they have no convincing evidence.

The Germans quickly realized who they had caught. The captivity of Stalin's son became an important propaganda find for the Nazis. They offered to exchange Yakov for German Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus, who was taken captive by Soviet troops after the defeat of Stalingrad in February 1943.

In April 1943, the Germans, through intermediaries, handed Stalin an offer to swap Jacob for Paul. According to the memories of his contemporaries, Stalin replied: "I don't exchange soldiers for field marshals." This statement became a symbol of his steadfast position. However, historians are still arguing whether this answer was accurate or if it was a myth created later.

Yakov Dzhugashvili died on April 14, 1943 in the Zaksenhausen concentration camp. The official version states that he was shot by a camp guard after trying to escape. However, there are other versions of his death, including suicide or execution by Gimmler's order.

For a long time, the Soviet government hid the facts about Yakov's fate. Only in 1977, after Stalin's death, was it officially confirmed that he died in captivity.

 In the 2000s, documents were published confirming the circumstances of his death. 

Whatever the circumstances of his death, the facts are that Yakov chooses a low tier member of the Russian Army who was engaged in front line battles, isntesdnof taking up an officers rank and kept away from the main battle lines for propaganda  purposes  

Yakov was an Immortal  Hero for the Motherland  and his father lost a Son !

text:
In August 1942, at a late-night dinner in the Kremlin during Winston Churchill’s visit to Moscow. Churchill asked Stalin whether the personal stresses of fighting World War II had been as difficult for him as enforcing the policy of agricultural collectivization. Churchill remarked that he thought collectivization would have been worse because it meant fighting millions of small farmers and peasants rather than a defined class of aristocrats or large landowners....

Winston Churchill asked Stalin whether destroying peasant resistance had been harder than fighting Germany. The question came during Churchill's visit to Moscow in August 1942, when Britain and the Soviet Union were military allies against Nazi Germany. According to Churchill's later account, Stalin acknowledged that collectivizing Soviet agriculture had involved an enormous struggle affecting millions of people. He nevertheless defended the policy as necessary for the country's development. The conversation offered an unusual glimpse of how the Soviet dictator justified one of the most destructive campaigns of his rule.

Churchill had travelled to Moscow on an uncomfortable diplomatic mission. The Red Army was under immense pressure, and Stalin wanted Britain and the United States to open a second major front against Germany in Western Europe. Churchill had to explain why such an invasion could not take place in 1942. Their discussions were frequently tense, with Stalin criticizing Allied military strategy and Churchill defending decisions made in London and Washington. Yet the two leaders also needed each other. Their governments were separated by deep ideological hostility, but defeating Hitler required cooperation despite those differences.

During their discussions, Churchill raised a question about Soviet collectivization. Stalin had imposed the policy beginning in the late 1920s, replacing much of private peasant farming with collective agricultural enterprises controlled by the state. The campaign involved coercion, mass deportations, executions, confiscation of property and the destruction of established rural communities. Resistance was met with severe repression. Agricultural disruption and state grain procurement policies contributed to catastrophic famine in the early 1930s, particularly in Ukraine and other agricultural regions. Churchill knew that the policy had caused immense suffering, but he was now speaking directly to the man who had ordered and defended it.

In his wartime memoir The Hinge of Fate, Churchill recalled asking Stalin whether the struggle over collectivization had been more difficult than the war. Stalin reportedly responded that it had been extraordinarily severe and had continued for several years. When Churchill referred to the millions of ordinary peasants involved, Stalin answered by invoking ten million people. That figure has sometimes been repeated as though Stalin had confessed to killing exactly ten million peasants. Churchill's account does not support such a precise interpretation. The number arose in a discussion of the scale of upheaval, repression and resistance, not as a verified statistical accounting of deaths.

Stalin's explanation, as Churchill remembered it, centered on economic necessity. He argued that Soviet agriculture had to be mechanized and reorganized to prevent future shortages and improve production. The peasants had resisted because the new system threatened their traditional way of life and control over their land. Stalin described the campaign as a terrible struggle but insisted that the government had been compelled to carry it out. His justification treated collective farming as a requirement of national modernization, even while acknowledging the suffering associated with its introduction. The distinction between acknowledging hardship and accepting personal responsibility for crimes remained fundamental.

text:
October 17, 1346. The King of Scotland was found hiding under a bridge because English soldiers spotted his reflection in the water. He had two arrows in his face. When they dragged him out he knocked two of his captor's teeth out.

That is how David II, son of Robert the Bruce, ended up spending the next eleven years as a prisoner in England.

The reason he was in County Durham at all was a letter from Paris. Edward III had just destroyed the French at Crécy in August, and Philip VI of France wanted the pressure taken off. So he leaned on the Auld Alliance and told David that northern England was, in his words, a defenceless void.

It was not. That is the whole story in one sentence.

David crossed on October 7 with around 12,000 men, a lot of them carrying French-supplied weapons and armour. What Philip either did not know or did not care about was that the English had left a northern command in place precisely because they expected this. Ralph Neville pulled together three or four thousand northern troops, picked up another three thousand Yorkshiremen on the march, and met the Scots west of Durham with maybe six or seven thousand men.

Half the Scottish numbers. On worse paper.

The Scots took the high ground, which sounds right until you look at it. The ground was broken, cut up with ditches and old field walls, and it was murder on a formation trying to move across it.

And the Scots were not going to move. They remembered Dupplin Moor and Halidon Hill, where charging English positions had got Scottish armies slaughtered, so they sat and waited for the English to come to them.

The English, holding the better ground, also sat and waited.

So for most of the day nothing happened. Two armies looking at each other.

Then the English longbowmen walked forward and started shooting, and that broke the deadlock, because an army being shot at from a distance it cannot answer has to either advance or come apart. The archers drove off the Scottish light horse and put arrows into the flank of Moray's division. The Earl of Menteith led a cavalry charge at the archers to clear them, it failed, and he was taken.

Worth noting that the English archers that day were not the veterans of Crécy. Those men were in France. A lot of these were in their first fight and the accounts call their performance uneven. It was still enough. The Lancashire longbowmen each got a £10 bonus for it, which in 1346 was a serious amount of money.

Goaded into it, the Scots attacked.

Moray's division went in first and the broken ground tore its formation apart before it arrived. English men-at-arms finished it hand to hand. Moray was killed.

The third division, under the Earl of March and Robert Stewart, saw the first attack fail, took some arrows, and left. Most of them got away, which is the only reason Scotland had an army left at all.

That left David II in the centre, standing, and the English came in on him with arrows and then with men-at-arms until his division broke too.

Then the king of Scots was shot twice in the face.

Surgeons got one arrowhead out. The other one stayed in his face. He lived with that for decades and with the headaches it gave him.

The dead included the Constable, the Marischal, the Chamberlain and the Chancellor of Scotland. Four of the great offices of the kingdom, killed on the same afternoon. Also the Earl of Moray, the Earl of Strathearn, and Niall Bruce of Carrick, an illegitimate son of Robert the Bruce. More than fifty barons were killed or captured.

Scottish chroniclers put the dead at about a thousand. Modern historians put it closer to three thousand with fewer than a hundred prisoners taken, which tells you what kind of day it was for the men who could not pay a ransom.

And here is the cold part. Edward III did not want ransoms. He had the Scottish nobles shipped to London and refused to release them on parole or sell them back, because a Scotland without its leadership could not invade anybody. He even paid individual captors to buy out their own ransom rights, giving up money to keep men in cells.

Menteith had previously sworn fealty to Edward. He was tried for treason and executed.

John de Coupland, the man who pulled the king out from under the bridge and lost two teeth doing it, was knighted and given £500 a year for life.

Edward offered to release David for £40,000 if Scotland would accept one of Edward's sons as heir to the Scottish throne. He made that offer three times. David refused it three times, from a prison cell, with an arrowhead in his skull.

He was eventually released in 1357 for 100,000 marks over ten years. The truce that followed held for roughly forty years and effectively finished the Second War of Scottish Independence.

The English also took the Black Rood of Scotland off him, a reliquary said to hold a piece of the True Cross, and gave it to the shrine of St Cuthbert in Durham Cathedral.

1346 is one of the most lopsided years in English military history. Crécy in August, Neville's Cross in October, Calais under siege the whole time. Two kingdoms wrecked in ten weeks by an island everyone had written off as overextended.

text:
The 2015 Strategic Defence and Security Review and Strike Brigades

8/25 The 2015 Strategic Defence and Security Review announced the creation of two new Strike Brigades as a core part of Army 2020 Refine. These brigades were to be centred on the new Ajax vehicle fleet and enabled by the acquisition of a new Mechanised Infantry Vehicle to provide a better protected, more agile force capable of self-deploying over large distances. The MIV was explicitly framed as an 8×8 wheeled platform. 

The concept acknowledged the real limitations of the existing force, both operational and economic, and offered infantry brigades the ability to march and manoeuvre under armour at far greater distances than tracked formations could match. Strike was predicated on a completely different starting point from FRES: there was no demand for air deployment by C-130.

text:
The Post-Cold War Search for a Role

2/25 At the end of the Cold War the British Army fielded four divisions and a substantial armoured inventory optimised for high-intensity warfare on the North German Plain. Within a decade that force had been reoriented toward expeditionary operations, peace support and, ultimately, prolonged counter-insurgency. Doctrine evolved accordingly. The emphasis moved from massed armoured manoeuvre to rapid deployability, network-enabled effects and the ability to operate across the spectrum from stabilisation to limited intervention. Programmes such as the Future Rapid Effect System (FRES) sought a family of medium-weight vehicles that could be air-transported and still offer meaningful protection and firepower. 

The institutional memory of sustained peer-level armoured operations began to atrophy long before any replacement vehicles arrived.

text:
Curve Finance: Still the King of Low-Slippage Stablecoin Swaps

Project Type and Narrative

Curve Finance is a decentralized exchange (DEX) and automated market maker (AMM) protocol built for stablecoins, pegged assets, and correlated pairs. 
It sits at the heart of DeFi as the specialized liquidity layer for assets that should trade near 1:1, powering everything from stablecoin routing to lending and yield strategies.

The Problem and the Solution

General DEXes like early Uniswap versions created high slippage when swapping large amounts of stablecoins or liquid staking tokens. Traders lost value on every big trade.
Curve solved this with its StableSwap invariant, a custom bonding curve that stays nearly flat near the peg and only steepens when a pool becomes heavily imbalanced. 
The result is capital-efficient, low-slippage swaps that have become foundational infrastructure for DeFi.

Uniqueness and Competition

Curve pioneered the vote-escrow (ve) tokenomics model that launched the famous “Curve Wars.” Locking CRV for veCRV gives users fee share, gauge voting power, and boosted rewards. This long-term alignment remains distinctive.
Competition has intensified. #Uniswap, #PancakeSwap, and newer designs like #Fluid now offer low-fee stablecoin tiers and concentrated liquidity. Yet Curve still dominates deep stablecoin and LST liquidity thanks to its specialized design, multi-chain reach, and the sticky liquidity created by veCRV incentives.

Recent Developments

LlamaLend v2 has driven strong growth. Active loans rose roughly 68% in Q3 2026 to around $71 million, outpacing the broader DeFi lending recovery, with most of the increase coming from the new isolated lending markets.
In August 2026 the protocol entered Epoch 6, cutting annual CRV emissions below 100 million for the first time. Curve also expanded to the Arc network, introduced Savings crvUSD (scrvUSD), and began enabling borrowing against Curve LP tokens, letting liquidity providers stay in pools while accessing credit.

Upcoming Developments

Expect more LlamaLend v2 markets, additional LP-token collateral options, and continued multi-chain expansion. 
The next programmed emissions reduction arrives in August 2027, further slowing dilution while the protocol keeps refining its lending and stablecoin tools.

Tokenomics and Market Snapshot

ethereum:0xd533a949740bb3306d119cc777fa900ba034cd52 is the governance and incentive token. Maximum supply is approximately 3.03 billion. Circulating supply sits near 1.57 billion. 
Initial team, investor, and community allocations finished vesting in 2024; the remaining tokens are emitted to liquidity providers and lenders over roughly 200 years, with the rate declining about 16% every August.
Holders lock CRV for up to four years to receive non-transferable veCRV. This grants a share of protocol fees, gauge weight voting that directs emissions, governance rights, and up to 2.5x boosts on their own liquidity rewards.
At the time of writing, CRV trades around $0.34 with a market capitalization near $540 million.

The Curve Edge

Beyond the DEX, Curve runs crvUSD (a decentralized stablecoin with soft-liquidation protection) and LlamaLend. The combination of deep stablecoin liquidity, programmable incentives, and expanding credit markets keeps Curve tightly woven into DeFi’s plumbing.

Community

A battle-tested DeFi-native community that still shows up for gauge votes, protocol upgrades, and the long game.

text:
Adon Shuler's father was his first football coach.

Four years ago, before his son had a single scholarship offer, he told a reporter exactly where he wanted him to end up.

"You can't go wrong with Notre Dame. You will be set for life."

He lost his father days before this season started. He played in the opener anyway.

Here is the whole thing.

Irvington, New Jersey. Don Shuler played at Irvington High himself, then coached his three boys in the backyard.

He ran a football camp named after his oldest. He and his wife Fran ran a foundation out of Irvington that handed out toys and book bags.

Here is the rest of what he told that reporter.

"Me, him, my wife talked about this years ahead of time since he played youth football."

"Before he got any offers, we were all on the same paths to understand what we wanted to accomplish."

So his boy went to Notre Dame.

And then, days before the first game of his senior year, his father was gone.

Adon played. Seven tackles.

Here is why.

"He would be mad if I didn't. That's what he wanted. That's what he expected."

Here is the thing his father used to tell him.

"Life is a card game. You get dealt the cards you get dealt."

"It's your job to change your circumstance, to change what you're going through, what you're around."

And here is what he says about him now.

"I used to tell him that every room he walked in, he lit it up."

Here is his head coach, Marcus Freeman.

"He is such a strong young man. His focus wasn't on himself. It was on making sure that he's there for his mom and his brothers."

That is Fran, and Donte and Donovan.

He has started every game since. He is a team captain. He forced a fumble that went back for a touchdown against Rice, he picked off a pass against Michigan State, and he led the team in tackles at Purdue.

He talks about where he is from more than he talks about any of that.

"I live in a tough town. I just want to always give the young kids hope."

"I always say I want a statue in Irvington by the time I'm done giving back."

Now the honest part. Football does not fix this and he has never once said it does. He is a safety having a good year on an unbeaten team, and that is all a stat line can tell you.

But a man planned out a whole life for his kid before anybody else wanted him. He said out loud where that kid should go. And he did not get to watch the last year of it.

Today his son starts at safety in Provo. Notre Dame at BYU, both of them unbeaten, 63,000 people in the building.

For the school his dad picked out before anybody else wanted him.

Oregon’s Catholic bishops have expressed heartfelt condolences and offered prayers for the victims and families affected by a tragic shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, that left five people dead and two others critically injured.

The shooting occurred on the afternoon of October 15, when a 16-year-old opened fire at the elementary school, killing three children, aged 5, 8 and 11, and a teacher. A 7-year-old child and another teacher were also hospitalized with critical injuries.

Bishop Thomas J. Hennen of the Diocese of Baker, which includes Bend, expressed his “heartfelt prayers for those whose lives were taken in the shooting” in a letter dated October 15. He also offered prayers and spiritual support to those grieving the loss of their loved ones.

“We expect that our schools are safe places for our children and all who pass through their doors. When a tragedy like this occurs, it shakes us to our core,” Bishop Hennen wrote.

Archbishop Alexander K. Sample of Portland also expressed his solidarity with the victims and their families in a statement released the same day. “No family should ever have to experience such fear and heartbreak. Please know that you are not alone, I hold you close in prayer, and the Church stands with you in this time of sorrow.”

text:
30-SECOND PHOTOREAL FANTASY ACTION COMEDY. 9:16.
THE LAST FISH
Seven connected shots with intentional cuts. No dialogue or music.

REFERENCES
Image 1 defines the orange cat warrior: fur markings, face, scar, ear notch, armor and green scarf.
Image 2 defines the slim CRT traveler: television head, single antenna, petrol coat, clothing and boots.
Reference the characters only. Each sheet shows several views of ONE character. Exclude the studio backgrounds and panel arrangements.

CHARACTERS AND CONTINUITY
Exactly two characters.
The armored orange cat stands upright and reaches the traveler's knee.
The CRT traveler is tall and slender, with narrow shoulders, long limbs and a compact ivory television head. His convex screen stays pale blue-grey, without a face or symbols.
Each carries one sword in a scabbard at the left hip.
CRT carries one cream cloth bundle containing one cooked fish.

LOCATION AND OPENING
One straight weathered stone bridge leading to a distant castle gate. Low stone parapets and one flat-topped square stone pier beside the action. Dry paving, warm late-afternoon sunlight, quiet valley below.
CRT walks toward the gate, carrying the bundle in his LEFT hand.
Cat blocks his path, staring at the bundle. Keep their position relative to the gate consistent throughout the duel.

SHOT 1 [00:00–00:04]
Frontal full two-shot, gate behind CRT.
Cat draws his short sword with his RIGHT paw and plants his feet.
CRT stops, tilts his head, then draws his sword with his RIGHT hand. His left hand keeps the bundle behind his hip.
Wind, small armor rattles and blades leaving scabbards.

SHOT 2 [00:04–00:09]
Cut to a low side full two-shot.
Cat advances with two quick, clearly separated slashes.
CRT retreats two short steps, blocking each strike with his right-hand sword. Blades meet visibly, then separate.
Keep both bodies and their feet readable.
Two sharp metal contacts, boots scraping stone.

SHOT 3 [00:09–00:14]
Cut closer from the same side of the action axis.
Cat ducks beneath CRT's blade and makes one upward strike.
CRT blocks, recoils and bumps his LEFT hand against the square stone pier.
The bundle drops onto its flat top. Its loose cloth unfolds, exposing one grilled fish.
Both freeze mid-confrontation, then lower their blades.
Cloth lands softly. The fighting sounds stop.

SHOT 4 [00:14–00:18]
Cut to a low close two-shot beside the pier, fish visible between them.
Cat stares at the fish. His ears lift.
CRT looks from the fish to the cat, then slowly tilts his head.
One awkward pause.
Cat gives one small, demanding meow.
Neither attacks.

SHOT 5 [00:18–00:23]
Cut to a medium two-shot.
Their swords are now visibly secured in their original scabbards.
CRT breaks the cooked fish into two portions with his gloved hands over the open cloth.
He offers the larger portion.
Cat accepts with both paws, suddenly polite.
Soft cloth movement and a small armor creak.

SHOT 6 [00:23–00:27]
Cut to a low frontal two-shot.
They sit shoulder-to-leg on a low stone ledge beside the pier.
Cat holds the larger fish portion and leans comfortably against CRT's leg.
CRT looks down. Cat answers with a slow blink.
Hold their relaxed familiarity. This was an argument over lunch between old companions.

SHOT 7 [00:27–00:30]
Cut to a rear wide view along the bridge.
Both walk together toward the castle gate, swords sheathed.
Cat carries his fish with both paws.
CRT carries the smaller portion in the folded cloth in his LEFT hand.
Cat takes quick little steps beside CRT's long stride.
End while they are still walking. No fade or black frame.

CAMERA AND LOOK
Panavision 35mm film aesthetic, photographic fantasy, subtle grain, warm highlights and natural cool shadows.
Vertical compositions keep the small cat and tall traveler visible together.
Stable framing for blade contacts. Brief lateral tracking during Shot 2. No orbit or slow motion.
Detailed fur, scratched armor, worn coat fabric and aged stone. Believable balance and contact.

PERFORMANCE AND SOUND
Play the duel seriously, with no exaggerated facial comedy.
CRT reacts through posture and television-head angles.
Cat changes from fierce determination to quiet satisfaction.
Native synchronized sound: valley wind, birds, footsteps, armor, sword contact, cloth and one meow. No speech, narration or music.

AVOID
Extra characters, bulky CRT body, extra antennas, human face inside the screen, identity changes, extra limbs, swapped hands, duplicate props, blood, injury, changing bridge geometry, glowing effects, text, subtitles and logos.
